title: Dolly Parton’s six-decade love story with Carl Dean began at a laundromat
summary: Dolly Parton and Carl Dean's private love story began at a Nashville laundromat in 1964 and endured nearly 60 years away from the spotlight.
story: Kathie Lee Gifford shares personal memories from her close friendship with Dolly Parton on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’
Dolly Parton lived much of her life in the spotlight, but her greatest love story unfolded almost entirely away from it.

The country music legend, who died on Tuesday at the age of 80 after a "brief battle with cancer," was married for almost 60 years to her late husband Carl Dean. Parton's death comes less than 18 months after she lost Dean, who died in March 2025 at age 82.
While announcing her passing, her nephew Bryan Seaver shared their family's belief that she had been reunited with the man she called the "star of my life story."
TRUMP MOURNS DOLLY PARTON, ORDERS US FLAGS LOWERED NATIONWIDE AFTER COUNTRY MUSIC ICON DIES
"Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by Carl, her parents and countless others who have watched her and longed to meet her in the heavens," Seaver said.
Dolly Parton's love story with her husband Carl Dean began at a laundromat and lasted more than 60 years. (Getty Images/Getty Images for ACM; Dolly Parton Instagram)
Despite being married to the internationally famous singer, Dean was a very private man who steered clear of the limelight and was rarely seen in public.
The couple's romance began with a chance meeting on Parton's first day in Nashville in 1964. At the time, Parton was 18 and Dean was 21.

Parton, who hailed from rural East Tennessee, previously shared she had been so eager to leave home that she arrived in Nashville with dirty clothes and went to the Wishy Washy Laundromat. While her clothes were in the wash, she bought a cold drink and walked around looking at her new city.

Dean drove past in a Chevrolet and warned her that she was going to get sunburned. Parton, who said she greeted everyone because she was "straight from the country," answered him. He soon circled back and joined her at the laundromat.

"I was surprised and delighted that while he talked to me, he looked at my face, a rare thing for me," Parton recalled in a 2016 post on her official website. "He seemed to be genuinely interested in finding out who I was and what I was about."
Parton died on Tuesday, 17 months after Dean passed away. (AP Photo/Andres Kudacki, File)
During his lifetime, Dean rarely gave interviews. However, in 2016, he spoke lovingly of Parton while the couple were celebrating their 50th wedding anniversary.

"My first thought was, 'I'm going to marry that girl,'" Dean told Entertainment Tonight about meeting Parton for the first time. "My second thought was, 'Lord, she’s good-looking.' And that was the day my life began. I wouldn't trade the last 50 years for nothing on this Earth."

Two years after their first meeting, Parton and Dean married in a private ceremony in Ringgold, Georgia, on May 30, 1966. Parton’s record label had reportedly urged her to postpone the wedding for a year while launching her career, but the couple chose to marry quietly across the state line to avoid coverage in the Nashville press. Parton's mother, Avie Lee, was the only wedding guest.
"It was just my mother and Carl and me," Parton told CMT in 2016. "We went across the state line to Ringgold, Georgia. My mother made me a little white dress and a little bouquet and a little Bible."

Parton said she rejected the idea of a courthouse ceremony because she feared she would not "feel married." The couple instead found a small Baptist church, where Pastor Don Duvall married them before they posed for photographs on its steps. According to Parton’s official website, the pastor’s wife also attended.
Parton and Dean married during a private ceremony in Ringgold, Georgia in 1966. (DollyParton.com)

While Parton pursued her dream of country music stardom, Dean remained firmly outside the entertainment industry. He owned an asphalt-paving business in Nashville and preferred a quiet life on their farm away from the limelight, though Parton said he always supported her ambitions.

Early in their marriage, Parton persuaded Dean to accompany her to the BMI Awards, where she won her first songwriting award for 1966's "Put It Off Until Tomorrow," which was named song of the year. During a December 2024 appearance on Bunnie Xo’s "Dumb Blonde" podcast, Parton recalled renting Dean a tuxedo and begging him to attend.
"And, oh, he was so uncomfortable the whole night," Parton said.
DOLLY PARTON’S ONGOING HEALTH BATTLE FORCES COUNTRY LEGEND TO MISS MAJOR DOLLYWOOD EVENT
Parton remembered that Dean "started pulling off stuff" immediately after they returned home.

"He said, ‘Look, now I want you to do everything you want to do, and I wish you the best, but don't ever ask me to go to another one of these damn things because I ain't going.’ And he never did," she said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"So we just kind of have that respect, and I respected that because I didn't know he was gonna be that uneasy, but he doesn't even like to go out to, you know, to big dinners or anything like that," she added.
Over time, Dean's absence became so conspicuous that there was speculation that he didn't exist, and she had made him up to ward off admirers.
During a 2020 interview with Entertainment Tonight, Parton weighed in on the longtime rumors.
Dean shunned the spotlight throughout their marriage. (Dolly Parton Instagram)

"A lot of people have thought that through the years, because he does not want to be in the spotlight at all," she shared. "It's just not who he is. He's like, a quiet, reserved person and he figured if he ever got out there in that, he'd never get a minute’s peace and he's right about that."

"I've always respected and appreciated that in him and I've always tried to keep him out of the limelight as much as I can," Parton continued. "He said, 'I didn't choose this world, I chose you, and you chose that world. But we can keep our lives separate and together.' And we do and we have."

While Parton's career required constant travel, she previously said that Dean preferred staying at their Tennessee home and taking care of their ranch. While speaking with ET, Parton shared that the time spent apart strengthened their relationship.

"Our joke about the fact, when people ask me why it's lasted this long, I say, ‘Because I stay gone,’" she told ET. "And there's a lot of truth in that — the fact that we're not in each other's faces all the time.
"But we do have a great respect and admiration for each other. We both have a great sense of humor. So, we have a lot of fun," she added.
During a 2015 interview with People magazine, Parton shed some light on their favorite shared activities and their low-key home life.
DOLLY PARTON CANCELS LAS VEGAS RESIDENCY AS HEALTH ISSUES FORCE HER TO STEP BACK FROM STAGE PERFORMANCES

"We like to get out in our little RV and just be simple," she said. "I love to read, I love to cook, I love to be with my husband. I put on my little comfy clothes – I call them my baby clothes – and we just relax."
Dean only accompanied Parton to one industry event during their marriage. (David Redfern/Redferns)

"He loves to go on vacation or on little trips, but he doesn’t want to be gone a long time," Parton continued. "He wants to be mostly around the house. He knows I’m just the opposite. I can’t go enough places. I can’t do enough things. He loves that. He’s independent."
"But when we’re together, we have enough things in common that it works," she added. "We love the simple life. We can be calm and just have a good time."

Though Dean stayed out of the spotlight, his influence could be heard throughout Parton’s music. The country star previously said that a flirtatious red-haired bank teller’s interest in her husband helped inspire the story behind her 1973 hit "Jolene," while an early disagreement about Parton’s romantic past led her to write 1968's "Just Because I’m a Woman." She later said she thought of Dean while writing her 2012 song "From Here to the Moon and Back."

Dean’s love of rock music, particularly Led Zeppelin, also helped inspire Parton’s 2023 album "Rockstar." Shortly after his death, she paid tribute to him with "If You Hadn’t Been There," a song crediting him with supporting her and encouraging her dreams.
Parton called Dean the "star of my life story." (Terry Wyatt/WireImage)

Parton and Dean never had children, though she said they had imagined becoming parents early in their marriage and even chosen names. In 2017, Parton told The Guardian that they would have named a daughter Carla.

The "9 to 5" star previously said that she later came to believe not having kids allowed her to pursue her career and devote herself to other children, including her nieces and nephews and goddaughter Miley Cyrus, as well as those reached through her early-childhood literacy program Imagination Library.

"I didn’t have children because I believed that God didn’t mean for me to have kids, so everybody’s kids could be mine, so I could do things like Imagination Library, because if I hadn’t had the freedom to work, I wouldn’t have done all the things I’ve done," she said while appearing on 2020 episode of Apple TV+’s "The Oprah Conversation." "I wouldn’t be in a position to do all of the things I’m doing now."

"We’re going to get married again!" Parton told People magazine at the time. "I’ll have a beautiful wedding dress, ’cause I didn’t have a big, long wedding dress when we got married, and we've got a suit for him, so we’re going to dress up and take a bunch of pictures."

Parton later celebrated their vow renewal ceremony in a June 2016 statement. "If I had it to do all over, I’d do it all over again, and we did," she said. "I’m dragging him kicking and screaming into the next 50 years."
On March 3, 2025, Parton announced Dean's death on social media, writing, "Carl and I spent many wonderful years together."
"Words can't do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years," she added. Thank you for your prayers and sympathy."
Days later, Parton released "If You Hadn't Been There" in honor of her husband and the cover art for the song featured a vintage photo of the couple.

title: Busy Philipps diagnosed with rare brain tumor after undergoing body scan her doctor told her she didn't 'need'
summary: Busy Phillips revealed her grade 2 oligodendroglioma diagnosis came after a Prenuvo scan her primary care doctor initially said she didn't need.
story: Samantha Harris tells Fox News Digital people need to be their own "best health advocate." The TV personality was first diagnosed with breast cancer in 2014, then again in 2024.
Busy Philipps is sharing how she was diagnosed with a rare brain tumor.

During a recent interview with People magazine, the 47-year-old "Cougar Town" actress shared the terrifying moment her doctor told her she had a brain tumor, the day after her "Dawson's Creek" co-star, James Van Der Beek, died after a battle with colorectal cancer.
"Dr. Devinsky says to me, 'I'm just going to say this to you the way I would want someone to say it to me,'" she recalled.
'BACHELORETTE' STAR REVEALS BRAIN TUMOR DIAGNOSIS AFTER ROUTINE HEALTH SCAN

"And that was when the wind like sort of knocked out of me, and I had to sit down. He was like, 'I need you to breathe. I can hear that you're not breathing.' And I was like, 'Just tell me what's happening.' And he's like, 'This isn't any of those other things that they said it could be. This is a real tumor, and it's inside your brain, and Busy, it's got to come out. We got to take it out.'"
She was then connected with Dr. John Golfinos of NYU Langone and scheduled the five-hour surgery for March 2, during which surgeons removed a 2.6-centimeter mass from her brain.
Philipps shared she was diagnosed with a rare brain tumor in February. (Gilbert Flores/WWD via Getty Images)

The mass was then biopsied and revealed to be a grade 2 oligodendroglioma, a rare tumor that Dr. Alexandra Miller, Philipps’s neuro-oncologist at NYU Langone told People, affects 1,100 to 1,300 people a year in the U.S. She added that "it is considered malignant, but it has the best prognosis of all of the malignant gliomas."
"It’s sort of defined as a cancerous tumor based on the ability of the tumor to regrow over time, rather than it looking very malignant under the microscope," Miller said.

The diagnosis came after Philipps told her cousin’s husband, a doctor in Los Angeles, that she was interested in getting a Prenuvo scan but that her primary care doctor had told her in 2025, "You're super healthy. We've done all this other blood work. We've done, like, all kinds of tests. You're super healthy. There's no need for you to get one."

"'Oh, I love them,'" he told Philipps about the scan. "And I was like, 'OK, cause my doctor just a few months ago said that I shouldn't get one.' He's like, 'Oh, like respectfully, don't know your doctor, but disagree. I think knowledge is power.'
"And what he said really resonated with me. And I was like, 'That was kind of what I was feeling, too. I think I want to get one.' He's like, 'Well, I'd be happy to help you set that up.'"
Philipps' primary care doctor originally told her she didn't need a Prenuvo scan that detected her tumor. (John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images)

After getting the scan, the "Freaks and Geeks" star went to an audition and later that night got a call from her cousin's husband, who let her know there was a lesion on her brain and that she should get an MRI.
Dr. Devinsky later told her the MRI showed a tumor that needed to be removed.

Philipps’ neurosurgeon, Dr. John Golfinos, told People that the early detection of the tumor ultimately made the surgery much easier, adding that had the tumor been found later, it "would have been two or three times the size."
Over a month after recovery, Philipps was back on the operating table after her dermatologist flagged that her incision site looked concerning.

Philipps filmed the upcoming legal drama, "Cupertino," in between dealing with her health scares. (Unique Nicole/Getty Images)

She had contracted staphylococcus, which required another surgery to cure, leaving Philipps feeling "really upset" and "like I was back at square one."
Despite her health scares, Philipps still managed to film her upcoming legal drama, "Cupertino," in which she plays the ex-wife of an AI billionaire who becomes the financier of a new law firm.
Philipps does not need chemotherapy or radiation but will get regular scans to monitor any potential reoccurrence. Through this experience, the actress learned to trust her instincts.

title: Tim Curry, 'The Rocky Horror Picture Show' actor, dead at 80
summary: Tim Curry, the British actor who portrayed Dr. Frank-N-Furter in "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," died Tuesday at 80 after years of stroke recovery.
story: Fox News’ William La Jeunesse looks back at the life and career of actor Tim Curry, known for memorable roles in ‘The Rocky Horror Picture Show,’ ‘Clue,’ ‘It’ and more.
Tim Curry, best known for playing Dr. Frank-N-Furter in "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," has died. He was 80.

Curry's death was confirmed by his publisher, Jimmy Franco, senior director of publicity at Grand Central Publishing. "Yes, it is true and very sad indeed." Franco added that he did not have a statement to share at this time.

The LAPD confirmed to Fox News Digital that officers responded at approximately 11:20 p.m. Tuesday for a death investigation involving a male described as being in his 80s at home. No foul play is suspected.

Curry became a pop-culture icon after starring as Frank-N-Furter in the 1975 film "The Rocky Horror Picture Show," having originated the role in the original 1973 London stage production before taking it to Broadway and the big screen.
DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80

Tim Curry is remembered for his unforgettable roles on stage and screen, including his iconic turn as Dr. Frank-N-Furter in "The Rocky Horror Picture Show." (Walt Disney Television Photo Archives/Walt Disney Television via Getty Images)
The cult classic, which also starred Susan Sarandon, Barry Bostwick and Meat Loaf, became known for midnight screenings, audience participation and songs including "The Time Warp."

Curry also was known for playing Pennywise in the 1990 miniseries "It," Wadsworth in "Clue," the concierge in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York" and the villainous Cardinal Richelieu in "The Three Musketeers."

His career spanned theater, film and television. Curry earned three Tony Award nominations for "My Favorite Year," "Amadeus" and "Spamalot." He won a Daytime Emmy Award, and also received a Primetime Emmy nomination.
"I like playing the more curious corners of the human mind and human behavior, partly because they’re a tad more interesting," Curry told the Associated Press in 1993.
'HOME ALONE' STAR CATHERINE O'HARA DEAD AT 71
Tim Curry, nominee for best performance by a leading actor in a musical for "Monty Python's Spamalot."  (Robin Platzer/FilmMagic/Getty Images)
The British actor had a major stroke in 2012 that left him using a wheelchair. He continued working in voice acting and returned to live-action film in 2024 with "Stream."
Curry was born in Cheshire, England, the son of a Navy chaplain and a school secretary. His father died when Curry was 12.
He discovered acting as a teenager and studied at the University of Birmingham before heading to London, where he landed his first West End job in "Hair."
"I took an academic course, which I largely ignored, I’m afraid, and just acted all the time," he said to the Associated Press.
His work with the Royal Shakespeare Company and Royal Court Theatre eventually led to "The Rocky Horror Show."

From right to left, actors Richard O'Brien, Tim Curry and Patricia Quinn as Riff Raff, Dr. Frank-N-Furter and Magenta from the 1975 musical comedy "The Rocky Horror Picture Show", produced by 20th Century Fox. ( Movie Poster Image Art/Getty Images)
In his 2025 memoir, "Vagabond," Curry reflected on the difference between his private life and the characters he played.

"The distinctions between who I really am and who I've pretended to be as an actor have proven to be a source of great disappointment to some audiences. It has not caused me much personal distress beyond the periodic necessity to deter stalkers," he wrote.

Tim Curry as William Shakespeare appearing in the miniseries "Will Shakespeare." (David James /Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
Following news of Curry’s death, tributes began pouring in from fellow actors who remembered the actor and the iconic characters he created.

Michael McKean, who proudly called Curry his friend, shared on X, "My last conversation with Tim Curry was about life and love and laughter. The grim physical state he found himself in has now ended, a blessing. Our blessing was that we had Tim Curry in our lives. RIP, my friend."
Tim Curry, the one-of-a-kind star behind "Clue," "It" and "Annie" has died at 80. (Djamilla Rosa Cochran/WireImage)
Luke Evans, who recently played Frank-N-Furter on Broadway, revealed he had written Curry a letter just three weeks ago.
"There will only be one Tim Curry," Evans wrote, describing him as "a force, a bright fierce flame" and an inspiration.
"I hope, wherever you are, you’d approve of one more Frank having the time of his life in those heels," Evans wrote in part.
Lesley Ann Warren, Curry’s "Clue" co-star, called him "the brilliant, hilarious, hysterically funny, magician of artistry."
"I adored him. Bless his wild and inspired soul. Love you Tim," she wrote.
Actor Tim Curry attends the premiere of "The Rocky Horror Picture Show: Let's Do The Time Warp Again" at The Roxy Theatre on October 13, 2016. (Jason LaVeris/FilmMagic/Getty Images)
Fellow British actor Robin Askwith also paid tribute to Curry on X, writing, "RIP Tim Curry. Seems like yesterday Royal Court Upstairs. Seriously good….."

"Few humans have earned the title of honorary Muppet more than the legendary Tim Curry. As a performer he was unparalleled – witty, charming, unnerving, and deeply funny," the Instagram account wrote.
Tim Curry's career spanned theater, film and television. (Dimitrios Kambouris/WireImage for GLAAD)

title: Dolly Parton's life in her own words: from Smoky Mountains poverty to country music immortality
summary: Dolly Parton's life in her own words reveals her Smoky Mountains childhood, faith, marriage to Carl Dean and her views on aging and what comes after.
story: Fox News senior national correspondent William La Jeunesse goes through the legacy of country music legend Dolly Parton on 'The Story.'

Country music icon Dolly Parton died peacefully in Nashville on Tuesday at 80 years old. Parton's team shared a statement with Fox News Digital on Tuesday night and confirmed that she died after a "brief battle with cancer."

Parton's death sparked mourning across the world. Parton’s catalog included enduring hits such as "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "Here You Come Again," "9 to 5" and "I Will Always Love You." The latter song became a global phenomenon again when Whitney Houston recorded it for 1992’s "The Bodyguard."

Throughout the span of her career, which ignited as a performer on "The Porter Wagoner Show," Parton always shared what mattered most to her – her Tennessee upbringing, her faith, her beloved husband, Carl Dean, and family.
Dolly Parton passed away peacefully on Tuesday. (Shirlaine Forrest/WireImage)
Below is a look at Parton's life, in her own words, over the years.
DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80
Smoky Mountains upbringing
Born in 1946 in rural Sevier County, Tennessee, Parton grew up in a large, poor family in the Smoky Mountains. She began singing in church as a child and started writing songs at a young age.
Dolly Parton in 1955. (Getty Images)

In 2015, Parton told Entertainment Tonight that her upbringing shaped who she became in her adult years. "I think my childhood made me everything I am today. I would trade nothing for being brought up in the Great Smoky Mountains. I’ve never been ashamed of my people no matter how poor or dirty we might have been," she said at the time.
Parton added, "I’ve always loved being from where I am, and having the folks that I’ve had."
During an interview with Rolling Stone in January, Parton shed a little more light on her poor childhood and said that her mother would make her clothes out of "feed sacks or scraps."
Country singer Dolly Parton in 1970. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
"We didn’t have anything. Mama used to sew all of our quilts and curtains for the windows, remake our clothes, and make clothes out of feed sacks or scraps," she said.
Parton was one of 12 children. Her parents were Robert Lee Parton Sr., known as Lee, a sharecropper and construction worker, and Avie Lee Caroline Parton, who raised their family.
Dolly's faith
Parton was very outspoken throughout her life about her Christian faith. During an interview with Fox News Digital in 2023, Parton said that her faith impacted everything she did.
GRAMMY-NOMINATED SINGER ANNE WILSON SAYS SPEAKING ABOUT JESUS COST HER OPPORTUNITIES, BUT SHE WON'T BACK DOWN

"My faith impacts everything I do because I do believe that, through God, all things are possible," she said at the time. "I always ask God to bless everything that I do and the people that I work with and to bring all the right things and right people into my life and to take the wrong ones out."
WATCH: Dolly Parton discusses the important role faith plays in her life
She added, "My spirituality has been a guiding light in my life and my strength, really, in my creative energy."
On the "WorkLife with Adam Grant" Ted Talk series in 2022, Parton shared that her religious beliefs were instilled in her at a young age.

"My grandpa was preacher. My mom was very religious, very spiritual. So I learned all the good lessons about loving your neighbor as yourself and judge not lest you be judged. Through God, all things are possible," she said.
WILLIE ROBERTSON'S FAITH-BASED ADVICE THAT'S KEPT HIS 34-YEAR MARRIAGE TO WIFE KORIE STRONG
WATCH: Dolly Parton: ‘I pray a lot and God's been really good to me'
Fox News looked back on Parton's history speaking about God in public. "I pray a lot and God's been really good to me," she said in March. In 2018, Parton said that music is "everything to me."
"It's my gift, it's my joy, it's my job," she continued.
Marriage to Carl Dean

Parton met Carl Dean outside the Wishy Washy Laundromat in Nashville on her first day in the city in 1964, when she was 18. They married two years later, on May 30, 1966, and remained together for nearly six decades until Dean’s death in 2025.
Dolly Parton and Carl Dean were married for nearly 60 years. (Dolly Parton Instagram)
After Dean died at the age of 82, the "Jolene" singer explained why she couldn't get herself to do what she loved: write songs.
DOLLY PARTON'S HUSBAND, CARL DEAN, DEAD AT 82

"I can’t afford the luxury of, you know, getting that emotional right now," she said during an appearance on Khloé Kardashian’s podcast, "Khloé in Wonder Land." "There are times like that, things like that, that will stall you a little bit. But I’ll write something else though, if it comes."
"I’m just putting that all on hold," Parton said.
Also, shortly after Dean's death, Parton told People that she would always keep him close to her heart.

"Ours is a great old love story. Most people don’t stay that close that long. That’s a loss. Nobody can ever know that unless you’ve experienced it yourself. He will always be in my heart and in my memories," she said.
Speaking to Fox News Digital in 2023, Parton said that part of the reason she believes their marriage lasted as long as it did was because she kept it private.
WATCH: Dolly Parton shares the secret to her long-time marriage

"The fact that he's not in show business at all, so we're not in competition on that. We don't have to deal with it. He's kind of a homebody. He loves working on the farm. He loves workin' on his tractors and his trucks and all that. He was in asphalt paving for years, and then he went into kinda doin' some real estate. But he don't wanna be in the spotlight, but he's very proud of and for me," she said at the time.

"When I first won an award, when we first married in '66... he just started taking clothes off before we even got out of the building. Before we got to the car, he had that bowtie off from that tuxedo. Had that shirt, jacket off, and he said, 'I want you to be successful. Do whatever you want to do, but leave me out of this. I ain't doing any more of these things, so don't ask me.' So I never did it," Parton said.
Shortly after Dead died, Parton told The Associated Press that she "truly believe[s] that I’m going to see him again someday."
Dolly's legacy
Parton built a seven-decade career as a singer, songwriter, actress, author, businesswoman and philanthropist, winning 11 Grammy Awards and becoming one of country music’s most enduring stars.
Beyond music, she created Dollywood, founded the Imagination Library and brought her larger-than-life personality to films including "9 to 5" and "Steel Magnolias."
Dolly Parton in a publicity picture for the movie "Rhinestone" in 1984. (Getty Images)
In 2025, Parton spoke to People about how she was able to not only maintain a country music career, but crossover to Hollywood successfully and find the time for her charitable efforts.

"I don’t try to tell other people how to do it, how to be, but I know who I am. I’m a star to everybody but me. I’m just a working girl. I always just say that I’m a workhorse that looks like a show horse," she said at the time.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I’m at that point in my life where I just want to be able to do good things that can be carried on. I’m proud of my legacy so far, and I hope to just continue to do things that might be of use to other people," Parton added.
Parton died on August 25 at the age of 80. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
In 2022, Parton said part of the reason she found the time to do the things she loved was because she didn't sleep much.

"I don’t need a whole lot of sleep," the singer insisted to Insider. "I go to bed pretty early, but even if I’ve been up late – it’s just kind of like a little clock inside of me that says, ‘It’s 3 o’clock!’"
"I do some of my best work there, but I get enough sleep. I don’t require as much sleep as a lot of other people do. That’s kind of a Parton family trait," she continued.
Parton's stance on aging
After Parton turned 77 in 2023, she spoke to Insider about how she viewed getting older.
The singer said she's come to terms with the idea that "wisdom comes with age, and you can't stop the aging process, nor the numbers."
Dolly Parton passed away on Tuesday, August 25 at 80. (Getty Images)
DOLLY PARTON SAYS SHE’D ‘RATHER BE’ IN HER 70S THAN BE YOUNG AGAIN: ‘I MEAN THIS FROM THE BOTTOM OF MY HEART’

"Honestly — and I mean this from the bottom of my heart — when I see young people today and I see what they're going to have to go through, especially in this day and time, I would honestly rather be this age than that age," Parton explained.

The legendary singer acknowledged she's no different from "everyone (who) would like to stay 35 forever," but she doesn't spend her life thinking about her age and doesn't let it get in the way of her doing what she wants.
Parton performed at the halftime show at the Dallas Cowboys’ Thanksgiving Day game in 2023, dressed as a Dallas Cowboy Cheerleader. (Ron Jenkins/Getty Images)

"The way I live, the way I work, the way I feel, I'm going to make every moment count," Parton said. "I may live to be 100 or I may die tomorrow, but whenever that is, I will know I died trying, and I will know I've done everything I could to make the most of everything."
"As long as I stay healthy, the numbers shouldn't matter. I don't feel my age, I don't work my age, I don't think my age and, hopefully, I don't look my age," she noted.
"I may live to be 100 or I may die tomorrow, but whenever that is, I will know I died trying, and I will know I've done everything I could to make the most of everything."
Just before her 80th birthday this year, Parton told People that she felt like she was "just getting started."

"If you allow yourself to get old, you will. People say, ‘How come you don’t seem to get old?’ I say, ‘I ain’t got time to get old,’" she said. "I ain’t got time to dwell on that. That’s not what I’m thinking about," she told the outlet.
What Dolly believed came after death
In 2019, Parton shared rare comments on what she believed would happen after she died during an episode of the "Dolly Parton's America" podcast.
Dolly Parton believed in life after death. (Getty Images)

"As far as what happens after we go on, like I say, I’m no saint so I’m hoping just as a Christian faith person, that we go on to a greater thing. I believe that we’re all part of that great divine plan, and I’m hoping to get on up there, and do some more writing, and singing, and playing with those golden harps, and write some more songs, and have my own mansion, and walk them golden streets of glory, and keep doing it forever and ever and ever.

"So I’m going to get in the angel band, for sure. I want to play in the angel band and I want to maybe play the harp up there. I don’t know," she said.
Dolly Parton appeared on the Phil Donahue Show in 1977. (Getty Images)
On the podcast, Parton said that she "kind of" believed in reincarnation and was "open to things."

"You just hope and you have faith. That’s what faith is. But I believe that it’s going to be better. I think it’s not the end of me. I don’t think it’s the end of any of us. title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle won’t ‘hijack’ Prince George’s historic Eton debut, royal expert says
summary: Royal experts say Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will likely "lay low" when Prince George starts at Eton College this September.
story: Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair royal correspondent and co-host of "The Royals Uncensored," says Prince George passed Eton's admissions process like other applicants before accepting his place at the prestigious school.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are expected to steer clear of releasing photos, making comments or generating other news that could overshadow Prince George’s highly anticipated first day at Eton College, according to a royal expert.

"The Sussexes have assured the king that they will not hijack or derail major royal events, notably the first day of school term for Prince George at Eton," royal broadcaster Neil Sean told Fox News Digital. "By that, no pictures or comment from either one on that day in September."
A representative for Archewell told Fox News Digital: "This is not something we would comment on." Kensington Palace did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The reported understanding comes as the Prince and Princess of Wales prepare for a major family milestone. Kensington Palace confirmed in June that George, 13, will attend Eton beginning this September, following in the footsteps of both his father, Prince William, and his uncle, Harry.
PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON WRESTLED WITH MAJOR DECISION OVER PRINCE GEORGE'S FUTURE: EXPERT
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle won’t "hijack" Prince George’s start at Eton, according to a royal expert. (Getty Images)
Royal commentator Amanda Matta told Fox News Digital that George’s arrival at the prestigious boarding school carries significance beyond a typical first day.

"Prince George’s start at Eton isn’t just a personal milestone; it’s the beginning of his public-facing path as heir to the throne," Matta said. "The Palace is incredibly protective of that narrative, and any competing headline — especially one involving Harry and Meghan — threatens to distract from the ‘steady, future-focused’ brand the Prince and Princess of Wales have worked so hard to build."
PRINCE WILLIAM ‘BLINDSIDED’ BY HARRY, MEGHAN RETURN AS KATE FEARS NEW TURMOIL FROM ROYAL FEUD: EXPERTS
She added that, while the matter may not weigh heavily on Prince William and Kate Middleton personally, it could be important to palace staff working to keep the focus on the future king.
Prince George of Wales is said to be excited that he'll be attending Eton College in the fall. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
"It would certainly be a shame for his first days at Eton to see him embroiled in a ‘feud’ narrative with his uncle and aunt," Matta said.

In a statement shared with The New York Times last week, a spokesperson for the Sussexes said, "On the heels of a wonderful trip with family and friends this summer, Harry and Meghan have decided to spend an extended period in the U.K. this autumn. They are excited to have their children spend more time in the country that’s such an important part of their family’s story."

The spokesperson confirmed that the couple’s businesses will remain unchanged and based in the U.S. Meghan and Harry will also keep their home in California.

Matta said the reported agreement may reflect an informal attempt to avoid competing headlines during significant occasions, though the couple's public profile makes a complete break from the royal news cycle unlikely.
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex will be returning to the U.K. this fall. (Chris Jackson - Pool/Getty Images)
"The Sussexes generate headlines simply by existing in public space," she said. "That’s been true since 2018 and hasn’t changed with their location or job titles."
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE'S UK RETURN SIGNALS ‘SPECTACULAR DEFEAT’ AS ROYAL EXPERTS WARN OF WILLIAM SHOWDOWN

"If they also want to avoid collisions, it would require a level of coordination with the Palace that seems very unlikely given the current climate," she said. "Harry and Meghan have not conferred with the Palace about their personal or professional plans for several years now."
The more realistic outcome, Matta said, may be "an informal understanding of when to lay low, and when an overlap could be workable."
While palace aides may be concerned about maintaining the royals' carefully planned media strategy, Matta cautioned that not every competing headline is the Sussexes’ doing.

Prince Harry and Markle have been residing in Montecito, Calif., with their two children. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Palace aides know better than anyone how quickly a delicate PR plan and media cycle can be dominated by a competing story," she said. "It’s not necessarily even about the Sussexes’ actions, but it’s completely up to the editors running headlines."
MEGHAN MARKLE RETURNS TO BRITAIN WITH PRINCE ARCHIE AND PRINCESS LILIBET FOR FIRST TIME IN YEARS
She added, "Meghan stepping outside will generate headlines even if it’s just to buy groceries or ice cream with the kids."
British broadcaster Hilary Fordwich echoed that concern, telling Fox News Digital that even the absence of a Sussex appearance can fuel coverage and public speculation.
"Just their mere presence or lack thereof will now be making headlines and, indeed, likely to clash with royal priorities and media focus on causes," she said.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle stepped away from royal duties in 2020. (Matt Dunham - WPA Pool/Getty Images)
Fordwich said George’s first term at Eton should remain "private" and serve as "a life transition for both him and the family," who live nearby in Windsor.

"The U.K. tabloid press will manufacture that narrative regardless of what the Sussexes do," she said. "What they can control is their own family and their own goals."

title: Dolly Parton's ‘all-American heart’: How country icon forged special bond with US military
summary: Dolly Parton's bond with the military included troop performances, patriotic art on a KC-135 Stratotanker and a fiery message to Saddam Hussein.
story: Country music star Lee Greenwood remembers Dolly Parton’s life, legacy and lasting impact following her death. He reflects on her ‘humble beginnings’, her rise to stardom and the tributes honoring the country music icon on ‘America Reports.’
Dolly Parton wore rhinestones and fringe, not a military uniform, but the American music legend spent decades finding her own ways to serve those who served America.
Parton, who died Tuesday at 80 in Nashville, forged a lasting connection with the military during her seven-decade career.

Her iconic blonde likeness appeared on U.S. military aircraft, she performed for troops and military families, recorded patriotic music and once took the Grand Ole Opry stage as American service members watched from Iraq.
TRUMP MOURNS DOLLY PARTON, ORDERS US FLAGS LOWERED NATIONWIDE AFTER COUNTRY MUSIC ICON DIES

Dolly Parton smiles as she arrives for a special event held Sept. 8, 2004, at McGhee Tyson Air National Guard Base, Tenn. She unveiled a patriotic nose art featuring her image on one of the 134th Air Refueling Wing’s KC-135 Stratotanker air refueling aircraft. The "Miss Dolly" nose art was autographed by the legendary singer, and she performed several songs for the Airmen and families in attendance at the special event. (U.S. Air National Guard photo by Senior Master Sgt. Kendra M. Owenby)

The connection was personal, too. Carl Dean, Parton's husband of nearly six decades, enlisted in the Army shortly after they began dating and served for two years, according to Biography.com. The couple married in 1966, and remained together until Dean's death in 2025.
Parton once described her patriotism in simple terms.
"I've got an all-American heart," she told Vanity Fair in a 1991 profile.

Vanity Fair accompanied Parton to Fort Hood, Texas, for that profile, where she met service members, including soldiers who had returned from the Persian Gulf only weeks earlier. The magazine also reported that Parton's likeness appeared on a KC-135 and an A-10 Thunderbolt during the Gulf War era.
During her Fort Hood visit, Parton climbed onto the shoulders of an Army major near two M-1 tanks and delivered a pointed message to Saddam Hussein in a way only she could.
COUNTRY STAR CHRIS JANSON SAYS RESPECTING THE FLAG IS THE NUMBER ONE LESSON HE WANTS HIS KIDS TO LEARN
Dolly Parton seen performs in a photo shared by the U.S. Marines. (U.S. Marines via X)
"Saddam Hussein, you son of a b----!" Parton shouted, according to Vanity Fair. "You touch one of my men again and see what happens!"
Later, Parton posed for photographs with soldiers and their families and signed autographs inside a Fort Hood theater, the magazine reported.
The service members eventually began chanting: "Dol-ly! U-S-A! Dol-ly! U-S-A!"
More than a decade later, Parton's connection with the military produced another memorable tribute.

At a September 2004 event at McGhee Tyson Air National Guard Base in Tennessee, Parton unveiled patriotic nose art bearing her likeness on a KC-135 Stratotanker assigned to the 134th Air Refueling Wing, according to an Air National Guard photo record preserved by the Defense Visual Information Distribution Service.
LEE GREENWOOD RECALLS SURVIVING ENEMY FIRE IN PANAMA AFTER WHITE HOUSE SENT HIM TO ENTERTAIN TROOPS
Country star Dolly Parton sings on stage during a Grand Ole Opry live broadcast in Nashville, Tenn., as U.S. soldiers watch the show via a video feed in Iraq. (Tech. Sgt. Cherie A. Thurlby, USAF)
The aircraft was dubbed "Miss Dolly." Parton autographed the artwork and performed several songs for airmen and their families at the event.
The appearance followed the release of Parton's For God and Country on Veterans Day 2003. The album combined patriotic standards with original Parton songs.
"I’m not a bit political, but I’m extremely patriotic," Parton said of the album, according to her official website, as cited by Military.com.

Parton's music had addressed war and military families before that album. Military.com noted that her 1970 song "Daddy Won’t Be Home Anymore" concerned a mother preparing to tell her children their father had died at war, while "Welcome Home," from For God and Country, centered on a parent waiting for a son to return from overseas.
In April 2005, Parton performed during a Grand Ole Opry live broadcast in Nashville while U.S. troops watched by video feed from Iraq, according to DVIDS.
STEVE DOOCY: THE DOLLY PARTON I SAW WHEN THE CAMERAS STOPPED ROLLING
Country music star Dolly Parton performs at the Cordell Hull Dam dedication on Oct. 13, 1973, on the shore of the Cumberland River at the dam in Carthage, Tenn. (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers)

Then-Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld also joined Parton onstage. According to DVIDS, Rumsfeld visited Nashville to thank Parton, the Grand Ole Opry and the American people for supporting U.S. troops.

Parton's work with military families continued later in her career. She participated in a virtual USO program in December 2022 that allowed service members around the world and their families to speak with her and ask questions, according to Military.com.

Her Imagination Library also blessed military families. In 2024, the program's Washington affiliate partnered with the Government Employees Health Association on a $15,000 grant to expand free books for young children in military families, Military.com reported. The effort served families at Naval Base Kitsap, Joint Base Lewis-McChord and Naval Station Everett.
The military community was among those mourning Parton following her death Tuesday.
Boot Campaign, a nonprofit that works with veterans and military families, remembered Parton's support in a tribute posted to X.

"We are so heartbroken to hear of the passing of @DollyParton who used her platform to support so many, including Veterans, military families and our work at Boot Campaign," the organization wrote. "Rest in peace, Dolly."
The group accompanied the tribute with an image of Parton saluting while wearing camouflage pants and combat-style boots beneath the hashtag "#LaceUpAMERICA."
The official U.S. Marine Corps account offered an even simpler farewell Tuesday, sharing a photograph of Parton singing in camouflage.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"RIP Dolly Parton."

Parton's family said a small, private service will be held for immediate family at her request. Fans and friends around the world were encouraged to pay tribute to Parton on social media by tagging @DollyParton or by leaving a message at DollyParton.com.
In lieu of flowers, the family asked that donations be made to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, the literacy program she founded in 1995.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Hayden Panettiere’s rep slams ‘gossip and speculation’ as death investigation deepens

story: Hayden Panettiere's 'Guiding Light' co-star Beth Chamberlin says she believed actress would overcome troubles

title: Dolly Parton dead at 80
summary: Dolly Parton, country music legend, has died after months of battling unknown health issues. Her nephew announced the news in a video posted to her Instagram page.
story: Music icon Dolly Parton has passed away at the age of 80 due to health complications in Nashville, Tennessee.
Legendary country singer and songwriter Dolly Parton died. She was 80.
Parton died peacefully in Nashville, Tennessee on Tuesday, according to a press release obtained by Fox News Digital. Her representatives confirmed she faced a "brief battle with cancer."
"Our beloved Dolly Parton spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched," her team said in a statement.
DOLLY PARTON ADMITS HUSBAND CARL DEAN'S DEATH HAS BEEN 'BIG ADJUSTMENT' AFTER 60-YEAR ROMANCE
Dolly Parton has died. She was 80.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand. Whether it be the hundreds of millions of books donated through her invaluable Imagination Library or funding research that helped create a lifesaving vaccine used around the world, Dolly’s unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact.
"After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones," the statement concluded.
Her nephew revealed the news in an Aug. 25 Instagram video. The news comes after Parton spent months battling an unknown health issue.

"My name is Brin Seaver, son of Cassie Parton, and I’m representing the Parton and Owens family today announcing the passing of my aunt, Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean, Sister, Sis and Granny to one generation and Gigi to the next," he says in the video. "This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality. As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it until now."

"It is an honor, an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness. But sadness lies with us, not with Dolly. Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by Carl, her parents and countless others who have watched her and longed to meet her in the heavens."

"I first went on the road with Dolly as a kid, getting a taste of the road life in the early 1980s. Dolly opened doors not just for me, but for her entire family to reach the potential we didn’t even know was possible. Dolly also opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent," Seaver added in the video message. "By her example, we believed that anything is possible. She never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the doors she opened made and changed history."
Parton had been battling a series of health issues.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly, but so have you," Seaver continued. "She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family whether you liked it or not. Our family and the team she has entrusted with her legacy will work diligently to ensure her spirit will live with us forever. Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy; he farmed the soil, she farmed songs and happiness. Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because, after a life of wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest."
"Rest in peace, Aunt Dolly — Aunt, Granny, Gigi. May God bless Dolly Parton, and may God bless you all. She will always love you."

Born in 1946 in rural Sevier County, Tennessee, Parton grew up in a large, poor family in the Smoky Mountains. She began singing in church as a child, started writing songs at a young age and moved to Nashville after graduating high school to pursue music.

Her breakthrough came as a performer on "The Porter Wagoner Show," where she became a fan favorite before forging a solo path that would establish her as one of country music’s most prolific and influential songwriters.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
"I’ll always be a country musician because I’m a country girl," she told People in 1975. "My style is my soul and my feelings. I’ll tell the world in my songs what I wouldn’t have told my mother."

Parton’s catalog included enduring hits such as "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors," "Here You Come Again," "9 to 5" and "I Will Always Love You." The latter song became a global phenomenon again when Whitney Houston recorded it for 1992’s "The Bodyguard."
DOLLY PARTON UNABLE TO WRITE NEW SONGS AFTER LOSING HUSBAND OF NEARLY 60 YEARS
The legendary country music star built her career on talent, charitable work and charisma.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

Parton made her feature film debut opposite Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin in 1980’s "9 to 5." Parton later appeared in films including "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas," "Rhinestone," "Steel Magnolias" and "Joyful Noise."
Parton was also known for her decades-long marriage to Carl Dean, who largely stayed out of the public eye during their nearly 60 years together. Dean died in March 2025.
After Dean died at the age of 82, the "Jolene" singer explained why she couldn't get herself to do what she loved: write songs.

"I can’t afford the luxury of, you know, getting that emotional right now," she said during an appearance on Khloé Kardashian’s podcast, "Khloé in Wonder Land." "There are times like that, things like that, that will stall you a little bit. But I’ll write something else though, if it comes."
"I’m just putting that all on hold," Parton said.
Dolly Parton's husband, Carl Dean, died in Nashville in March 2025. He was 82. (Dolly Parton Instagram)

In November of that same year, the country music legend opened up about her impressive career spanning more than seven decades, got candid about the personal sacrifices she's made throughout the years and explained why she feels like she's "just getting started."

"You know, I have just been going so fast my whole life," Parton told People at the time. "And I just start thinking, ‘How in the world did I even have a life? How did I even get it done?’ I really realized when I was putting this book together just how much I had sacrificed in my life. I never had children, so at least I didn’t have a guilty feeling. I’m thankful that I got to see my dreams come true."

"People say, ‘Well, you’re going to be 80 years old.’ Well, so what? Look at all I’ve done in 80 years. I feel like I’m just getting started," said Parton. "I know that sounds stupid, but unless my health gives way, which right now I seem to be doing fine… I think there’s a lot to be said about age. If you allow yourself to get old, you will. I say, ‘I ain’t got time to get old!’ I ain’t got time to dwell on that. That’s not what I’m thinking about."
Parton canceled her Las Vegas residency in May due to ongoing health concerns.  (AP Photo/Andres Kudacki, File)
Parton has battled various health issues over the past couple of years.
In May, the country legend announced she was canceling her planned Las Vegas residency, which had already been postponed from 2025 to September 2026 because of health concerns.
Earlier this month, Parton missed a major Dollywood event per doctor's orders.
"I’m still in Nashville, and I’m sorry about that," Parton told the crowd during a video appearance at the event, according to video shared by the Knoxville News Sentinel.

"I’m supposed to be there in person, like we planned," she continued. "Now I’ve told you before, all my fans, that I have had a few little health issues. And sometimes I get a little dizzy, and I get dehydrated."

"And I’m dehydrated," Parton, who appeared on-screen wearing fairy wings, told the crowd. "And, so, my Nashville doctor clipped my wings, saying, 'You ain’t traveling this week.’"
Parton was also known for her charitable work through the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library. (David Redfern/Redferns)
Parton had previously discussed problems involving kidney stones, saying her immune and digestive systems had gotten "out of whack" and were being treated.

Beyond her impressive career, Parton built a business empire centered in her home state of Tennessee. Dollywood became one of Tennessee’s most popular attractions, while her charitable work through the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library left an equally lasting mark.

The Imagination Library, which sends free books to children from birth until kindergarten, was inspired by Parton’s father, who never learned to read or write. The program grew into an international literacy initiative and distributed millions of books to families around the world.

"With heavy hearts, the Dollywood family mourns the passing of our beloved Dreamer-in-Chief, Dolly Parton. Everyone at Dollywood shares the sorrow of countless people around the world touched by Dolly’s warmth, wisdom and generous spirit," a representative from Dollywood said in a statement. "Dolly’s heartfelt wish was that Dollywood always remain a place of joy, hope and togetherness—a space where families and friends could honor her memory, not with silence, but with laughter, music and shared dreams.""Dolly’s enduring legacy extends beyond her music and generosity to her remarkable work ethic—an inspiration to people everywhere. In her spirit, Dollywood will be open Wednesday as Dolly wanted, always reminding everyone with her signature sparkle — 'the show must go on.' Together, we honor her by carrying forward her message of love, perseverance, and hope."
At Parton’s request, a small, private service will be held for immediate family.

title: Jennifer Garner says she 'panicked' about financial stability after divorce from Ben Affleck
summary: Jennifer Garner reveals she "panicked" about finances after her split from Ben Affleck, realizing she needed to become a serious earner for her kids.
story: Celebrity matchmaker Alessandra Conti told Fox News Digital that Garner and Affleck are incredible co-parents.
Jennifer Garner once "panicked" about her financial stability shortly after her marriage to Ben Affleck came to an end.

During an episode of the "Aspire with Emma Grede" podcast, Garner — who shares three children with Affleck — opened up about her past fear that she would no longer be able to financially support herself and her children post-divorce and explained how she pushed through.

"I panicked when I was first out of my marriage and realized I had taken such a step back in my work," said Garner. "Suddenly I realized I don't know how long I'll be able to work. This isn't a career that's like, 'Hey, you're 60, you're 55, you're 43, come on, let's pay you more than you've ever made.' You know what I mean? That's not been traditionally the role. I was suddenly like, 'Wait a minute, I have to take care of myself, I have to take care of these kids. So what is it going to be?'"
JENNIE GARTH ADMITS ‘SCARY’ FINANCIAL SPIRAL AFTER ‘90210’ FAME
Jennifer Garner said she "panicked" after her divorce from Ben Affleck. (Getty Images)
Garner said this was the time in her life where she couldn't pick up and leave for months at a time for a movie shoot. She had to be in Los Angeles for her children.
"I can't leave these kids for six months at a time," she said. "I would love to. I love going on location, but it's not this time in my career."
‘THE OFFICE’ STAR JENNA FISCHER EXPOSES THE GRUELING REALITY THAT FORCED HER OFF TV

Affleck and Garner met on the set of 2001's "Pearl Harbor," but didn't spark a romantic relationship until 2004, after starring alongside one another in the 2003 film "Daredevil." They married in 2005, but eventually called it quits in 2015.

"I was so lucky to be able to luxuriate and working some and being home and being a mom a lot of time," Garner said. "I was really grateful for that opportunity. I got to kind of have the best of both worlds, so I can't really look back and complain about any of it … it is what it is."

Jennifer Garner became a co-founder of Once Upon A Farm in 2017.  (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)

"It's not like you can just unfamous yourself. Life is expensive, and you still have to figure out how you're going to live," she added. "Just because you're well known by people does not mean that there is some great living being provided for you, and it became very serious to me, very quickly as someone who has never given a lot of thought to money, like, 'Oh I need to be an earner here.'"
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Two years after her divorce, Garner became a co-founder of the organic children's food company, Once Upon A Farm.
Earlier this year, the "Alias" actress opened up about the "upheaval" that consumed her and their three children amid her very public split from Affleck.
"When my kids were little, I worked so little, and then we had such an upheaval in our family, that I really hardly worked for a long time," she told the outlet.
While balancing her work and professional life, Garner said she learned there is beauty in imperfection.
Ben Affleck and Jennifer Garner were married from 2005 until 2015. (Getty Images)

"You have to raise yourself at the same time. And just be so radically kind to yourself about how imperfect it is," she said of trying to navigate life as a working mom of three. "And that it is just going to be imperfect. There’s no such thing as balance. There’s no such thing as doing it right. And when the big moments happen, you are okay, and that’s on you to know and understand so your child feels your okayness."

While expressing that same sentiment, Garner further opened up about the sacrifices made while raising their three children together.

"When your kids grow up in two separate households, I become mom and dad, and he becomes dad and mom," said Garner. "You kind of can't help it, right? Because you don't have the benefit of both sides, the yin and yang being in the same house, so you have to have a bit of both in the way you parent."

"There's a little bit of loss in that, but there's also something gained in that," she added. "You also just learn, it's made me let go and not focus so much on the bringing up."

title: Prince William ‘blindsided’ by Harry, Meghan return as Kate fears new turmoil from royal feud: experts
summary: Prince William was reportedly "blindsided" by the Sussexes' U.K. return, with royal experts saying he and Princess Catherine are concerned about the fallout.
story: Dan Wakeford, founder of Celebrity Intelligence, discusses Prince Harry's expected UK return, his relationship with King Charles, and why a meeting with Prince William remains unlikely.
Prince William was reportedly "blindsided" by Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s surprise decision to return to the U.K. with their children.

Several royal experts told Fox News Digital that the Prince and Princess of Wales are "concerned" about the Duke and Duchess of Sussex returning for an extended period beginning this month. Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet are set to begin school there in September, People magazine reported.
"Prince William was blindsided," Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube’s "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital.
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S UK MOVE PUTS FRESH SPOTLIGHT ON THEIR EXPLOSIVE CLAIMS AGAINST ROYAL FAMILY

Prince William, Prince of Wales, Catherine, Princess of Wales, Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex leave after escorting the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II to Westminster Hall from Buckingham Palace for her lying in state, on Sept. 14, 2022, in London. Royal experts told Fox News Digital the brothers haven't spoken since 2022. (Emilio Morenatti - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"He had found Harry’s recent eagerness to publicly signal that he wanted to spend more time in Britain unusual, but that is very different from anticipating a full return. William now has to navigate a situation he did not create, did not ask for and, given the state of their relationship, almost certainly would not have chosen."
A Kensington Palace spokesperson told Fox News Digital: "We would never comment on private family matters."
Prince William, Prince of Wales, Duke of Rothsay and Prince George of Wales attend a service at Crathie Kirk Church on Aug. 23, 2026, in Crathie, Aberdeenshire. (Peter Summers/Getty Images)

In a statement shared with The New York Times, a spokesperson for the Sussexes said, "On the heels of a wonderful trip with family and friends this summer, Harry and Meghan have decided to spend an extended period in the U.K. this autumn. They are excited to have their children spend more time in the country that’s such an important part of their family’s story."
Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, speaks at Scotty's Summer Festival at Maxstoke Castle near Birmingham, central England, on July 11, 2026. (Heathcliff O'Malley/AFP via Getty Images)
The spokesperson confirmed that the couple’s businesses will remain unchanged and based in the U.S. Meghan and Harry will also keep their home in California.
British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that the Waleses are "feeling uneasy" about facing another chapter in the "endless Sussex soap opera."
WATCH: PRINCE WILLIAM UNLIKELY TO RECONCILE WITH PRINCE HARRY SOON: EXPERT

"It’s about broken trust," Chard explained. "Prince William is said to feel that Harry and Meghan have spent years attacking the institution, then monetizing their grievances through a very lucrative media operation. From his view, it’s an ongoing campaign for maximum impact and self-gain. He’s not going to fuel it, and he’s not going to endorse behavior he sees as damaging."
Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, arrive for a service at Crathie Kirk Church in Crathie, Aberdeenshire, on Aug. 23, 2026. (Jeff J Mitchell/Getty Images)

William and Kate were seen arriving in Scotland on Thursday, where they’ll spend time with King Charles at Balmoral Castle. The royal family has spent summers at the Scottish estate since the reign of Queen Victoria, with family members traditionally hunting, fishing and horseback riding there.
The king learned about Harry and Meghan’s move three days before it was made public, according to reports.

King Charles III inspects the Balaklava Company, 5th Battalion, The Royal Regiment of Scotland, at the gates of Balmoral as he takes up summer residence at the castle on Aug. 18, 2026. (PA Images via Getty Images)

"Prince William, along with Catherine, is currently at Balmoral Castle visiting the king," royal broadcaster Neil Sean told Fox News Digital. "Harry and Meghan have, so far, not been invited to visit the king privately while on a holiday. This will not happen while William is there. I’ve been told he has no desire to connect on any level with his younger brother and simply has no time for [Meghan]."

A spokesperson for Archewell, which handles the offices of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, told Fox News Digital: "We do not comment on the family’s private travel arrangements or meetings with the extended family."

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, attend the David Foster Foundation 40th Anniversary Celebration on Aug. 7, 2026, in Victoria, British Columbia. (The David Foster Foundation via Getty Images)

The Daily Mail reported that the king and his heir held a "Sussex Summit" following the announcement. A source told the outlet that the Prince and Princess of Wales "have no interest in engaging with anything Harry and Meghan do or say."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Balmoral Castle in Scotland. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

"Things are projected to be tense at Balmoral," British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital. "... Princess Catherine is particularly guarded given how deeply hurt she was by both of them. Both she and Prince William are very determined to maintain their own family stability and remain focused on duty with their royal roles paramount."
Several royal experts previously told Fox News Digital that William and Harry haven’t been on speaking terms since at least 2022.

From left: Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, Prince William and Princess Catherine watch a Royal Air Force flypast from the balcony of Buckingham Palace on July 10, 2018, in London. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"My sources have described genuine concern within the Wales camp," Schofield said. "I don’t think Prince William and Princess Catherine are sitting at Balmoral panicking about Harry and Meghan returning, but they are understandably apprehensive about what their return could bring. The last several years have taught them that private family tensions have a habit of becoming very public."
King Charles III and Queen Camilla attend a service at Crathie Kirk Church on Aug. 23, 2026, in Crathie, Aberdeenshire. (Peter Summers/Getty Images)

"The concern isn’t simply that Harry and Meghan will be geographically closer," Schofield continued. "It’s the unpredictability that comes with the Sussexes. There have been interviews, books, documentaries and very personal allegations about members of the royal family. … My sources tell me the Wales camp has not forgotten the hostility directed at them after some of Harry and Meghan’s previous public accusations."
Schofield said unnamed sources told her Kate is also unsettled by the news.

Meghan Markle told Oprah Winfrey in 2021 that Kate Middleton made her cry during a disagreement over flower girl dresses ahead of her wedding to Prince Harry. Meghan said Kate later apologized and brought her flowers and a note. (Chris Jackson/WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"My sources tell me that Catherine does not want to revisit that chapter of her life," Schofield explained. "She has endured very personal allegations, an enormous amount of public scrutiny and a difficult few years. My understanding has always been that her priority is Prince William, their children and the future."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales attend the 2026 EE BAFTA Film Awards at The Royal Festival Hall on Feb. 22, 2026, in London. (Samir Hussein/WireImage/Getty Images)

"Meghan returning to Britain doesn’t mean Catherine suddenly has an obligation to reopen a relationship that has caused considerable hurt," she said. "Catherine can wish Harry and Meghan well without wanting them back inside her private life. ... The idea of resurrecting the ‘Fab Four’ is fantasy. Too much has happened, and too much has been lost."
The Sussexes are expected to live at a private, nonroyal residence outside London, The Associated Press reported. They won’t resume their royal duties, which they gave up in 2020.

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex are seen greeting members of the public at the Cruising Yacht Club of Australia on April 17, 2026, in Sydney, Australia. (Cameron Spencer/Getty Images)

The couple’s return to the U.K. comes as the king continues treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer diagnosed in 2024. In 2025, Harry said he didn’t know "how much longer my father has" and expressed a desire for his children to get to know their grandfather.

Prince William (pictured here) did not meet with his estranged younger brother, Prince Harry, who spent time with their father, King Charles III, at Highgrove House, the monarch's private residence, on July 10, 2026. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)
Last month, the king met with Harry, Meghan and their children at Highgrove House.
Vanity Fair royal correspondent Katie Nicholl reported at the time that, according to sources, "not even the Prince and Princess of Wales were made aware that the meeting was taking place."
Prince William, Prince of Wales and Catherine, Princess of Wales are seen here at the DMMI Royal Charity Polo Cup 2026 in Windsor, England, on July 10, 2026. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"The Sussexes played a blinder with the king welcoming them, having not told him last month of a plan they have had for ages as their children will soon be in school," royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital.
The move is understood to have come together relatively quickly, as Harry and Meghan waited to learn whether their children had been accepted to the private school they applied to.

Highgrove House, the king's private residence, in Doughton, Gloucestershire. (Neil Bennett/Mirrorpix/Getty Images)

"Since the brothers haven’t spoken in years, the imminent arrival of the Sussexes places William and Catherine in a pressured and difficult situation," said Fitzwilliams. "William is reportedly furious. But what is essential is that the king accepts that the Waleses and their children are the future of the monarchy."
Schofield doesn’t believe reconciliation between the brothers is likely, at least anytime soon.

Prince Harry (left) and Prince William (right) attend the unveiling of a statue of their mother, Princess Diana, at The Sunken Garden in Kensington Palace, London on July 1, 2021, which would have been her 60th birthday. Royal experts told Fox News Digital the last time the brothers spoke was in 2022 during Queen Elizabeth II's funeral. (Dominic Lipinski/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"Geography cannot repair a relationship where trust has been so badly damaged," she said. "Harry’s return could make that estrangement more obvious because people will inevitably ask why two brothers living in the same country still aren’t seeing one another. ... William and Catherine could suddenly find themselves under public pressure to perform a reconciliation that probably doesn’t exist behind closed doors."

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex sits in a car as she attends Queen Elizabeth's state funeral and burial in London on Sept. 19, 2022. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"... William may have reached the conclusion that distance is healthier than reconciliation, and he is entitled to make that decision," Schofield said. "The realistic goal at this stage probably isn’t friendship [with Harry]. I would argue it’s peaceful coexistence for the sake of their father. ... Harry and Meghan moving back to Britain creates proximity, not reconciliation. They can buy a house near London. They cannot buy back trust."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Kacey Musgraves divides fans with immigrant children’s plea, faces boycott calls to ‘shut up and sing’
summary: Kacey Musgraves asked fans to donate to the Young Center for Immigrant Children's Rights during her tour opener, sparking a divided reaction on social media.
story: Mickey Guyton said she "loves" both Reese Witherspoon and Kacey Musgraves and enjoyed working with them on the show "My Kind of Country."
Kacey Musgraves is facing backlash after asking fans to donate to an immigrant children’s rights group as her birthday wish while kicking off her "Middle of Nowhere" tour.

On Friday, the country music star marked her 38th birthday on the opening night of her tour at the United Center in Chicago, Illinois. At one point, Musgraves paused her show and urged concertgoers to contribute to the Young Center for Immigrant Children's Rights.

"It’s a wonderful organization, and they help give aid — legal aid — and money to children whose parents have been deported unfairly," Musgraves said. "It’s not a political thing. It’s just, these kids need help."

Kacey Musgraves sparked backlash on social media after asking fans to donate to an immigrant children’s rights group as her birthday wish during the opening night of her new tour. (Getty Images for Coachella)

She continued, "They have no guidance and no way to get through this thing without their homebase or their parents. So anyway, 50 cents, whatever the hell, I don't know, whatever you want to do but that would mean a lot to me."
KACEY MUSGRAVES FACES BOYCOTT CALLS AFTER ASKING FANS TO DONATE TO IMMIGRANT CHILDREN'S GROUP
"If you don't want to, that's totally fine too," Musgraves added.

The eight-time Grammy Award winner's appeal was immediately met with applause and cheers from the crowd in Chicago. However, Musgraves' request drew a divided response online, including criticism from conservative political commentators.
The country star said the Young Center supports children "whose parents have been deported unfairly." (Christopher Polk/Billboard via Getty Images)
"What is an unfair deportation?" Tomi Lahren, host of Outkick's "Tomi Lahren Is Fearless" podcast, wrote on X alongside a video of Musgraves' birthday request.
KENNY CHESNEY TELLS BILL MAHER THE KEY REASON HE REFUSES TO TELL HIS LISTENERS HOW TO VOTE

"Kacey Musgraves stopped her concert to ask the audience to donate money for legal aid to kids whose parents have been deported ‘unfairly.’ How about donating money the help kids who's parents have been killed by illegal immigrants! What happened to the country music industry?" conservative influencer Vince Langman commented.
"Another TRAITOROUS woman who wants nothing more than to see our country fall," an X user chimed in.
"Shut up and sing Kasey (sic)!! Why do musicians think they Can draw a line in the sand? You alienate 50% of your audience," another commented.
Some critics declared that they would no longer support Musgraves and called for a boycott of her music and concerts.
NATALIE MAINES’ ANTI-TRUMP TIRADE, ZACH BRYAN’S FENCE-CLIMBING CLASH FUEL COUNTRY MUSIC’S BIGGEST FEUDS
"You just earned yourself a big ol’ boycott, you traitor," one detractor wrote. "Illegal aliens and their kids don’t deserve our patronage and neither do you!"
"I’m deporting Musgraves from all my music playlists," another X user commented.
Critics slammed Musgraves' comments while her fans defended her. (Christopher Polk/Dick Clark Productions via Getty Images)
Other social media users argued that Musgraves should donate her own money rather than ask fans to contribute.

"Kacey Musgraves is worth $15 million. Yet she’s asking fans who already paid $150 to $350 for tickets to donate to support the children of illegal aliens," one social media user commented. "If she cares that much, she can fund it herself and let them live in one of her multi-million-dollar mansions."
MUSICIAN KENNY CHESNEY'S REFUSAL TO SPEAK OUT ON POLITICS SPARKS ARGUMENT ON 'THE VIEW'

"Everyone she is speaking too (sic) gave her their money when they bought tickets," another added. "She did not give the audience money. So now she has the money, shouldn't she donate to whatever cause she wants? She is actually on stage at a show that the audience had to pay to get admission to and now she is asking for more of their money. That's rude."
However, some of the "Dry Spell" singer's fans defended her on social media and praised her for speaking out on behalf of immigrant children.
POP STAR OLIVIA RODRIGO FELT 'ENRAGED' AFTER ICE USED HER HIT SONG, BRANDS AGENCY 'BARBARIC'
"Love this. 'It's not a political thing. It's just, these kids need help.' Exactly. More artists doing this please," one fan wrote on X.

"In all fairness, the kids didn’t do anything wrong," another wrote. "I don’t believe their parents were wrongfully deported, but I equally believe that their children, if retained in the United States by law, should be taken care of. We’re not f------ animals!"
"No boycott here!" an X user declared.

"Helping children caught in difficult circumstances is a worthy cause," one commenter argued. "At the same time, immigration enforcement and whether a deportation was lawful or justified are matters for the courts and policymakers not concert stages."
Fox News Digital has reached out to Musgraves' representatives for comment.
Musgraves stood by her support for the organization following the concert.  (Dan MacMedan/Getty Images)
Meanwhile, Musgraves stood by her remarks on social media, taking to her Instagram Story to upload a post that read, "Kinda chic when kids don't face immigration court alone."
The singer also reposted a message shared by the Young Center's Instagram page, in which the organization expressed its gratitude to her.
"Thank you," the nonprofit wrote. "We appreciate your support of our work and mission to see unaccompanied immigrant children safe, free, and with their families."

Based in Chicago, the Young Center describes its work as pairing volunteers with attorneys and social workers to advocate for unaccompanied and separated immigrant children in government custody. Its website lists family unity, release from custody, fair proceedings and children's best interests among its priorities.

The nonprofit reported serving 1,975 children from 53 countries in 2024 and opening 1,388 new cases. Its 2025 annual report said children's average detention time increased from 30 to 198 days and requests for assistance from detained parents quadrupled from 2024.

Friday’s appeal extended Musgraves’ support for the charity. In April, resale platform Depop announced that 20 pieces from her wardrobe, including clothing from music videos and tours, would be sold in capsule drops. Women's Wear Daily reported that all proceeds would benefit the Young Center.
In announcing the sale, Musgraves described the beneficiary without discussing immigration enforcement.
The eight-time Grammy Award winner wrote "Kinda chic when kids don't face immigration court alone." (Taylor Hill/Getty Images for ABA)
"I also adore the fact that the sales are supporting a really beautiful cause," Musgraves said.

Musgraves also invited three brothers, ages 18, 14 and 12, to open three Texas shows in May after their family was released from ICE custody. The mariachi performers' family said they entered through the now-defunct CBP One appointment system in 2023 and sought asylum after fleeing violence in Mexico, KSAT reported.
