title: Navy veterans reunite after 30 years for 'grueling' cross-country bike challenge honoring 9/11
summary: Two Navy veterans reunited after 30 years to bike from San Diego to Ground Zero, raising over $17,000 for Tunnel to Towers before 9/11's 25th anniversary.
story: Two Navy friends reunited after 30 years to bike from San Diego to New York, raising awareness for Tunnel to Towers and visiting fire stations along the way. Their journey became a moving tribute to service, sacrifice and unity.
Two Navy veterans recently reunited to complete a great expedition across America.
Jim Serger, 55, of Cincinnati, Ohio, and Cory Hardy, 51, of Ennis, Montana, hadn’t seen each other in 30 years since serving together overseas.
On July 14, the two friends embarked on a bike ride across the country, from California to New York City, in honor of the upcoming 25th anniversary of 9/11.
NEW JERSEY MAN WALKS ACROSS US TO RAISE NEARLY $100K FOR HOMELESS VETERANS: 'RESPECT AND REVERENCE'
After writing three books for the nonprofit Tunnel to Towers, Serger said he felt he needed to challenge himself "with something bigger."

"And why not wrangle in my old Navy buddy, who I hadn’t seen for 30 years, that I knew was a tremendous bicyclist," he told Fox News Digital. "Back in January, I said, ‘Would you like to go on this trip?’ And he said, ‘Absolutely, Jimmy, count me in.’"
Navy veterans Jim Serger (left) and Cory Hardy (right) set off to bike across the country, starting in San Diego July 14, 2026. (Jim Serger)
Hardy said he’s always viewed himself as "incredibly patriotic" because he’s been granted "so many opportunities" through the military to see the world and get an education.
"When Jim approached me about the idea of doing this, I was like, ‘Wow, this is awesome. This is something that I can do,’" Hardy shared.
"It's the 250th anniversary of our country and the 25th anniversary of 9/11, and I don't want to forget. And I want people to keep it at the forefront of their minds."
TUNNEL TO TOWERS 5K DRAWS 40,000 PEOPLE TO HONOR 9/11 FIRST RESPONDERS IN NYC
Serger trained for 10 months, logging 5,000 miles on an indoor trainer. When spring came, he hit the trails around Cincinnati.

A few months later, the duo began their journey in San Diego and headed east. They were met with 20 road closures, a fire and flooding in Colorado, two flat tires, three bike shop visits and lots of backroad maneuvering.
A map depicts Serger's and Hardy's bike route across America. (Jim Serger)

Serger and Hardy focused on staying hydrated, especially in the California and Arizona heat, with a collective three gallons of water each day, sometimes including electrolytes. They snacked on energy waffles, protein bars and "salt gummy bears" and ate lots of carbs at meals.
Hardy said he took 10-minute ice baths "every single day." Serger reported losing six pounds by the end of the mission, which he gained back by eating "good food" in New York.
AMERICA'S FIREFIGHTER SHORTAGE HITS CRISIS LEVEL AS EMERGENCY CALLS TRIPLE, PUTTING LIVES AT RISK
While Hardy was already accustomed to the elevation after living in mountainous Montana, Serger said the altitude posed a physical challenge.
"It was grueling ... so hard," he told Fox News Digital. "Cory had to take the mountains in Colorado. I stayed on flat ground. That was our game plan."
Serger and Hardy stopped at 25 firehouses along the way, connecting with first responders and community members from big cities to small towns. (Jim Serger)

Serger and Hardy met up with some of their old Navy buddies along the way. One fellow veteran, an Arizona state trooper, drove from Phoenix to Flagstaff to meet them on the route. Others opened their homes for the pair to stay the night.
The friends stopped at about 25 firehouses to hand out Tunnel to Towers books and to introduce themselves.

"Sometimes we were there for an hour, sometimes we were there for four hours," Serger said. "Talking about Tunnel to Towers, where they were on 9/11 … how much they train … it was just very heartwarming."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Serger said he and Hardy both foster the "patriotic mentality" of "what we can do for others." Hardy serves on city council and Serger's wife cooks for the fire department every month. These types of efforts were reciprocated on their journey.
"Every fire station, EMS, police station, they're all involved in the communities. We got patches. We got hats. we got pins. We got T-shirts," Serger said.
Hardy added that, at every firehouse, everybody was there to help, "regardless of their state’s political affiliation."
Serger and Hardy receive a grand welcome at the FDNY Ten House in Lower Manhattan Aug. 2, 2026. (Jim Serger)
"They're just another American out there willing to put their life on the line to save people," he said. "I thought it was super awesome to get to meet firefighters from East Coast to West Coast.

"The closer we got to Shanksville and the Pentagon and New York, it became very emotional, because then people said, ‘My mom was there’ or ‘My aunt was there' ... and then a firefighter said, ‘Three of our brothers went up there.’
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The closer we got, we knew we had hit the epicenter of how people responded to those terrorist attacks, and it really hit home."
At the Pentagon, Serger and Hardy got a police escort from the Pentagon Police and Pentagon Fire Department before receiving a five-hour tour, including the 9/11 memorial.
Serger and Hardy received a police escort in Shanksville, Pa., where they spent time at the firehouse. (Jim Serger)
Clocking about 170 miles a day, the pair made it to Lower Manhattan in 20 days.
They were welcomed by the FDNY, Port Authority and NYPD Honor Guard at FDNY Ten House, across from Ground Zero and the 9/11 Memorial & Museum.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"I started crying," Serger said. "My wife was there. She flew in. We had Sal Cassano, the [former] FDNY fire commissioner, there. Fire Station 10 had firemen, civilians were there. It was very, very moving."
Serger and Hardy’s cause has so far raised more than $17,000 for Tunnel to Towers.
(L-R) Jim Serger's wife, Gina, former New York City Fire Commissioner Sal Cassano, Jim Serger, Tunnel to Towers CEO Frank Siller and Cory Hardy. (Jim Serger)

In addition to raising funds for the organization, Serger said the expedition aims to generate continued awareness for those who sacrificed and risked their lives on 9/11 as the 25th anniversary approaches.
"We never forget 9/11," Serger said. "We never forget the sacrifice of our heroes, of our military, our first responders and gold star families," he said. "We never want 9/11 to fade away."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Serger described the bike ride as a "surreal" and emotional experience.

"It started off with, we're going to raise money for Tunnel to Towers, and I think our final [takeaway] was there's a lot of love and pride and patriotism in this country, from far west all the way to the east," he shared.
"Everybody welcomed us with open arms. That's all we talked about."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Woman accused of defacing WWII Memorial with spray paint indicted by federal grand jury
summary: U.S. Attorney for DC Jeanine Pirro called the World War II Memorial vandalism a "despicable attack" after Melissa Farris was formally indicted on two federal counts.
story: Fox News correspondent Madeleine Rivera reports on charges 41-year-old Melissa Farris faces after she allegedly admitted to vandalizing the World War II Memorial in Washington, D.C., on ‘Fox Report.’
The woman accused of vandalizing the World War II Memorial in Washington, D.C., was formally indicted Friday, Fox News Digital has learned.
Melissa Farris was charged on two counts, including destruction of a veterans’ memorial and destruction of government property.
The Kentucky woman allegedly spray-painted the words "Clean hands, dirty money" in bright pink paint and dumped bubble soap into the fountain at the center of the memorial, according to authorities.
WORLD WAR II MEMORIAL ON NATIONAL MALL VANDALIZED WITH PINK SPRAY; FOUNTAIN OVERFLOWING WITH BUBBLES
A vandal poured bubble soap and painted graffiti on the World War II Memorial in Washington, D.C., Aug. 13. (Andrew Leyden/ZUMA Press Wire)
Federal prosecutors allege that cleanup and restoration costs already exceeded $1,000.
Farris did a Facebook live before turning herself in and her arrest Aug. 14, in which she admitted to the alleged vandalism the day before.

"It's me. I am going to turn myself in," she said. "I'm outside district federal court. I am just trying to do the right thing. … I was trying to get people to listen. … I tried to reach the media. I tried to fight back. I tried to ignore it."
Farris claimed she lived in a paper-thin camper that she "boarded up with cardboard in the winter to feel a little bit warmer."
Fox News Digital has reached out to the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia for comment.
WWII MEMORIAL VANDALISM SUSPECT IN CUSTODY, CHARGED WITH TWO FELONIES, PIRRO SAYS
Police respond to the World War II Memorial in Washington, D.C., after an apparent act of vandalism at the national landmark. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

"Vandalizing our World War II Memorial is a despicable attack on a sacred monument honoring the Americans who fought and died for our freedom," U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said in a statement after Farris was charged.
"Those Americans include my father and grandfather."
Pirro said the charges carry penalties of up to ten years in prison.
"Our beautiful World War II Memorial was just hit by Spray Painting Vandals," President Donald Trump wrote earlier this month on Truth Social.
"THERE CAN BE NO GREATER INSULT TO THOSE AMERICAN HEROES WHO DIED IN WORLD WAR II. First the Reflecting Pool, now this. We are on their trail! Where do these animals come from???"

Several people, including Olympic canoeist David Hearn, were arrested in June for allegedly vandalizing the newly renovated Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, but the charges were dropped earlier this month.
TRUMP BLAMES VANDALS FOR DEAD GRASS ON NATIONAL MALL WHERE HE HOSTED 4TH OF JULY CELEBRATION
Prosecutors cited evidence indicating the damage may have stemmed from a botched renovation rather than vandalism.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche on Aug. 16 said he "absolutely" supported Pirro’s decision to drop the charges, "as does President Trump," he told NBC’s "Meet the Press."
Trump has spoken out against the decision this month, saying he "disagrees 100%" with Pirro’s decision.
Fox News' Robert McGreevy, Bonny Chu and Ashley J. DiMella contributed to this report.

title: Antifa-linked sites go dark after State Department terror designation of tech collective
summary: The Rose City Antifa and Jane's Revenge websites went dark after the State Department designated their tech provider, A/I Collective, a global terrorist.
story: Secretary of State Marco Rubio spearheads an international conference, rallying over 60 countries to confront far-left political terrorism. Websites tied to Portland’s Rose City Antifa and the militant abortion-rights group Jane’s Revenge began going dark in the days after the State Department designated their Italy-based technology provider a global terrorist entity.

Fox News Digital first reported this week that the State Department had designated Autistici/Inventati, known as the A/I Collective, as a specially designated global terrorist over its alleged support for violent far-left networks.
"Today’s news demonstrates the extent to which the A/I Collective was the digital infrastructure of the global Antifa terror network," a State Department official told Fox News Digital.
RUBIO PUTS ENTIRE WORLD ON NOTICE AGAINST RISE OF 'POISONOUS' FAR-LEFT TERROR 'MASKED AS EQUALITY'
Multiple groups, including Rose City Antifa and the Proud Boys protest in downtown Portland, Ore., June 29, 2019.  (Dave Killen/The Oregonian via AP)

"Just one day after the extremist collective was designated as a specially designated global terrorist, an untold number of servers and websites — used by far-left extremists to plot violent attacks, target federal agents, and conceal their crimes from law enforcement — have been shut down," the official said.

15 ANTIFA RADICALS INDICTED, 12 ARRESTED IN SWEEPING FEDERAL PROBE INTO MINNEAPOLIS ANTI-ICE OPERATIONS

title: Illegal immigrant tuition perks put 4 states in Trump DOJ crosshairs
summary: Arizona State University gave 432 illegal immigrants in-state tuition in Fall 2025, totaling $10.5 million in reduced costs, the Justice Department alleges.
story: Fox News correspondent David Spunt reports on the Justice Department’s lawsuits challenging laws in Vermont, Connecticut and New York that allegedly prioritize tuition benefits for illegal immigrants living in the United States over American citizens on ‘Special Report.’

The Trump administration filed lawsuits against four states Thursday over laws allowing illegal immigrants to receive financial benefits offered to state residents, including in-state tuition, state grants and state-funded student loans.

The Justice Department argued that laws in Oregon, Washington, New Mexico and Arizona allowing illegal immigrants to receive benefits are in violation of a federal law that states an illegal immigrant is ineligible to receive higher education in-state benefits unless those same benefits are available to every U.S. student.

"This is a simple matter of federal law: Colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens," Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division said in a statement.
"This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country."
DOJ SUES NEW JERSEY OVER LAWS GIVING ILLEGAL ALIENS IN-STATE TUITION, SAYS CITIZENS TREATED AS 'SECOND-CLASS'
Arizona State University is facing criticism for allegedly continuing DEI efforts. (Getty)

The latest lawsuits bring the number of states facing legal challenges over laws granting illegal immigrant students the same benefits as lawful residents to 21. The Justice Department has won its cases in Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska and Illinois.

"Our efforts will not cease until President Trump’s promise is fulfilled: Illegal aliens will not receive benefits denied to American citizens," Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. said in a statement.

The difference between in-state and out-of-state tuition costs at public universities in the four states is significant. The complaint showed that for the 2026-2027 school year, Washington residents would pay $13,406, compared with $44,460 for out-of-state students at the University of Washington.

This means illegal immigrants could receive a $31,054 discount if they earned a high school diploma or equivalent in the state, lived there for at least one year for reasons other than attending college and signed an affidavit saying they would seek permanent residency when eligible.
TRUMP'S JUSTICE DEPARTMENT SUES NEW YORK, OTHER BLUE STATES OVER TUITION FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS
Arizona State University’s downtown Phoenix campus in Phoenix Dec. 25, 2015. (iStock)

The Justice Department's lawsuit against Arizona also showed a significant difference between in-state and out-of-state tuition costs, with the largest gap at Arizona State University totaling $24,448.
The lawsuit alleged that in fall 2025, 432 illegal immigrants received in-state tuition benefits at Arizona State University amounting to $10.5 million in reduced tuition.
The lawsuit also cites a report from the Arizona Center for Investigative Reporting that estimates more than 3,600 illegal aliens per year could qualify for in-state tuition under Arizona’s law.
A spokesperson for the Arizona Board of Regents, a plaintiff in the lawsuit, said the school system follows state law.
"We are reviewing the lawsuit and will work closely with Arizona leaders on the appropriate next steps," a spokesperson said.
The benefits extend beyond tuition costs.
COURT CHECKS PRITZKER AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SCORES ANOTHER IMMIGRATION WIN
The Justice Department filed a lawsuit against Oregon over laws allowing illegal immigrants to receive in-state tuition. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

In Oregon, only in-state students enrolled at Oregon Health & Science University can receive a Rural Nurse Scholars Scholarship, which covers the full cost of tuition and a $1,500 travel stipend. The Justice Department alleges that illegal immigrants are eligible for the scholarship under state law.

In Washington, not only do illegal immigrants qualify for in-state tuition and grants, but the state also created a financial aid program for illegal immigrants living in the state who are unable to obtain federal financial aid. The program is known as the Undocumented Student Support Loan Program, and it was created under a bill passed in 2020.
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson said in a statement to Fox News Digital that he stands by the state's laws.
"Washington state won’t be bullied into changing how we provide opportunities for young people in our state," Ferguson said. "We’ll see them in court, and we expect to win."
A June 2024 report estimated that roughly 408,000 illegal immigrants were enrolled in higher education, with 29.1% arriving in the United States at age 17 or older.

title: Trump election fraud crackdown lands first arrest, putting longtime critics in White House crosshairs
summary: A Honduran national in Los Angeles faces felony charges and deportation after allegedly registering to vote, and officials promise more arrests to come.
story: First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli criticizes California Gov. Gavin Newsom for claiming credit for recent fraud crackdowns. Essayli highlights Newsom's prior dismissal of fraud and his administration's refusal to implement a state auditor's recommended fraud prevention regulations.

The first arrest in what a Trump administration prosecutor says will be a broader election fraud crackdown was announced Friday in Los Angeles, and the White House seized on the case to hit back at longtime critics.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli announced a Honduran national was charged with two felony counts and could face deportation if convicted, while criticizing California’s current voter registration safeguards and renewing DOJ demands for a voter roll audit.

"Today’s arrest is the first of many to come. Unfortunately, because states like California allow non-citizens to easily register to vote and receive a ballot by mail, there’s no telling how many non-citizens are currently registered to vote," Essayli said in a statement announcing the capture of Darwin Jonathan Rivera Flores.
CALIFORNIA ACCUSED OF BLOCKING FEDERAL VOTER ROLL AUDIT AS DOJ ESCALATES PROBE OF ELECTION FRAUD CLAIMS
Darwin Flores, center, is arrested in California as part of the federal government's voter integrity operations. (Credit: Office of Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli)
"We again renew our request that California immediately comply with our requests to audit their voter rolls so that all voters can have confidence in our elections."
Fox News Digital reached out to Gov. Gavin Newsom for comment.
Rivera Flores, of the Winnetka neighborhood west of Van Nuys, was charged with fraudulent voter registration and false claim of U.S. citizenship. He did not vote in an election, according to the DOJ.
Rivera Flores entered the U.S. during the George W. Bush administration and was a green card holder, but was not a U.S. citizen, according to an affidavit.
FOUR NONCITIZENS CHARGED WITH ILLEGALLY VOTING IN 2020, 2022 AND 2024 FEDERAL ELECTIONS IN NEW JERSEY

Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, answered questions during a news conference outside the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department April 10, 2026, in Rancho Cucamonga, Calif. (Anjali Sharif-Paul, The Sun/ via Getty Images)
He was previously charged with a misdemeanor for "disrupting immigration law enforcement operations" at a federal building in Camarillo, California, and sentenced to one year of probation.

Rivera Flores also allegedly sent a Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agent a slew of taunting text messages, calling the officer "not the good guy" and saying he could not "wait until the midterms" because he believed the agent would not have qualified immunity, legal protection that can shield law enforcement officers from certain civil claims arising from their official conduct.

Text messages between Rivera Flores and the agent reviewed by Fox News show several profane jabs directed at the officer, including, "How you f---ing treat people ... that’s not f---ing protecting, you’re hurting these people," and, "Chris, you know you’re a b----, right."
CLICK BELOW TO READ THE AFFIDAVIT
Rivera Flores obtained the agent’s number after the agent unblocked it on his government-issued phone to contact him during an investigation, according to the affidavit.
The White House said Rivera Flores’ case indicates mainstream media and political critics are off base in their countervailing reporting and allegations about the existence of voter fraud.

"Despite the media and Democrats claiming it never happens, the evidence of noncitizens registering to vote in our elections continues to pile up," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.
"Any non-citizens found registering to vote and voting in our elections will be held accountable. Only Americans should be electing American leaders."
WATCH: TRUMP DOJ VOWS TO PURSUE ‘EVERY SINGLE’ VOTING VIOLATION AFTER NJ ROLL SHOCKER
CNN HOST ADMITS HE WAS WRONG TO SAY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT VOTING 'NEVER HAPPENS' AFTER NEW JERSEY ERROR
Essayli said the case bolsters the DOJ’s demand that California comply with Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon’s request for a comprehensive voter roll audit.
Dhillon said in a statement that noncitizens who "commit fraud so they can vote in American elections" violate federal law and should expect to be prosecuted.
"Let this criminal complaint serve as a reminder that the Justice Department stands ready to enforce the laws Congress enacted to ensure only American citizens vote in federal elections."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Californians will decide in November whether to impose additional voter ID and citizenship-verification requirements. Under current law, people registering to vote must state, under penalty of perjury, that they are U.S. citizens and provide identifying information.
The initiative is being led by state Sen. Tony Strickland, R-Huntington Beach, and Assemblyman Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego.

Fox News’ Matt Finn contributed to this report.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Trump border wall construction kicks off in Arizona amid clash with Native American tribe
summary: The Tohono O'odham Nation claims masked CBP agents blocked tribal police as border wall contractors drilled on their sacred Native American land.
story: Aerial video shows authorities pursuing suspected human smugglers in Texas before the vehicle was disabled and the occupants fled. Officials said one suspect later carjacked a civilian at gunpoint. (@CBPCommissioner via X)
The Trump administration has started construction of a section of a border wall in Arizona despite objections from a Native American tribe.
The wall is part of a $46 billion effort to shore up the southern border with 30-foot steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers and technology designed to stop illegal immigration and smuggling.
However, the Tohono O'odham Nation has said the construction will damage land sacred to the tribe, The Associated Press reported.
MULLIN TELLS CONGRESS PRIMARY BORDER WALL WILL BE DONE BY JUNE 2027, SECONDARY WALL BY SUMMER 2028

Contractors drill at a border wall pre-construction site in Arizona on Tuesday. The project is part of a Trump administration effort to shore up the southern border, which came amid opposition from the Tohono O'odham Nation, which said contractors are trespassing on tribal land. (Tohono O'odham Nation via AP)
U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) said the desert spanning the Tohono O’odham Nation, which sits on both sides of the border, is a major corridor for drug smuggling.

"The project will close one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border — remote desert that has facilitated decades of drug loads, migrant deaths and cartel activity," said CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott.
TRUMP TO SHRINK 2 UTAH NATIONAL MONUMENTS BY 90%
The tribe, which has 37,000 members, including many who live in Mexico, sued the federal government in June in an attempt to halt the project.
The lawsuit argued the construction would cause "significant devastation" on the reservation, including the destruction of mountain peaks sacred to the tribe.
TRUMP SCORES MAJOR IMMIGRATION VICTORY AS JUDGE CLEARS WAY TO END TPS PROTECTIONS FOR THOUSANDS OF SOMALIS
Contractors drill at a border wall pre-construction site in Arizona Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Tohono O'odham Nation via AP)

A federal judge rejected the argument, siding with the government and noting that the border wall would be built on a 60-foot-wide buffer zone of federally owned land called the Roosevelt Reservation.
"Defendants have not yet articulated plans to construct outside the Roosevelt Reservation," U.S. District Judge Richard Leon in Washington, D.C., wrote in his opinion.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION NAMES ROSARIO 'PETE' VASQUEZ TO SERVE AS NEXT US BORDER PATROL CHIEF
Illegal Mexican immigrants walk through the Sonoran Desert after illegally crossing the U.S.-Mexico border border Jan. 19, 2011, into the Tohono O'odham Nation, Ariz. (John Moore/Getty Images)

The tribe said the construction still constitutes trespassing, even if the project is contained to the Roosevelt Reservation. The tribe set up "No Trespassing" signs this week and said masked CBP agents set up a vehicle blockade to stop tribal police from removing the contractors.

"The contractors, who are on the Nation illegally, were accompanied by agents as they worked on three separate locations near the border with drill trucks to conduct soil sampling and other activities," tribal officials said in a statement.
The U.S.-Mexico border fence ends at the eastern edge of the Tohono O’odham Reservation near Sasabe, Ariz., May 10, 2022. (Reuters/Rebecca Noble)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The tribe said it was exploring other legal means to remove the contractors.
Fox News Digital has reached out to CBP and the Tohono O'odham Nation for comment.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Trump signs order creating new Space Academy akin to West Point; its location will be determined
summary: President Trump signed an executive order Friday creating the U.S. Space Academy aimed at training students to enter the U.S. Space Force and serve the nation's growing space industry.
story: President Donald Trump announced a new U.S. Space Academy that will serve the Space Force, NASA and civilian spaceflight industry, saying a location will be chosen ‘very shortly.’
President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order to establish the U.S. Space Academy.

Trump said the location of the academy was yet to be determined but compared its significance to that of the United States Military Academy in West Point, N.Y., and the United States Coast Guard Academy in New London, Connecticut.

The U.S. Space Academy will be for students looking to enter the U.S. Space Force, a new branch of the military Trump created during his first term. The president said it will also serve NASA and the civilian spaceflight industry.
OUT-OF-THIS-WORLD FIX FOR DATA CENTER BACKLASH COULD BE ON NASA'S HORIZON

"We're going to have an academy for what the people in this room love the most. That's exciting. That's really exciting. And I'm going to be choosing a location very shortly," Trump said during remarks at NASA's Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.
The other purpose of the event was to award the four Artemis II astronauts with the Congressional Space Medal of Honor. More than a dozen astronauts stood behind Trump throughout his remarks.

President Donald Trump looks at astronauts as he arrives to present the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to Artemis II crew members Aug. 28, 2026, at the Johnson Space Center in Houston. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)
After signing the executive order, Trump presented the vaunted award, which was first given to Neil Armstrong in 1978, to all four members of the Artemis II crew.

The crew consists of NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman, the mission commander; NASA astronaut Victor Glover, the pilot; NASA astronaut Christina Koch, a mission specialist; and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, also a mission specialist.

"We gather here on these storied grounds to celebrate the immense courage and service of four intrepid space heroes whose sense of daring and adventure led them further from Earth and anyone has ever traveled before. Incredible," Trump said.
Trump called the crew members "great people," also thanking the engineers and scientists who worked on the Artemis II mission.

"Mr. President, it means a lot that you are here at the Johnson Space Center. It underscores the important work that is going on here in Mission Control, in furthering human exploration," Wiseman said when he was called up to speak. "Thank you for coming here today."

President Donald Trump, left, shakes the hand of Artemis II crew member Reid Wiseman after presenting him with the Congressional Space Medal of Honor Aug. 28, 2026, at Johnson Space Center in Houston. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)
NASA MOON BASE: ADMINISTRATOR JARED ISAACMAN DETAILS PLANS FOR LONG-TERM PRESENCE

The Artemis II astronauts launched aboard the Orion spacecraft April 1, 2026, and spent nearly 10 days traveling around the moon before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean April 10. Their trajectory took them as far as 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans had traveled before.

Unlike past missions to the moon, the Artemis II team did not touch down on the lunar surface. Its mission was to fly around the moon while testing the spacecraft and systems NASA plans to use for future lunar landings.

NASA says the mission served as a stepping stone for Artemis III, which is scheduled for 2027 and will involve a series of challenging tests in Earth's orbit. Artemis IV, slated for early 2028, is then expected to send astronauts to the lunar South Pole for the first time.
The Artemis program's overall goal is to establish a long-term human presence on the moon and eventually send astronauts to Mars.
President Donald Trump, left, presents the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to Artemis II crew member Victor Glover Aug. 28, 2026, at Johnson Space Center in Houston. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)
NASA OPENS FIRST MAJOR NEW WIND TUNNEL IN MORE THAN 40 YEARS AT VIRGINIA FACILITY

"America has always been a frontier nation, and space is the highest of all the frontiers. Our manifest destiny is to explore and settle this great unknown," Trump said. "Americans were the first in flight, the first to the moon and will certainly be the first in space, no matter where it is. And I know we're going to be looking at Mars very shortly."
Trump also revealed NASA has begun to work on the first ever nuclear-powered "interplanetary spacecraft" that the space agency will use for the planned 2028 mission to Mars.

"They have to go nuclear because they have essentially unlimited fuel. You don't have to fill up the tanks," he said. "This ship will be among the first of what will ultimately be a massive American Star fleet, making space travel almost as common as ocean travel today and bringing our military to a new level of excellence."
President Donald Trump participates in a Congressional Space Medal of Honor ceremony at NASA's Johnson Space Center Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, in Houston. (AP Photo/Karen Warren)
Throughout his speech, Trump blamed his predecessors for letting U.S. space programs languish.

"In particular, the Obama administration, we even lost our ability to send astronauts into orbit at all. We had no ability in space whatsoever. We totally lost it with everything we spent, with all of the talent and all of the genius and all of the money, we had nothing," the president said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Before the end of my term, American astronauts will return to the lunar surface," he said. "And when we do, they'll plant this very important flag to mark the site of the first permanent American settlement on the moon."
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Hochul ICE policy ‘written in the blood of victims,’ opponent says as sheriffs sue
summary: The clash comes as another top Republican declared Hochul 'doesn't give a s— about public safety'
story: Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman blasts Gov. Kathy Hochul and New York lawmakers over restrictions on ICE cooperation, arguing the policy will make communities less safe and calling it a "total disgrace." (Credit: WNYW)

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul faces new legal and political challenges over a law restricting local law enforcement cooperation with ICE after her Republican gubernatorial opponent warned it was "written in the blood" of crime victims.

Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, whose county borders sanctuary New York City, warned more New Yorkers will be hurt by Hochul’s move, pointing to recent cases of people maimed by illegal immigrants.
"I want to be very clear about this law: This law is written in the blood of the victims, past, present and future," Blakeman said.

"This law is completely misguided and will make our communities less safe," Blakeman said. "We have a governor and a legislature [wherein] every major criminal justice initiative makes it easier for criminals to prey on our communities."
DEM GOVERNOR IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER TESTING LIMITS OF AUTHORITY WITH MAJOR MOVE AGAINST ICE
New York Governor Kathy Hochul speaks at a press conference in Manhattan in New York City, Feb. 20, 2025. (REUTERS/Brendan McDermid)
Blakeman’s warning came as a coalition of 15 sheriffs representing counties from the shore of Lake Champlain to the Massachusetts line filed a lawsuit challenging the ban on 287(g) ICE agreements.
His campaign referred Fox News Digital to his remarks when asked for additional comment.

In a memo outlining the "Local Cops, Local Crimes Act," Hochul argued that "current federal immigration efforts have made communities less safe" and that using local officers and assets for federal civil immigration enforcement draws resources away from local public-safety functions.
A Hochul spokesperson told Fox News Digital that Blakeman’s "understanding of New York’s bail and immigration laws is incorrect," and said the governor’s top priority remains public safety.
BLAKEMAN CUTS INTO HOCHUL'S NEW YORK GOVERNOR'S RACE LEAD IN NEW POLL, AS LIKELY VOTERS GIVE DSA JUDGMENT
Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, left, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul. (NDZ/Star Max/GC Images/Getty Images; Alexander MacDougall/Albany Times Union via Getty Images)

"The Local Cops, Local Crimes Act does not tie the hands of our police or stop them from apprehending dangerous criminals, and local law enforcement can and will continue to work with federal authorities on criminal investigations and violent crime just as they always have," the spokesperson said, adding that the law doesn't prevent cooperation on "ordinary criminal investigations."
EXCLUSIVE: LEGAL GROUP TELLS NYPD COPS THEY CAN CONTACT ICE DIRECTLY DESPITE BLUE CITY'S SANCTUARY RULES

A Homeland Security operation at a New York confectionery arrested 57 illegal immigrants, some with prior convictions, as Gov. Hochul condemned the raid for separating families. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images and Richard Drew/AP Photo)

Hochul recently signaled she'd enlist Attorney General Letitia James to take action against counties that do not comply with the law, while quipping that police should not be converging on churches and schools to help "Stephen Miller reach his quotas." Miller is a White House aide credited with crafting much of President Donald Trump's immigration policy.

"We have reviewed this law with the county attorneys and we looked for every possible way not to comply with this law," Blakeman said in his recent remarks. "However, it was concluded that we would have to abide by the law. I am a law-and-order county executive. I believe in the rule of law, even when it's a bad law," he said.
ICE EYES $20M PURCHASE OF ELECTRIC SHOCK GLOVES AS HOCHUL WARNS OF LEGAL CONSEQUENCES

Blakeman said the law makes it harder for police to keep communities safe, pointing to the recent killing of Westchester County resident Sheridan Gorman, which authorities have attributed to an illegal immigrant, while she was attending college in sanctuary Chicago.
Blakeman cited Illinois’ restrictions on state and local participation in federal immigration enforcement as he argued that New York was moving in a similar direction.
Closer to home, Blakeman said an illegal immigrant from Honduras was charged days ago in his county with second-degree rape and endangering the welfare of a 14-year-old.

Rep. Michael Lawler, the Rockland County Republican who has often warred with Hochul, tweeted this latest law shows she is "the worst governor in America" and "doesn't give a s— about public safety or the rule of law."
Rensselaer County Executive Steve McLaughlin opposed the 287(g) ban before it took effect, calling the agreements "common sense."
McLaughlin, whose Capital Region county is one of the 15 challenging the law, invited Hochul to follow through:

"We don’t really care what this legislature did, we are not going to let them endanger our citizens," he told ABC’s Troy affiliate in June. "I dare you to confront me on this, governor. We’re not stopping."
Late Thursday, Hochul announced a countersuit against Rensselaer County’s sheriff for noncompliance.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Protestors gather outside the federal immigration center at Delaney Hall, where ICE is housing detained illegal immigrants, on June 3, 2026, in Newark, New Jersey. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

Blakeman said he similarly sought a route to noncompliance, pointing to the recent seizure of dozens of illegal handguns and several kilograms of drugs, as well as one of the "largest gang takedowns" in the U.S., which netted 42 gang members in 2025.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Blakeman argued Wednesday that ICE involvement allowed authorities to keep some suspects in custody who otherwise might have been released under New York's cashless bail and other laws. The law-and-order debate is also playing out elsewhere on the statewide GOP ticket, where former Brooklyn federal prosecutor Saritha Komatireddy, who is vying against James, is in a faceoff over criminal justice policies.
Fox News Digital's Kiera McDonald contributed to this report.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Newsom targets major affordability squeeze in ‘striking’ convergence with Trump
summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom's housing push mirrors Trump's supply-side playbook on permitting and zoning, but key policy differences remain.
story: Heritage Foundation economist Peter St. Onge argued Gov. Newsom is embracing housing reforms long championed by free-market economists, but questions whether California can overcome its regulatory barriers.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom is making affordability a focal point of his agenda as the potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender moves to tackle housing costs — seizing on an issue that hurt Democrats politically while converging with pieces of President Donald Trump’s deregulatory housing agenda before the midterms.

Newsom’s biggest recent housing reforms in California came before Trump’s March 2026 executive order on regulatory barriers, but the two are pushing some of the same ideas, including faster approvals, fewer regulatory hurdles and more housing construction.

"This is a pattern that we've seen a couple times with Democrats, where they will fight tooth and nail against economic common sense, but if it starts pulling the wrong way for them, then they'll come around to reality. So you know he's focusing on a lot of things that Trump has been championing," economist Peter St. Onge told Fox News Digital. "...These are things that the free-market economists have been championing for decades."
St. Onge said while Newsom’s "transformation has been certainly striking," California’s struggle to rebuild after the Palisades fire underscores whether that shift will translate into results.
THE KEY STRATEGY RED STATES ARE USING TO LOWER HOUSING COSTS REVEALED

California Gov. Gavin Newsom and President Donald Trump. The Trump administration this week announced a pause on more than $10 billion in childcare funds to five blue states. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images (left); Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images (right))

"We saw this with the Palisades fires where thousands of houses were burned. And people go through… and look at exactly how many houses are under construction and it’s pretty close to zero. The regulatory blockade is insurmountable," said St. Onge.

Newsom has embraced some of the same supply-side housing tools Trump has pushed nationally, including faster approvals, fewer regulatory barriers and efforts to reduce construction costs. California enacted its major recent reforms in June 2025, before Trump issued a housing-specific executive order targeting regulatory barriers in March 2026.
The push comes after Democrats notched big wins in 2025 by campaigning on affordability, reclaiming ground on an issue that had worked in Trump’s favor in 2024.

The Golden State governor signed a housing package in June 2025 to exempt certain projects from California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and streamline environmental review for qualifying housing and infrastructure development. Some Coastal Commission housing appeals were limited and new residential building standards through 2031 were placed on hold.
Newsom followed those changes in July by signing another housing package aimed at streamlining affordable-housing financing and project reviews.

"We can’t speak to the Trump administration’s approach, because he hasn’t done anything. Trump’s failed economic policies and tariffs (also called taxes on Americans) have increased prices and shut down supply chains – slowing building across the country," Newsom director of communications Tara Gallegos told Fox News Digital when approached for comment.

"In contrast, in California, Governor Newsom has enacted historic reforms in California to boost affordability, accelerate housing production, and hold local governments accountable for planning and building the housing their communities need," Gallegos added.
$104,200 SALARY IN ORANGE COUNTY, CALIFORNIA CONSIDERED 'LOW-INCOME' BY STATE OFFICIALS
California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks during a press conference for a housing affordability reform bill signing on July 13, 2026, in Oakland, Calif. (Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Trump already made reducing regulatory barriers to home construction part of his federal housing agenda. He signed an executive order in March directing agencies to identify ways to speed permitting, reduce regulatory costs and encourage state and local governments to ease barriers to new construction.

The White House’s Economic Report of the President, published in April, went further by recommending specific state and local reforms, including by-right approval for code-compliant projects, deadlines of no more than 60 days for a right-to-build decision and 30 days for later permits and inspections, limits on certain fees, third-party inspections and fewer green-energy mandates.

"Unlike incompetent Governor Gavin Newscum, President Trump has been laser-focused on making housing more affordable. The President signed an Executive Order prohibiting large Wall Street firms from purchasing single-family homes, directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to purchase $200 billion in mortgage bonds that helped drive rates to four-year lows, and cut unnecessary red tape at a historic pace to boost supply, speed construction, and lower costs," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital .

"The President will not stop fighting until the American Dream of homeownership is within reach for every American, which is why he continues to sign bold new executive orders and calls on Congress to pass further legislation," added Ingle.
John Gibbs, Thomas A. Roe Institute for Economic Policy Studies Director at The Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital that housing is better handled by state and local governments.
.TRUMP SCORES MAJOR WIN AS CONGRESS PASSES HOUSING CRACKDOWN ON WALL STREET INVESTORS

Governor Gavin Newsom speaks during a press conference for a bill signing of housing affordability reforms event in Oakland, California, United States on July 13, 2026. (Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"While California's recent efforts to streamline approvals and limit local barriers to development reflect policies to increase housing supply that many economists across the political spectrum support, it is important to recognize that housing supply is ultimately governed primarily by state and local governments, not Washington," said Gibbs.
The president and governor both have different powers in their pockets they can use.

Newsom can directly use state power to override local zoning, streamline CEQA/permitting and pressure cities to build. Trump’s levers are largely federal — mortgage finance, federal regulation, GSEs and incentives/guidance to states.

"Federal policymakers have far greater control over demand-driven housing policies such as mortgage guarantees, federal mortgage insurance programs, the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs), and monetary policy, than they do over local zoning and land-use decisions," Gibbs explained.
Manhattan Institute senior fellow Judge Glock also Fox News Digital there are contrasts to the president and Newsom’s plans.
TRUMP’S AFFORDABILITY PLAN FACES CONSERVATIVE PUSHBACK AS POCKETBOOK ISSUES LOOM OVER MIDTERMS

"One problem is that many of Newsom's housing laws contain handouts to unions or to environmental groups that further drive-up housing prices, such as requirements for union labor or for solar-paneled roofs," said Glock. "The Trump administration, by contrast, has tried to limit such requirements for new housing."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The Trump administration has also focused more on trying to expand cities outward and allowing more single-family homes, while Newsom has focused on densifying existing areas and building more apartments," he added.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Kamala Harris dives into midterm fight only to get roasted for never having 'an original thought in her life’
summary: Kamala Harris urged Democrats to turn out in "big numbers" and be "too big to rig" in midterms, drawing mockery for echoing Trump's signature phrase.
story: Gene Hamilton explains what the ruling allows the administration to do next, when states could return to court and how federal agencies may move to implement Trump’s mail-voting order ahead of the midterms.

Critics mocked former Vice President Kamala Harris after she warned Republicans are "trying to cheat" in the midterms while echoing President Donald Trump’s signature "too big to rig" rallying cry in a new video urging Democrats to turn out in force.
"We are two months away from the midterms. Get out and vote. Let’s get everyone out to vote. They are cheating," said Harris in a recorded video Thursday posted on X.
"They are trying to cheat, and we have got to turn out in big numbers and be too big to rig. I’ll see you out there," Harris added.

Trump repeatedly used "too big to rig" during the 2024 campaign, after years of casting doubt on U.S. election integrity following his loss in the 2020 election. Harris is using the same phrase while accusing Republicans of trying to cheat in the 2026 midterms.
2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN
Vice President Kamala Harris, former Democratic presidential nominee, speaking at a campaign rally in Chandler, Arizona, on October 10, 2024 (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
"Kamala Harris has never had an original thought in her life," wrote TPUSA Spokesman Andrew Kolvet.
"47 seconds. 15 jump cuts. She must be high as a kite," wrote popular account End Wokeness.
"Nice to know she's still stealing Trump's ideas," said conservative commentator Shawn Farash.
"Sounds familiar," said Turning Point show host Jobob Taeleifi.
FEDERAL JUDGE AGAIN BLOCKS TRUMP'S MAIL BALLOT ORDER JUST BEFORE MIDTERMS

An absentee ballot for the 2020 U.S. election. A federal judge on Tuesday blocked the U.S. Postal Service from implementing part of President Donald Trump's executive order tightening mail-in voting rules ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. (Caroline Brehman/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, File)

In her video, Harris pointed to Monday’s Supreme Court ruling allowing parts of Trump’s mail-voting order to move forward while the legal fight continues. The court did not rule on whether the restrictions themselves are legal.

A federal judge on Thursday again temporarily blocked the Postal Service from enforcing the new mail-ballot requirements, setting up another round of litigation over the policy ahead of November’s midterms.
FOX NEWS POLL: AS ECONOMIC PAIN DEEPENS, DISAPPROVAL OF TRUMP HITS NEW HIGH
Former Vice President Kamala Harris speaks during a panel discussion at the Austrian World Summit of the Schwarzenegger Climate Initiative on June 16, 2026, in Vienna, Austria. (AFP via Getty Images)
Harris urged Democrats to turn out in large numbers while arguing that Trump’s mail-voting policies could make it more difficult for some voters to cast ballots.

"By the way, he votes by mail from Mar-A-Lago, but he doesn’t want you to vote by mail. Just this week the U.S. Supreme Court backed up the president’s agenda. He’s trying to make it more difficult for you to vote by mail," Harris said in the video.

Fox News Digital reached out to Harris for comment.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Chinese bot farm caught red-handed trying to influence heated AI data center debate
summary: X uncovered 200,000 inauthentic Chinese accounts pushing anti-AI and anti-data center narratives in the United States amid energy policy debates.
story: AI executive and former election whistleblower Brittany Kaiser warns foreign actors may be fueling backlash to U.S. data centers, saying the campaigns could slow development, send sensitive data overseas and weaken America in the global AI race.

The social media platform X, formerly known as Twitter, has uncovered a massive suspected Chinese bot farm conducting "influence operations" online in the United States, including pushing an anti-artificial intelligence and anti-data center narrative.

This comes as a national debate rages over the costs and benefits of continuing to develop artificial intelligence at breakneck speed and the massive data centers required to power it. The debate also has immense political implications, dividing parties internally as many members of the GOP break with President Donald Trump on AI and data centers.

As this national conversation unfolds, X’s Global Government Affairs account said the platform’s safety team identified a bot farm of approximately 200,000 inauthentic Chinese accounts "involved in influence operations."
The X team said that within the bot farm, 200 accounts were found posting "in a manner that could manipulate a legitimate debate about American AI and energy policy."
BLANCHE URGED TO INVESTIGATE ALLEGED FOREIGN INFLUENCE IN FIGHT AGAINST DATA CENTERS
X has uncovered a massive suspected Chinese bot farm conducting "influence operations" online in the United States. (Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto via Getty Images; Kevin Frayer/Getty Images)

According to the platform, posts by these accounts contained claims that AI data centers are driving up household electricity prices and straining the grid. The X team said other accounts also posted AI-generated cartoons depicting data center developers enriching themselves at the public's expense.

One image shared by the team depicted horrified citizens across from data center developers with bags of cash with the caption, "Data centers get subsidized while we foot the bill!" Another image read that "the AI industry is booming, but the costs are being borne by ordinary people."

Earlier this summer, OpenAI announced that it had banned a "cluster of ChatGPT accounts that likely originated in China" that were being used to generate a "covert influence operation" primarily targeting U.S. audiences. OpenAI said the accounts generated short comments and images similarly claiming that data centers and AI were increasing electricity demand and causing higher costs.

The influence campaigns were discovered as debate rages over AI. Critics of AI development say the data centers required to power it harm the environment, drive up electricity costs and decrease neighborhood property values. Proponents, meanwhile, say AI data center development is critical to national security and boosts local economies by creating jobs.

He said that local communities and states should want to welcome data centers because "the jobs are enormous, and the money paid, the taxes paid are just enormous."
"And if you don't take it, you're going to be left behind because there are plenty of places that want it," he added.

title: Trump admin blocks more than $1.6B in potentially improper Medicare lab payments, agency says
summary: Dr. Mehmet Oz says labs billed Medicare for tests never performed as President Donald Trump's CMS uses AI to flag suspicious billing patterns.
story: Dr. Mehmet Oz vows to eliminate multi-billion dollar billing scams and systemic waste within the healthcare system.

FIRST ON FOX: Federal officials and the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud have blocked or clawed back more than $1.6 billion in potentially improper Medicare laboratory payments since President Donald Trump returned to office, including $732 million tied to 157 lab providers booted from the program for alleged fraud.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) said the labs were suspected of billing Medicare for tests that were never performed, tests patients did not need and services billed at higher rates than they should have been.
"When laboratories bill Medicare for tests they never performed, it drains the Medicare Trust Fund and diverts resources away from beneficiaries who need them," CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said.
DOJ CHARGES 19 DEFENDANTS IN ALLEGED $4M PHILADELPHIA MEDICARE AND MEDICAID FRAUD

President Donald Trump speaks as Administrator for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Mehmet Oz looks on during an event on drug pricing in the South Court Auditorium on the White House campus on Feb. 5, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Nathan Howard/Getty Images)
In one case, the owner of a consulting company enrolled 14 labs in Medicare and billed the program more than $24 million, even though CMS said none of the labs appeared to be operating.

CMS has since held back $12 million in payments to the labs and recovered another $7 million. Eleven of the 14 labs have been removed from Medicare, while the remaining three are still under investigation.
CMS said it is using artificial intelligence and other technology to sift through Medicare claims and spot unusual billing that could be a sign of fraud.
The technology looks for billing that falls outside normal patterns and can flag suspicious claims for closer scrutiny. CMS can then hold, reject or deny a claim before Medicare pays it.

Vice President JD Vance speaks next to Administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Mehmet Oz about combating fraud at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in Washington, D.C., Feb. 25, 2026. (REUTERS)
Of the $1.6 billion cited by the agency, more than $500 million in suspected fraudulent payments were stopped through 185 payment suspensions after CMS investigated 600 labs.

"The previous administration treated our taxpayer-funded programs as piggy banks for fraudsters," the White House told Fox News Digital. "That is no longer the case, thanks to President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and Dr. Oz, who is an anti-fraud superstar."
TREASURY HAILS SUCCESS OF ANTI-FRAUD PROCESS THAT FLAGGED AND PREVENTED $99 MILLION IN PAYMENTS TO DEAD PEOPLE

The agency also recovered more than $276 million in overpayments made to 442 suspect labs and said another $127 million in potentially fraudulent payments was prevented after 85 cases were referred to law enforcement.
CMS pointed to two recent cases in Texas as examples of labs suspected of billing Medicare for services they did not provide.
One lab began billing Medicare in late February. CMS said it caught the suspicious activity early and denied $1.2 million in claims.

The lab then changed the way it billed Medicare in early April in an apparent attempt to get around the agency’s safeguards, according to CMS. Officials continued watching its claims and stopped more than $150,000 in additional payments before removing the provider from Medicare later that month.

Vice President JD Vance looks on as Medicare and Medicaid Administrator Mehmet Oz speaks about combating fraud at the White House complex in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 25, 2026. (Oliver Contreras/AFP via Getty Images)
DR OZ SAYS 800 HOSPICE PROVIDERS SUSPENDED IN CALIFORNIA OVER ALLEGED $1B MEDICARE FRAUD SCHEME

Another Texas lab began billing heavily in May after submitting test claims two days earlier in the year. CMS denied $1.9 million in claims and captured another $1.7 million in payments. The lab remains under review and could be removed from Medicare.
The lab cases are part of a wider Trump administration push to combat improper Medicare billing involving medical equipment, hospice care, skin treatments and other services.

CMS said its Medicare fraud prevention efforts saved $42 billion in fiscal year 2025. So far in 2026, the agency says it has identified $1.8 billion in Medicare overpayments and recovered $378 million in overpayments from post-payment reviews.

Since Jan. 1, CMS has also frozen more than $371 million in Medicare payments involving 267 providers and suppliers. That includes more than $226 million in suspected improper billing for medical equipment, more than $53 million involving skin treatments and more than $23 million involving hospice providers.

"We won't stop until we've restored program integrity and ensured that fraudsters have nowhere left to hide," Oz said.

title: Biden-honored Iraqi official lands on US terror watchlist as Trump State Dept revokes visa
summary: Taif Sami Mohammed received the International Women of Courage Award in 2022 but now appears on the U.S. terrorist watchlist with her visa revoked.
story: Former Biden special assistant Meghan Hays, Bloomberg News senior White House reporter Josh Wingrove and 'Ruthless Podcast' co-host Josh Holmes join Shannon Bream to analyze the ideological battle within the Democratic Party.

FIRST ON FOX: Four years ago, Taif Sami Mohammed was being celebrated by the United States as one of the world’s most courageous women. Secretary of State Antony Blinken praised the senior Iraqi official as the country’s "Iron Woman," crediting her with stopping bribes, uncovering schemes that enriched corrupt officials and fighting corruption despite threats against her.
Today, Mohammed is believed to be outside Iraq on the U.S. terrorist watchlist and can no longer enter the United States.

A State Department official told Fox News Digital the department revoked Mohammed’s visa this week, marking a dramatic reversal for an official who received one of the Biden administration’s highest-profile awards for women in 2022.

"While the Biden State Department shamefully celebrated and awarded foreigners who threaten our nation, the Trump State Department revokes their visas and ensures these individuals are removed from our country," Assistant Secretary of State for Global Public Affairs Dylan Johnson told Fox News Digital.
TRUMP ADMIN EYES HISTORIC MASS VISA REVOCATION TARGETING UP TO 200K ASYLUM SEEKERS: REPORT
Taif Sami Mohammed, Iraq's former finance minister who received an award from President Joe Biden's State Department, now has no U.S. visa and is on the FBI's terror watchlist. (US State Department)
"Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio, suspected terrorists will never be allowed to remain in the United States."
The State Department did not immediately provide details about when Mohammed was placed on the terrorist watchlist or the intelligence that led to that determination.
Mohammed’s fall from Washington’s favor had been building publicly for more than a year.

Republican lawmakers previously accused her of helping facilitate terrorist financing through Iraq’s financial system and urged the Trump administration to take action against her. Reps. Joe Wilson, R-S.C., and Greg Steube, R-Fla., called Mohammed a "key enabler of terrorist funding in Iraq" and pushed the administration to impose sanctions.
Those allegations stand in stark contrast to how the Biden administration described Mohammed when it selected her for the State Department’s International Women of Courage Award in 2022.

At the time, Mohammed was Iraq’s deputy finance minister and director general of its budget department. The State Department described her as a "frontline leader against corrupt practices" who had been integral to preventing corruption in Iraq’s budget.
Blinken went further during the March 2022 awards ceremony, saying Mohammed had "stopped bribes" and uncovered efforts to inflate government payrolls and enrich corrupt officials.
The State Department praised Mohammed as a woman of courage. (X/State Department)
The ceremony, hosted by Blinken and featuring remarks from then-first lady Jill Biden, honored 12 women the State Department said had shown extraordinary courage and leadership.
Mohammed later rose to become Iraq’s finance minister, overseeing the federal budget, government spending and Baghdad’s financial relationship with Iraq’s Kurdistan region.
Her troubles have since spread beyond Washington.

An Iraqi court summoned Mohammed and placed her on a judicial wanted list as authorities widened a corruption investigation into former senior government officials, IraqiNews reported Aug. 9, 2025, citing sources familiar with the proceedings.

U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken discusses Russia's invasion of Ukraine during a news conference at the State Department in Washington March 2, 2022. (Reuters/Elizabeth Frantz/Pool/File Photo)

title: House Dem Debbie Dingell places Trump's Lake Ontario name change in the crosshairs

story: President Donald Trump signs an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America and speaks to reporters in the Oval Office.

"The change will begin occurring in printed documents over the next several days. This change has also been made official in the Geographic Names Information System."
Dingell's post on X linked to a Politico report, which stated that Dingell noted in an interview that she plans to introduce a measure on Monday to nullify Trump's move to change the lake's name.

title: One of the world's hottest industries is sparking a blue-collar jobs boom
summary: AI infrastructure spending is projected to drive U.S. industrial construction to $684 billion by 2031, creating massive demand for skilled trades workers.
story: The AI boom is driving a massive infrastructure buildout across the U.S., creating new opportunities for skilled workers as demand for data centers and chip plants surges.

The race to build the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence is creating a new boom for America's blue-collar workforce, as construction firms scramble to fill jobs building data centers, power systems and the facilities that keep the technology running.

The rapid buildout is putting a new premium on skilled trades, with data centers requiring armies of workers to prepare sites, pour concrete, install electrical systems and handle the infrastructure needed to bring them online.

"For many years, there's been a lack of focus just in general from what is the benefit of a career in the trades," explained Cole Renken, general manager of Merlo America, the U.S. division of Italian construction equipment manufacturer Merlo Group.
"It's a very stable income, very stable lifestyle that you can provide for," he added.
ONE OF AMERICA'S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS SAYS AI IS CREATING JOBS — NOT REPLACING THEM

The boom is creating demand for electricians, plumbers, heavy-equipment operators and other skilled tradespeople needed to build and maintain the infrastructure powering the technology. (Mark Wilson/Getty Images)
Now, the AI infrastructure boom could bring renewed attention to those careers.

U.S. construction spending is projected to climb from $2.22 trillion in 2026 to $2.85 trillion by 2031, according to a new report from Merlo America developed with predictive sales intelligence firm BiltData.ai. Industrial construction, which includes factories and data centers, is projected to reach $684 billion by 2031, representing 24% of total U.S. construction spending.

Much of that growth is being driven by the infrastructure needed to power AI, cloud computing and 5G, with data centers emerging as a major source of construction and industrial activity. And building those facilities requires skilled workers at nearly every stage of a project.

Renken said large projects require heavy-equipment operators to prepare sites and logistics workers to coordinate materials, followed by concrete workers, electricians, plumbers and other skilled trades as construction progresses. Electrical workers, he said, could face particularly high demand.
A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD’S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES

Data center development is surging across Texas, with North Texas taking the top spot in a new global ranking of the industry’s leading markets. (Mikala Compton/The Austin American-Statesman/Getty Images)
And the jobs don't necessarily disappear once construction is complete.

Brittany Kaiser, CEO of AI infrastructure company Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital that data centers require workers not only to build the facilities and energy infrastructure, but also to install equipment, monitor operations, perform maintenance and support future expansion.
"These are projects that can provide hundreds or thousands of jobs over many, many years," Kaiser said. "It's not a quick construction project."
She described data centers as "a constant construction project," requiring workers across construction, electricity, energy development, monitoring and maintenance as facilities grow and expand.
That ongoing demand could create opportunities for surrounding communities, particularly for workers who can be trained for specialized positions.

"It's jobs that can also be taught and trained," Kaiser said. "So it's very possible to engage with the community on education and training initiatives to allow people to get access to these higher paying jobs that they didn't have a skill set for before."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The rapid buildout of data centers and other infrastructure could intensify an existing shortage of skilled workers as construction demand grows. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images)
But as projects multiply, finding enough skilled workers could become a challenge.
Renken said shortages in the trades have persisted throughout much of his career and could intensify as more projects come online.

The boom, he said, is also a reminder that even the most advanced technology depends on physical infrastructure and the skilled workers needed to build and maintain it. That need, he said, could bring new attention to skilled trades that have long been overshadowed by the focus on high-tech jobs.
"To me, it has been kind of an overshadowed market that hasn't gotten the attention that it needs," he said.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Socialist mayoral candidate ignites online mockery for touting basic city service
summary: Los Angeles councilmember Nithya Raman faces online mockery from the right after celebrating a supposed win that critics said led them to question if it was a parody.
story: Los Angeles residents express their frustration with the remaining mayoral candidates as some express they believe they are "both bad."

A Los Angeles councilwoman’s celebration of a newly painted neighborhood crosswalk has drawn online mockery after critics seized on the months-long timeline and glossy "street infrastructure" rollout for what they said amounted to a basic city service.

Los Angeles Councilmember Nithya Raman, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, is facing online mockery after celebrating the completion of a neighborhood crosswalk project, which was first raised by the Los Feliz Neighborhood Council late last year, in a post on X. The post featured before-and-after images and thanked her field team for "continuing to problem-solve, push for solutions, and make our streets safer."

"Dear Lord, Nithya. Your standards are so incredibly low," responded Richard Grenell, Presidential Envoy for Special Missions amid Donald Trump's second term. "They didn’t even fix the street, they painted over cracks. And it took them a year….."

"Holy s—t, my sides...Nithya Raman's big accomplishment is taking 9 months to paint 7 yellow stripes over a cracked street?" quipped former L.A. mayoral candidate and reality television star Spencer Pratt. "How dumb do you have to be to post this? BAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHA"
DEM'S MELTDOWN OVER ‘TERRORIST SYMPATHIZER’ HASAN PIKER TRIGGERS INSTANT CONSERVATIVE MOCKERY: ‘YIKES’

Former L.A. mayoral candidate and reality television star Spencer Pratt mocked L.A. city councilwoman Nithya Raman after she touted a local win that others thought didn't deserve the credit she was trying to give it. (Getty Images)
"This is beyond parody," responded conservative commentator Ben Shapiro. "Eight months to paint some yellow lines. Huge infrastructure victory! Make her mayor!"
"They're calling it the most ambitious infrastructure project since the Golden Gate Bridge," added the Manhattan Institute's Chris Rufo.
AOC'S SOCIALIST CREDENTIALS FACE FRESH SCRUTINY AFTER GLARING 7-YEAR GAP SURFACES: ‘VERY CONVENIENT’
Daily Wire Co-Founder & The Ben Shapiro Show Host Ben Shapiro (Brendan McDermid/Reuters)
Fox News Digital reached out to Raman’s office and Pratt for comment but did not receive a response before publication.

Raman’s announcement labeled the work "Improving Our Neighborhood Street Infrastructure" and included before-and-after photos showing yellow crosswalk markings across the cracked roadway. She said the Los Feliz Neighborhood Council had brought the issue to her office in late 2025.
Los Angeles councilwoman Nithya Raman drew online mockery after touting a recent 'win' in her role representing her constituents. (Getty Images)

The post did not specify the project’s cost, when physical work began, which city department performed it or whether the work involved safety improvements beyond the painted markings.
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Dems derided Trump’s midterm gamble — until he ended up winning big
summary: President Donald Trump's mid-decade redistricting push netted Republicans at least 10 more right-leaning congressional seats ahead of the midterms.
story: Fox News congressional correspondent Bill Melugin reports on voter sentiment ahead of the 2026 midterm elections and breaks down the battle for control of the House and Senate on ‘Special Report.’

One year ago this week, Texas passed a new congressional redistricting map, giving President Donald Trump his first major victory in his push to give Republicans a big boost heading into the midterm elections by drawing more right-leaning districts.

One year later, as they fight to hold their razor-thin House majority, Republicans are the big winners, with partisan redistricting netting them at least 10 additional right-leaning congressional seats in time for the midterms.
Democrats and left-leaning pundits repeatedly railed against Trump's efforts and charged they would "shred our country’s democracy."

Top Democrats aimed to fight fire with fire but fell short. Their efforts to keep pace with the GOP were derailed following major court rulings by the Supreme Court and Virginia's top court earlier this year, which were seen as major legal victories for Republicans. And the GOP scored another redistricting win earlier this month in Missouri, when a judge allowed a new map, backed by Trump and passed last year by Republican state lawmakers, to be used in November's elections.
BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WARS ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES
U.S. President Donald Trump has been the driving force behind a Republican effort for mid-decade congressional redistricting ahead of the midterm elections. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
Progressive pundits that cast Trump’s push for Texas to redraw its congressional map before the 2026 midterms as a threat to voting rights and democracy. Among them was former MSNBC anchor Joy Reid.
She branded the fight a "Voting Rights 911" and later titled a segment on "The Joy Reid Show" as "Texas’s War on Democracy Through Gerrymandering."
John Oliver, host of "Last Week Tonight" on HBO, was also among a group of pundits that criticized the redistricting push as a power grab by Trump and the GOP.
Oliver said gerrymandering was the practice of manipulating maps "to get the outcome you want," and called it "putting a heavy thumb on the scale of who gets elected."
Fox News Digital reached out to representatives for Reid and Oliver to see if they continue to stand by their criticism, but didn't receive responses by the time this story was published.
It wasn't just pundits who spoke out.

Top Democrats also took action, after Trump, aiming to prevent what happened during his first term in the White House when Democrats reclaimed the House majority in the 2018 midterms, first floated the idea of rare, but not unheard of, mid-decade congressional redistricting.

After Texas led the way last summer, Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin called a ruling by the conservative-dominated Supreme Court to greenlight the redistricting a victory for a "rigged map" meant to protect the GOP from midterm accountability.
"But it will backfire," Martin predicted.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led a successful redistricting effort in his Democrat-dominated state last year to negate the GOP gains in Texas, emphasized, "California will not sit idle as Trump and his Republican lapdogs shred our country’s democracy before our very eyes."
TWIN COURT RULINGS RESHAPE HOUSE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS FIGHT UPHILL REDISTRICTING BATTLE
California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced a plan for a special election on November 4, 2025, to seek voter approval for a new congressional map, on August 14, 2025 in Los Angeles. (AP)

And Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York, who considered but decided against redrawing congressional maps in the blue-leaning state, charged that Trump and Republicans were aiming to "erode our democracy and drag us toward authoritarianism."
A veteran Republican strategist sees the Democrats' arguments as hypocritical.

"The left’s overcharged political rhetoric is undermined by Governor Gavin Newsom’s willingness to spearhead a power grab in his state that eliminated at least 5 GOP congressional seats," Colin Reed told Fox News Digital.

Reed argued that "Democratic leaders had the same goal as Republicans with mid-decade redistricting; they just weren’t as successful, but their intent makes any complaints about democracy ring hollow."
But Democrats stand by their resistance.

"Elected leaders in every state should respond aggressively to this unAmerican attempt to rig control of congress for a generation," John Bisognano, executive director of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, told Fox News Digital.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
While Texas and California were the first major battlegrounds in the redistricting war, the fight quickly spread from coast-to-coast.
Republican-controlled Florida, Missouri, and Ohio and swing state North Carolina, where the GOP dominates the legislature, drew new maps as part of the president's push.

But in blows to Republicans, a Utah district judge late last year rejected a congressional district map drawn by the state's GOP-dominated legislature and instead approved an alternate that created a Democratic-leaning district ahead of the midterms.
And Republicans in Indiana's state Senate in December defied Trump, shooting down a redistricting bill that had passed the state House.

But Democrats were dealt a major blow this spring when the Virginia Supreme Court struck down the Democrat-controlled state's congressional redistricting ballot measure, which would have produced up to four more left-leaning House seats.
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Concurrently, a blockbuster decision by the U.S. Supreme Court that gutted key portions of the landmark Voting Rights Act – ruling that race should not dictate the redrawing of legislative districts – gave a handful of GOP-dominated Southern states the greenlight to move forward with redistricting.
The legal rulings locked in an advantage for Republicans in this year's battle for the House. Now it's up to voters to decide which party will control Congress.
But the redistricting fight is far from over.
Democrat-controlled New York is taking steps toward redistricting in time for the 2028 elections.

So is blue state Maryland, but a court ruling on Wednesday dealt Democrats a setback. A Maryland court blocked Democrats from adding a congressional redistricting initiative to the November ballot on Wednesday. The Democrat-backed effort would have allowed Maryland residents to vote on an amendment to the state constitution to let lawmakers redraw district maps ahead of the 2028 elections.
Meanwhile, battleground Georgia, where Republicans currently control the governor's office and state legislature, is also mulling a move.
