"The gerrymandering crisis Trump started last year is is not over. We expect him to continue demanding new congressional maps that manipulate voting districts to protect Republicans despite what American voters want," Bisognano told Fox News Digital.
He urged state leaders to speak out and draw "responsive maps to ensure the national congressional map reflects the make up and the will of the American people."
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Mail-voting crackdown moves ahead as Trump court win opens door to federal action
summary: Gene Hamilton says federal agencies like USPS can now move forward with Trump's mail-in ballot safeguards after the Supreme Court's ruling.
story: Gene Hamilton explains what the ruling allows the administration to do next, when states could return to court and how federal agencies may move to implement Trump’s mail-voting order ahead of the midterms.

The next phase of President Donald Trump’s effort to change America’s mail-in-voting system is taking shape after the Supreme Court issued a largely favorable ruling for the White House in a challenge to Trump's mail-in ballot restrictions.

Former White House deputy counsel Gene Hamilton said federal agencies such as the Postal Service can now move forward with parts of Trump’s election-integrity order, including new ballot-mail standards and efforts involving state citizenship lists, as opposing states wait to see which concrete federal actions could form the basis of new lawsuits.
"It’s really interesting what the court did [and] it’s actually exactly what you would expect the court to do," Hamilton told Fox News Digital.
TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS
Protesters demonstrate in front of the home of then-Postmaster General Louis DeJoy over mail-in balloting concerns. (Eric Lee/Getty Images)
Hamilton said that when Trump directed USPS, DHS and DOJ to prepare for the new protocols, several states immediately claimed harm, but the court’s majority rejected their challenge.
Originally, a Boston federal judge agreed with them, but the Supreme Court effectively said "you can’t enjoin [the feds] from thinking" — in Hamilton’s words — because no action had taken place yet.
JACKSON RIPS INTO SUPREME COURT COLLEAGUES' 'SERIOUS LEGAL ERROR' ON TRUMP MAIL-IN VOTING ORDER

US President Donald Trump displays a signed executive order in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, March 31, 2026. Trump signed an executive order Tuesday intended to make it harder for voters to cast mail-in ballots, escalating his long-running campaign against a practice used by millions of Americans. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"It reminds the American people … just because something might happen in the future [it] doesn't mean that you're actually harmed today, and that's really the crux of what the court did."

Hamilton quipped that if the states challenging the order were proven right — and the possibility of future harm were enough to obtain a legal stay — his organization would "have a field day across the country" trying to head off new policies he and his clients oppose.

In that regard, he added that the district judge ultimately overruled by the Supreme Court made an "egregious" misread of Article III powers and essentially said states can dictate which cases the attorney general and DOJ try to prosecute.

He emphasized that the legal landscape could change quickly once Trump’s actions get underway, but said states challenging executive action must show a concrete or sufficiently imminent injury rather than rely on predictions about what agencies might eventually do.
DHS APPROVES PLAN TO VERIFY VOTER CITIZENSHIP, MONITOR MAIL BALLOTS AS TRUMP PUSH INTENSIFIES

California Attorney General Rob Bonta speaks after a hearing about Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco's seizure and recount of more than half a million 2025 election ballots on Monday, Aug. 24, 2026, at California Supreme Court in San Francisco. (Alicia Ramirez/The Riverside Record, Pool)

Besides USPS, Trump’s order directs DHS to compile and provide states with lists of adult U.S. citizens, while DOJ was told to prioritize investigations and potential prosecutions involving ballots issued to ineligible voters.
"Let’s see what the departments and agencies actually do. Well, let's see what they say they're going to do," Hamilton told Fox News Digital, as new concrete federal rules will come next.
USPS WOULDN'T DELIVER BALLOTS IN STATES THAT REFUSE TO FORK OVER MAIL-IN VOTER INFO UNDER PROPOSED RULE
The clock is ticking to implement the plan and respond to further legal challenges as states distribute mail ballots progressively earlier than in past decades.

USPS first proposed its ballot-mail rule in June and has since finalized it, requiring standardized ballot envelopes and unique tracking barcodes while directing states to use a federal portal to identify voters receiving mailed federal ballots. States that fail to comply could see outbound federal ballot mail refused or returned.

But the agency signaled at the time that it won’t implement the rule for the midterms unless the litigation is resolved. A separate injunction obtained in litigation by the League of Women Voters currently blocks USPS from implementing the rule.
"Why wouldn't you take steps like getting a list of eligible voters, like asking the USPS to use standard mail security measures that they use for other things," Hamilton commented.

Asked which provisions of Trump’s order the administration plans to implement following the ruling, when those actions would begin and how states would be directed to comply, the White House did not provide specifics.

"These are commonsense measures that protect the security of mail-in ballots and ensure only Americans are electing American leaders. This administration will continue to lawfully enact the agenda President Trump was elected on — which includes the safety and security of our elections," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta — who led the plaintiffs from 23 states along with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro — criticized the Supreme Court for letting Trump "try to make it harder for Americans to vote."
Shapiro was listed separately because Pennsylvania Republican Attorney General David Sunday had not signed the state onto the suit.
"Not so fast," the potential 2028 presidential candidate said in a statement. "Donald Trump does not run elections here in Pennsylvania — or in any state."
"[The] SCOTUS decision does not deal with the substance of Trump’s unconstitutional Executive Order and does not mean his illegal attempt to restrict mail-in voting will go forward."

On Wednesday, Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes responded to the ruling, declaring, "Over my dead body is that rule going to go into effect. We are going to fight this tooth and nail in the courts."
Bonta pledged to continue the fight and noted that Obama-appointed Judge Indira Talwani of Boston had originally sided with the plaintiffs.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Postmaster General David Steiner testifies before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee during a June 24 hearing on reforming the U.S. Postal Service's business model in Washington, D.C. (Valerie Plesch/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Hamilton predicted such disputes would produce another round of litigation as agencies make their next moves.
"We have to get through the arbitrage of lower court proceedings, and I'm sure there's going to be a lot more fighting to come," he said.
Shapiro echoed the plaintiffs’ opposition to the ruling, tweeting:
"We’ll see the Trump Administration in court."
Fox News Digital's Hannah Brennan and Melissa Chrise contributed to this report.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: GOP firebrand targets booming business letting foreigners exploit US citizenship laws
summary: The House Oversight Committee subpoenaed the top doctor at Have My Baby in Miami to testify before Rep. Brandon Gill's panel on birth tourism.
story: Fox News host Will Cain discusses President Donald Trump's efforts to end birthright citizenship and birth tourism through two executive orders on ‘The Will Cain Show.’
House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., is subpoenaing a doctor allegedly behind a sprawling birth tourism scheme based in Florida.

It comes as Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, is setting his sights on a new target after his crackdown on the Smithsonian Institution made headlines and thrust fresh scrutiny onto its teaching of American history.

Gill's task force on investigating institutional abuses, which is part of the House Oversight Committee, is now gearing up for a hearing on the practice of birth tourism — something the White House sounded the alarm on just this month.

As part of the hearing, Comer sent a subpoena to Dr. Wladimir Lorentz of Have My Baby in Miami, a South Florida business that's aimed at helping foreigners give birth in the United States. The hearing is expected to take place Sept. 1.

Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, arrives for the House Oversight and Government Reform Delivering on Government Efficiency Subcommittee hearing titled "Rewriting American History: Examining the Smithsonian's Efforts to Reshape the Past" in the Rayburn House Office Building on July 21, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Comer accused Lorentz of refusing to voluntarily appear via his attorney, and in a letter sent with the subpoena on Tuesday, Comer said Lorentz's attorney argued he could not speak with the committee due to a pending criminal probe being conducted by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida.

"As the Founder and Chief Medical Officer of a company doing business as 'Have My Baby in Miami,' your knowledge regarding the company’s marketing practices and direct observations relevant to the birth tourism industry is vital to the immediate investigation," Comer's subpoena letter read.
SEN ERIC SCHMITT SEEKS TO END BIRTH TOURISM, REVOKE CITIZENSHIP FOR BABIES OF FOREIGN DIPLOMATS

"Furthermore, given the national security concerns raised by birth tourism, delaying the hearing or deferring your testimony to some unknown date in the (potentially far) future would be an extraordinary action that would curtail the Committee’s ability to glean valuable information that will inform its oversight and further its legislative goals."
Meanwhile, Gill echoed Comer's concerns over national security.
House Republicans are eyeing a Florida-based company accused of promoting birth tourism in the U.S. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)
BIRTH TOURISM FIGHT SHIFTS TO US ‘TROPICAL MATERNITY WARD’ WITH HISTORY OF CHINESE EXPLOITATION

"A growing industry is openly marketing American citizenship to foreign nationals who travel here for the express purpose of giving birth on U.S. soil. This abuse of our immigration system also raises serious national security concerns, particularly given the number of birth tourists traveling from adversarial nations like China and Russia," the House GOP firebrand said.

His panel's Sept. 1 hearing is also expected to feature testimony from Dr. Steve Camarota of the Center for Immigration Studies. The medical director and owner of a company called International Maternity Services, Dr. Julio César Novoa, was also invited.

Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., chairman of the House Oversight and Accountability Committee, told "Fox & Friends Weekend" that he had sent letters to the leaders of several government agencies seeking information related to the mysterious deaths and disappearances of scientists in recent years. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
TEXAS GOV ABBOTT SIGNS EXECUTIVE ORDER CRACKING DOWN ON 'BIRTH TOURISM,’ SAYS US CITIZENSHIP NOT FOR SALE
Gill's new task force, which was founded this year, has largely focused on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) efforts across various sectors of American life.

He's held hearings on whether the Smithsonian's teaching of U.S. history involved overly ideological and political leanings, and whether DEI plays a role in running the American Bar Association (ABA).

Birth tourism is the colloquial term for the general practice of foreign nationals coming to the U.S. on temporary visas for the purpose of having a child who then automatically becomes an American citizen.

President Donald Trump targeted birth tourism in a recent executive order after the Supreme Court struck down his efforts to curb birthright citizenship writ large. He also signed an order banning specific categories, such as children born to foreign government workers, from automatically getting U.S. citizenship.
Have My Baby in Miami is just one company that appears to make it more accessible for foreigners to give birth in the U.S. Its website and social media pages appeared to be disabled as of Thursday.

But a YouTube page that appears to be associated with the business states, "Many people have questions about how to have a child in the United States, and we can help clarify how to deliver in Miami, how to live in the United States during your pregnancy, how to have a baby in the United States, how much it costs to deliver in the United States and how to go through pregnancy in the United States."
"Children who are born in the United States, with rare exceptions, have US citizenship," the summary states.
President Donald Trump in the Oval Office after signing an executive order on Aug. 10, 2026. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
An October 2025 article by Local 10 in Florida appears to have obtained information from the now-deleted pages, including that the company reportedly touted that it helped deliver 2,000 babies.
It's not yet clear if Lorentz will appear. But defying a congressional subpoena could risk criminal charges.

Fox News Digital reached out to his lawyer for comment.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: Federal judge again blocks Trump's mail ballot order just before midterms
summary: President Donald Trump's mail-in voting executive order faces a new two-week block from a federal judge as voters prepare for the midterm elections.
story: Fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn joins 'Fox & Friends' to analyze lawsuits filed by 24 states and Washington, D.C. against the United States Postal Service regarding mail-in voting rules. Urbahn breaks down the Supreme Court decision and details agency rules requiring barcodes on mail-in ballots.

A federal judge on Thursday again blocked President Donald Trump's executive order limiting mail-in voting, halting the directive, at least for now, for a second time with only about a week before the first mail ballots are expected to be sent out for the upcoming midterm elections.
U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani issued a 14-day temporary restraining order blocking enforcement of the new U.S. Postal Service rule implementing the order.

The ruling is likely to be quickly appealed and could soon make its way back to the Supreme Court, days after the nation's highest court handed down a procedural decision that allowed the administration to move forward.

Thursday's ruling comes after Democrats and voting rights groups refiled their lawsuits to comply with the recent Supreme Court decision. The high court did not address the legality of Trump’s order, only finding that Talwani had acted too soon.
JACKSON RIPS INTO SUPREME COURT COLLEAGUES' 'SERIOUS LEGAL ERROR' ON TRUMP MAIL-IN VOTING ORDER
A federal judge again blocked President Donald Trump's executive order limiting mail-in voting. (Caroline Brehman/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, File)
The administration has now issued a formal rule governing how states must prepare and submit mail ballots for USPS acceptance, effectively taking the legal fight back to square one.

The case will have a significant impact on November's midterms, as nearly one-third of Americans vote by mail and election officials argue there is not enough time to amend their systems to comply with the new directives.
The Postal Service said it will not accept outbound mail ballots if states do not submit required recipient information through its portal and meet the rule’s envelope and barcode requirements.

"Plaintiff states have neither time nor funds to design new mail ballots, seek approval of the new designs, order production of mail ballots, update their own election management systems, train election officials to use the USPS portal and upload citizen data to the portal, all before the midterms," Talwani wrote in Thursday's ruling.
A hearing in the case is scheduled for Sept. 3.
USPS WOULDN'T DELIVER BALLOTS IN STATES THAT REFUSE TO FORK OVER MAIL-IN VOTER INFO UNDER PROPOSED RULE
U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani ruled that the Trump administration cannot enforce the order for two weeks. (REUTERS/Evan Vucci)

Democrats and voting rights groups argue that the Postal Service rule and Trump’s order are unconstitutional. They say the Constitution grants states, as well as Congress in some cases, the authority to establish election rules, noting that the president and Postal Service do not have that power. USPS, however, says the rule does not determine voter eligibility or compare submissions with state voter rolls, and that states retain control over who may vote by mail.

"This rule is a clear attempt by the federal government to interfere in elections it has no power to control. Today, a federal court halted it before this administration could wreak havoc on our elections," New York Attorney General Letitia James, one of two dozen Democrat attorneys general who filed one of the lawsuits, said in a statement.
Trump’s first executive order, which was issued last year, was blocked on those grounds.

The order attempted to change election procedures, including by requiring additional physical documentation to register to vote, such as a U.S. passport, a REAL ID or military ID indicating U.S. citizenship or a government-issued photo ID accompanied by proof of citizenship.

Trump has long criticized mail-in voting, which he falsely attributes to his 2020 election loss to former President Joe Biden. But Trump himself uses mail-in voting to cast his ballot as a registered voter in Florida.
FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FROM RESTRICTING MAIL-IN BALLOTS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

The case will have a significant impact on November's midterms, as nearly one-third of Americans vote by mail and election officials argue there is not enough time to amend their systems. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

According to a 2025 report by the Brookings Institution, mail-in voting fraud was recorded in only about four cases out of every 10 million mail ballots cast, contradicting claims by Trump and his allies that election fraud is widespread. The analysis covered general elections from 2016 through 2022 and relied in part on a database that its source says is not comprehensive.
Trump issued the executive order targeting mail-in voting in March, leading to legal challenges.

In a separate case, a federal judge in Washington declined earlier this year to block the order at that stage, finding the challenge premature because the administration had not yet implemented the directive.
The Supreme Court struck down one of those holds earlier this week.

Talwani removed the second injunction a short time later. The plaintiffs then refiled their challenges, pointing to the Postal Service’s publishing of its final rule, in an effort to build a stronger case.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Fox News AI Newsletter: The industry sparking blue-collar jobs boom
summary: Stay up to date on the latest AI technology advancements and learn about the challenges and opportunities AI presents now and for the future.
story: The AI boom is driving a massive infrastructure buildout across the U.S., creating new opportunities for skilled workers as demand for data centers and chip plants surges, according to Cole Renken, general manager of Merlo America.
IN TODAY’S NEWSLETTER:
- One of the world's hottest industries is sparking a blue-collar jobs boom
- From Netflix to GPS: 10 ways this hidden tech infrastructure quietly powers modern life
- OpenAI, 100+ companies warn of coming surge in AI-powered cyberattacks, call for global defense push

The boom is creating demand for electricians, plumbers, heavy-equipment operators and other skilled tradespeople needed to build and maintain the infrastructure powering the technology. (Mark Wilson/Getty Images)

HARD HAT HYPE: The race to build the infrastructure behind artificial intelligence is creating a new boom for America's blue-collar workforce, as construction firms scramble to fill jobs building data centers, power systems and the facilities that keep the technology running.

HIDDEN HARDWARE: Data centers are the hidden infrastructure behind much of modern life, powering everything from the apps on your phone and the shows you stream to online shopping, banking and artificial intelligence.

DIGITAL DEFENSE: OpenAI released a letter Thursday warning that within months, artifical intelligence (AI) models could become powerful enough to allow bad actors to launch increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks on hospitals, water treatment plants and other critical infrastructure.

BEYOND THE GRID: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said Wednesday that solar-powered facilities in space could tap the sun’s energy without competing for the land, water and grid capacity required by sprawling data centers proposed across the country.

BIG BROTHER: Automatic license plate reader (ALPR) companies have been brought under scrutiny by lawmakers in Washington as privacy hawks warn that the growing sophistication of artificial intelligence technology is testing the bounds of what ALPR devices can legally learn about drivers on the road.

COST CRUNCH: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang defended his decision to "rip the Band-Aid off" on the company’s gross margins as the chip giant continues to power some of the world’s most advanced artificial intelligence models.

OPINION: Data centers have gone from a niche policy issue to one of the most controversial topics of the midterm elections. Fewer than 30% of Americans support a data center being built in their community and the reason why is simple; the industry forgot about consumers.
AI apps Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini. (Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

DIGITAL DOSSIER: AI companies are giving their assistants more ways to remember what you tell them. In some cases, AI can also draw from activity beyond a single conversation. That raises a bigger privacy question. What happens when an AI assistant can build a more detailed understanding of you over time?

MONEY TALKS: There’s an ugly political fight brewing in the Lone Star State over data centers, and both candidates running for Senate are racing each other to unveil their plans to slow the AI boom in Texas.
OPINION: The progressive left is working hard to derail America’s AI dominance by blocking data center construction. So is China.

DOUBLE-EDGED AI: Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates warned that the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) will present major challenges as it reshapes industries and work, suggesting that it could be helpful to explore ways to reserve work in certain areas for humans to ease the transition.
ROOFTOP REVELATIONS: AI could potentially be the wealth-of-knowledge generator that places practical expertise directly in the hands of young people failed by the current systems.

'AMERICA MUST LEAD': Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., on Saturday dismissed "AI doomsdaying," warning that China benefits from "overreaction" by the United States as the two countries compete for dominance in artificial intelligence.

title: Chinese hackers target NASA and key US agencies, DOJ alleges
summary: The FBI and Justice Department seized domains tied to QScan and QTRouter, tools allegedly used by China-linked hackers to breach NASA and other agencies.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Some cyberattacks start with a suspicious email. Others begin somewhere you would probably never think to look. It could be an old router in someone's home. Maybe it is a forgotten security camera that still connects to the internet. Hackers can compromise vulnerable connected devices and use them to disguise where an attack really comes from.
That tactic played a role in a China-linked hacking operation that U.S. authorities say took aim at some of America's most sensitive networks.

On Aug. 26, the Justice Department and FBI confirmed intrusion attempts since 2018 against NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Justice Department and the U.S. Senate. Other targets included the Department of Energy, Department of Health and Human Services and National Institutes of Health.
FBI WRAPS UP CYBERCRIME OPERATION TARGETING GLOBAL NETWORKS PREYING ON AMERICANS

Four unnamed companies in the United States and South Korea were reportedly targeted as well. The names behind the operation sound like something from an IT department: QScan and QTRouter. Yet what these tools allegedly did should get your attention.
Here is how the hacking operation worked, how authorities shut it down and what you can do to keep your own connected devices from becoming part of an attacker's network.

No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.
Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.
China-linked hackers used shared network infrastructure to disguise malicious traffic and make attacks harder to trace (Donato Fasano/Getty Images)
Chinese hackers breached NASA and other US targets

According to the Justice Department, a Chinese state-sponsored group known as QTFY created and operated QScan and QTRouter. Federal officials say the group worked for the China-based Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Company. The Justice Department alleges that the company offered hacking services to paying customers, including China's Ministry of State Security and People's Liberation Army.

Authorities say QTFY infrastructure has been used to compromise critical infrastructure and other sensitive networks since at least 2018. Court documents also describe targets that included hospitals, telecommunications providers, financial institutions and defense contractors.
CyberGuy reached out to NASA about the Justice Department's announcement.

"NASA is committed to the cybersecurity and the protection of our systems," NASA spokesperson Jennifer Dooren said. "We work closely with our federal partners, including the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, to quickly address identified vulnerabilities. We continuously collaborate with software partners and actively monitor and assess our networks, software and data for potential risks.

"For security reasons, NASA does not comment on specific reports of potential vulnerabilities or incidents. For additional information regarding this matter, please contact the Department of Justice."
Flight controllers monitor the Artemis II Orion spacecraft from the White Flight Control Room at the NASA Johnson Space Center on April 8, 2026, in Houston, Texas.  (Getty Images)
We also reached out to the Chinese Embassy in Washington about the Justice Department's allegations.

"I am not aware of the specifics you mentioned," an embassy spokesperson told CyberGuy. "China is a firm defender of cybersecurity. The Chinese government firmly opposes and combats all forms of cyberattacks in accordance with the law. We urge the U.S. side to stop using cybersecurity issues to smear or discredit China.

"China firmly opposes the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security and using it as a pretext to impose discriminatory restrictions on Chinese companies and will firmly safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies."

After we sent the embassy the specific Justice Department release outlining the allegations involving QScan and QTRouter, the embassy told CyberGuy it had "no further information to add at the moment."

China has repeatedly denied accusations that it sponsors malicious cyber activity. What stands out here is the infrastructure behind the attacks. Federal investigators describe a system designed to find vulnerable devices and then use some of those devices to help hide malicious activity.
How QScan and QTRouter worked

QScan handled the hunting. The Justice Department says the platform scanned for vulnerable systems and automatically infected thousands of internet-of-things devices around the world. Those compromised devices could then become part of QTRouter.

QTRouter served as what investigators call an obfuscation network. In everyday language, it helped conceal where an attack really came from. The network included compromised IoT devices along with commercial proxy devices and leased virtual private servers.

Attackers could route malicious communications through that infrastructure. As a result, the activity could appear to originate outside China or even near the network being targeted. That creates a serious challenge for security teams trying to track an attacker.

Think about all the internet-connected equipment people rarely touch after setting it up. A router might sit in the corner for years. A security camera could keep running long after its manufacturer stops releasing updates. Hackers pay attention to forgotten devices because those devices can give them somewhere to hide.
FBI Director Kash Patel emphasized how the infrastructure helped conceal the attackers.
"These tools were used by PRC cyber actors to hide the origin of their attacks," Patel said.
TRUMP PLAN TAPS US FIRMS TO FIGHT FOREIGN CYBERCRIME
Why your connected devices enter the picture

You were probably nowhere near the hackers' list of targets. NASA and the Federal Reserve operate in a very different security world from your living room. However, the infrastructure behind these attacks creates a connection to everyday technology.

QScan allegedly infected IoT devices and pulled them into a larger network. Those compromised devices then helped disguise malicious traffic. So, an insecure connected device can become useful to an attacker even when the attacker has little interest in its owner.

You may never see a ransom note. Your smart device could continue working normally. Yet vulnerable equipment can potentially provide infrastructure for malicious activity happening somewhere else. That is one reason I keep telling you to pay attention to the router sitting behind the couch.
How federal agents pulled the plug

The Justice Department obtained court authorization to seize domains used by QScan and QTRouter. Those domains turned out to be a critical weakness. Federal officials say the domains were hard-coded into the malware and used for essential functions, including communication and authentication. Once authorities seized them, the Justice Department says QScan and QTRouter became inoperable. Investigators went after infrastructure that the hacking platforms needed to work.

Black Lotus Labs says targeting shared infrastructure like this can damage more than one cyber operation at a time. Its researchers wrote that "taking down a single quartermaster's obfuscation network systematically degrades the capabilities of multiple active threat campaigns at once."

Black Lotus Labs also says it shared threat intelligence with U.S. government agencies about emerging risks and null-routed traffic to known infrastructure used by the operators. The researchers describe the operation as a kind of cyber "quartermaster," providing shared reconnaissance, routing and concealment infrastructure that multiple China-linked threat actors could use. That approach has become a recurring part of the U.S. response to China-linked cyber operations.
This follows years of China-linked hacking warnings

The latest operation follows several previous federal efforts targeting Chinese hacking groups. In 2025, the FBI removed PlugX surveillance malware from more than 4,000 U.S. computers infected by the China-sponsored Mustang Panda group. In 2024, federal agents disabled a botnet made up of hundreds of thousands of infected IoT devices associated with Flax Typhoon.

The FBI previously disrupted another botnet used by Volt Typhoon to conceal attacks targeting U.S. and foreign critical infrastructure. CyberGuy has also reported on Salt Typhoon, the China-linked hacking campaign that penetrated major American telecommunications networks. These operations work differently. However, they show how valuable compromised infrastructure can become for state-backed hackers.
Vulnerable smart home devices such as security cameras can become useful to attackers if they are left unpatched or poorly secured. (kazakova0684/Getty Images)
How to protect your router and connected devices
You cannot personally stop a nation-state hacking operation. However, you can make your own devices much harder for attackers to compromise or use as part of their infrastructure.

Your router runs software called firmware, and security fixes are often delivered through firmware updates. Open your router's app or administration page and check for updates. If your router supports automatic updates, turn them on.

An old router can keep working long after the manufacturer stops protecting it. Check your router's model number on the manufacturer's website to see whether it still receives firmware and security updates. If it has reached the end of its life, replace it with a supported model. The FBI has previously warned that cybercriminals actively exploit aging routers that no longer receive security patches.

Do not leave the router's administrator account using its original or default password. Create a long, strong and unique password that you have never used for another account. A password manager can help you generate and securely store it. If your router offers two-factor authentication (2FA) for administrator access, turn it on.

Your Wi-Fi network should also have its own strong, unique password. Avoid names, addresses, phone numbers or other information someone could easily guess. Do not reuse the password you use to administer the router.

Check your router's wireless security settings. WPA3-Personal offers stronger protection and should be your first choice when your router and devices support it. If WPA3 causes compatibility problems with older devices, use WPA2-Personal with AES or a WPA2/WPA3 compatibility mode. Avoid older WEP and WPA security.

Most people have no reason to change their router settings while away from home. Look for a setting called Remote Management, Remote Administration or WAN Access. Disable it unless you specifically need it. The FBI has specifically warned that exposed remote administration can give attackers another way to target vulnerable routers.

Wi-Fi Protected Setup, or WPS, can make connecting devices easier. However, most people do not need to leave it enabled after setup. Also check Universal Plug and Play, or UPnP. It allows devices to automatically request network access and open connections through your router. If none of your devices require it, turning UPnP off can reduce unnecessary exposure.
Most routers include a built-in firewall. Check your router settings and make sure the firewall remains enabled. Avoid changing advanced firewall settings unless you understand what they control.

If your router supports a guest network or dedicated IoT network, consider putting security cameras, smart plugs, speakers and other connected gadgets there. Separating those devices from the laptops and phones where you keep sensitive information can limit an attacker's reach if one smart device gets compromised.

Your router is only one piece of the network. Check security cameras, doorbells, smart TVs and other connected devices for software or firmware updates. Enable automatic updates when available. If a smart device has reached the end of its support life and no longer receives security fixes, consider replacing it.
Some cameras, smart home hubs and other IoT gear come with preset administrator credentials. Change those passwords during setup. Use a unique password for each important device or account.

Open your router's app or administration page and look at its list of connected devices. Make sure you recognize what is there. If you see a device you cannot identify, investigate it. Change your Wi-Fi password if necessary and reconnect only the devices you trust.

An old security camera in the garage or smart plug sitting in a drawer can still be connected to your network. Remove devices you no longer use from your Wi-Fi. Disconnect or reset the hardware before getting rid of it.

Install operating system and security updates on your computers, phones and tablets as soon as practical. Strong antivirus software can also help detect malware, malicious downloads and dangerous links before they create another route into your devices. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Unexpected settings changes, unfamiliar devices appearing on your network, repeated connectivity problems or unusual router behavior deserve attention. If something looks wrong, reboot the router and check its settings for changes you did not make. If suspicious activity continues, contact your internet provider or router manufacturer. You may need to factory-reset the router and set it up again using trusted settings.
Kurt's key takeaways

What catches my attention here is how much effort went into hiding the origin of these attacks. The hackers allegedly built infrastructure that could scan for vulnerable devices, compromise them and then use those devices as cover. Federal agents eventually found a pressure point by seizing domains the malware needed to operate. That is a significant win. Still, one disruption leaves a much larger cyber fight in place.

State-backed groups keep looking for vulnerable infrastructure because forgotten connected devices are everywhere. Your router may seem like nothing more than a box keeping Netflix running and your phone online. To an attacker, an unpatched device can have an entirely different purpose. For you, the lesson is surprisingly practical.

That router you have ignored for five years deserves a checkup. The same goes for old smart home gear that still connects to the internet. If a manufacturer stopped protecting a device, think carefully about whether you want to keep giving it access to your network.
Do you think the U.S. is doing enough to stop China-backed hackers from targeting American networks and using vulnerable devices to cover their tracks? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Uber Eats drone delivery could soon reach your home
summary: Uber Eats drone delivery launches later this year through a Zipline partnership, starting in Dallas and Houston with a goal of one million daily flights.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Your next Uber Eats order could arrive without a car pulling up outside your home. Uber Eats drone delivery is moving closer to everyday life through a new partnership with Zipline, one of the most established names in autonomous delivery.

Uber and Zipline announced the deal earlier this month. The companies say the first deliveries will begin later this year in existing Zipline markets. From there, they plan to expand into dozens of U.S. cities. Their long-term target is huge: 1 million drone deliveries per day by the end of 2029.

That does not mean a drone will show up with your meal tomorrow. The rollout will start in markets where Zipline already operates, including Dallas and Houston, before expanding to additional areas. Zipline already has commercial delivery systems operating in the U.S., which gives this partnership a running start. Here's how the system works and what you could expect if drone delivery reaches your neighborhood.
THIS SATURDAY! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats

Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.
Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.
PAPA JOHNS DRONE DELIVERY SKIPS THE PIZZA
Zipline’s autonomous delivery system could soon bring Uber Eats orders directly to customers in select U.S. markets. (Zipline)
How Uber Eats drone delivery with Zipline will work

The experience should eventually feel much like placing any other Uber Eats order. The companies say eligible Uber Eats customers will have the option to receive their orders through Zipline when the service launches later this year. Today, customers in Zipline's existing U.S. service areas can download the Zipline app, enter their address and browse available restaurants and stores. Once someone places an order, the business prepares it and loads it into Zipline's autonomous delivery system.

Zipline handles the flight with its Platform 2 system, also called P2. The electric aircraft can carry up to 8 pounds and has a 10-mile service radius. Zipline says the system can make some 10-mile deliveries in about 10 minutes. Its current fact sheet lists a cruise speed of about 70 mph. When the aircraft reaches the delivery location, it hovers around 300 feet above the ground. A smaller delivery unit descends on a tether, steers toward the selected drop-off spot and gently places the order on the ground.

The delivery unit then returns to the aircraft, and the drone flies back to recharge for its next order. Zipline told CyberGuy that the entire process happens autonomously. So you do not need a drone landing pad next to the house. Zipline can place deliveries in a yard or another approved location while the larger aircraft remains overhead.
Zipline already delivers to real homes

According to the joint announcement, Zipline has completed more than 2.7 million commercial deliveries. Its aircraft have flown more than 135 million autonomous commercial miles. Zipline also says it now makes a delivery somewhere in the world every 20 seconds. In the U.S., its P2 home delivery system has already been operating with Walmart and restaurant partners. Zipline's fact sheet says the service launched in Pea Ridge, Arkansas and more than 20 communities around Dallas-Fort Worth.

The company has been expanding quickly as well. In July, Zipline said the number of businesses offering delivery through its app had grown 13 times during the first half of 2026. Roughly 70% of its flights were taking place in the United States at that point.

CyberGuy recently looked at another side of that expansion when Zipline began carrying eligible prescriptions to Cleveland Clinic patients. The drone stays overhead while a tethered unit lowers the medication to the patient's property.
Your dinner could spend less time in traffic

The obvious appeal is speed. A drone can take a more direct path than a car crawling through traffic. It also avoids the hunt for parking near a busy restaurant. Zipline says its P2 system can make some 10-mile trips in about 10 minutes.

Of course, that does not mean every meal reaches your house 10 minutes after you tap Place order. The restaurant still needs to prepare the food. Severe weather or certain flight conditions could still affect whether a drone can complete a delivery. Local flight conditions may also change what the system can do. Still, cutting time on the road could help your dinner spend less time getting cold in the back seat of a car.
MISSOURI TESTS MEDICAL DRONES TO SPEED UP RURAL HEALTH CARE
Zipline says its Platform 2 drones can carry up to 8 pounds and complete some 10-mile deliveries in about 10 minutes. (Zipline)
Uber wants several ways to deliver your order

The Zipline deal also reveals a bigger part of Uber's strategy. Uber says it is building a delivery network that combines human couriers with autonomous technology. Depending on the trip, that technology could include a sidewalk robot or a drone. We have already seen pieces of this plan. Uber Eats uses autonomous sidewalk robots in some markets. CyberGuy previously looked at how those machines navigate streets and bring food directly to customers.

Uber also invested in drone company Flytrex in 2025. At the time, Uber called that its first investment in drone delivery technology. Now Zipline joins the picture. That suggests Uber wants the Uber Eats app to become the layer connecting customers with different delivery systems. A drone may make sense for one neighborhood. A robot may work better somewhere else. You may eventually care less about what carries your dinner and more about which option gets it there faster.
What about all that drone noise?

Noise could be one of the first things people notice when drone delivery arrives in their neighborhood. One delivery overhead may be easy to ignore. Regular flights throughout the day could be another story. Zipline says it has spent years working to make its aircraft quieter. The company says its drones now typically fly at least 300 feet above the ground. During delivery, the aircraft stays high while a smaller unit lowers the order on a tether.

Zipline says the full delivery takes about 90 seconds. Flying higher helps reduce how much sound reaches people below. Still, the real question is how noticeable these drones will be once they become part of everyday neighborhood traffic.
Safety could determine how fast drones spread

A delivery service flying over homes has a much higher bar than the hobby drone someone sends up at the park. Zipline's aircraft fly autonomously with onboard systems that help them understand their surroundings. The company has also received FAA approval for certain beyond visual line of sight, or BVLOS, operations. That allows approved flights without requiring ground observers to watch the aircraft along the entire route.

Zipline says it put P2 through extensive testing before launching home deliveries. That included tens of millions of simulated flights and more than 150,000 deliveries at test facilities. However, regulatory approval does not automatically mean drone delivery can appear everywhere. The companies still need the right operating area and infrastructure before a neighborhood can participate.
During delivery, the main aircraft stays overhead while a smaller tethered unit lowers the order to an approved drop-off spot. (Zipline)
Uber is putting money behind the idea

Uber is also making a strategic investment in Zipline as part of the agreement. The companies have not disclosed the size of that investment in their official announcement. However, they describe the relationship as a long-term effort to accelerate drone delivery across the U.S.

Zipline itself has plenty of money riding on this expansion. Earlier this year, the company announced that it had raised more than $600 million and reached a valuation of $7.6 billion. The companies now have a very ambitious benchmark in front of them. Reaching one million drone deliveries every day by the end of 2029 would require far more aircraft and participating businesses. The network would also need to reach many more homes. CyberGuy reached out to both Uber and Zipline for comment, but neither company responded before our deadline.
What this means to you

Most Uber Eats orders will continue arriving the familiar way for now. However, if you live in an area where Zipline already operates, watch the Uber Eats app later this year. The companies say qualifying customers will eventually have the option to receive an order by drone.

Before selecting drone delivery, pay attention to the drop-off location. You should also check what happens when weather prevents a flight. Then look closely at the price. Uber and Zipline have yet to explain whether customers will pay an additional fee for the drone option.

If the cost stays reasonable, speed could become the selling point. Waiting for dinner feels a lot longer when your phone says a drone could get it there in minutes. The larger change may happen almost without us noticing. Once people stop thinking of drone delivery as unusual, choosing one could eventually feel as routine as selecting a faster delivery window today.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've watched drone delivery go from something that felt years away to something people are actually starting to use. What jumps out to me here is how quickly Uber could help push it into the mainstream. Millions of people already know how to order dinner through Uber Eats, while Zipline already has drones making real deliveries. Put those two pieces together and this starts to feel a lot closer to everyday life. Of course, people will have questions once these drones start showing up over their neighborhoods. How much noise will they make? Will the delivery really be faster? And how much extra will Uber charge for the convenience? For me, that last part could be the dealbreaker. If a drone can get my food to me noticeably faster without adding a hefty fee or becoming a neighborhood nuisance, I can see a lot of people giving it a try. The real test will come when that drone delivery option actually pops up on your phone, and you have to decide whether you want dinner coming by road or through the sky.
Would you choose a drone if it could get your Uber Eats order to your door faster, or would you rather keep delivery traffic on the ground? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Why August is the most dangerous month to ignore your data
summary: Medicare Open Enrollment scams start with data broker targeting months before October. Learn why August is the time to remove your personal info.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Medicare Open Enrollment doesn't start until Oct. 15. So why am I telling you to worry about this in August? Because by the time Oct. 15 arrives, scammers aren't starting their work. They're finishing it.

The scam calls you may hear this fall, including fake Medicare card offers and urgent Social Security warnings, are only the final step. Scammers often build their target lists long before they make contact. Here is how that targeting process works and what you can do now to make yourself and your family harder to scam.

Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.
Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.
DR OZ WARNS MEDICARE SCAMMERS ARE STEALING BILLIONS — AND YOUR PERSONAL INFORMATION COULD BE NEXT

Medicare Open Enrollment begins Oct. 15, giving scammers a predictable window to target older Americans with fake benefit calls, texts and messages. (Sara Diggins/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)
The dates that shape fall benefit scams
Two major dates put Medicare and Social Security on the minds of millions of Americans each fall.

Medicare Open Enrollment begins on Oct. 15 and runs through Dec. 7. During that period, people can review their coverage and make certain changes that generally take effect Jan. 1. That also means beneficiaries expect to receive plan information, advertisements and calls about their coverage.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics currently plans to release September 2026 inflation data on Oct. 14. That release will complete the third-quarter CPI-W figures used to calculate the 2027 Social Security COLA. The Social Security Administration says the next COLA will be announced in October 2026. Based on the current schedule, the announcement is expected on Oct. 14. The Senior Citizens League currently projects a 3.8% increase for 2027. That estimate has been generating headlines, but it isn't the official number. The final percentage will depend on inflation data for July, August and September. Scammers do not have to guess when people will be thinking about benefits. These dates are public and repeat every year.
The part that happens before the phone rings

Here's what almost nobody thinks about. A scam call often comes near the end of the process, not the beginning. Before a fraudster dials, someone has to decide whom to target. Consumer lists can help make that decision. The Justice Department has already shown in court how marketing data can end up in the hands of scammers.

Epsilon Data Management maintained a database covering roughly 100 million American households. Two former employees, Robert Reger and David Lytle, spent about a decade selling targeted consumer lists to people running fraud schemes. Epsilon used consumer data and algorithms to identify people who were likely to respond to certain offers. One fraudster bought nearly 100 lists and used them to defraud more than 218,000 victims of over $23.7 million. Epsilon paid $150 million to resolve the case. That included $22.5 million in criminal penalties and $127.5 million for victim compensation. In September 2024, a federal court sentenced Reger to 120 months in prison and Lytle to 48 months.

Epsilon was not alone. KBM Group employees sold consumer data to clients involved in fraudulent mass-mailing schemes. The company entered into an agreement requiring it to pay $33.5 million for victim compensation and an $8.5 million criminal fine. Macromark pleaded guilty to knowingly supplying lists of potential victims to fraudulent mass mailers. Many of the victims were older and vulnerable. The company agreed to pay $1 million in fines and forfeiture. These companies did not operate from hidden corners of the dark web. They were established marketing businesses with employees, clients and offices.

Legitimate marketing companies still sell consumer lists online. Vendors advertise databases of Americans age 65 and older, along with lists created specifically for businesses that want to contact people approaching their 65th birthday. Buyers can often filter those lists by age, location, income, homeownership and other demographic details. Some products also include names, mailing addresses, phone numbers, email addresses and estimated home values. Selling a marketing list does not automatically make the vendor or buyer a scammer. However, the market shows how easily someone can identify and contact a narrow group of older Americans. That is why August and September matter. The personal data already exists, the enrollment dates are public and anyone planning a fall fraud campaign can begin researching potential targets before the calls start.
WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME
Removing personal information from data broker sites before fall can reduce the details criminals may use to make impersonation scams sound legitimate. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Where your data broker profile comes in

A purchased list gets a scammer a name, an age and an address. That alone makes for a generic call. What turns a generic call into a convincing one is everything else that's sitting on people-search sites like Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified and Intelius. As I've written before, those profiles routinely include address history, relatives' names and financial signals like property ownership and estimated home value. That's the difference between "Hello, I'm calling about your Medicare benefits" and "Hi Mr. Patterson, I'm calling about the plan at your address on Maple Street. Is your wife Linda still on the same coverage?" One of those calls gets hung up on. The other one gets answered.

You can run a quick free scan of how exposed you are online to get a better understanding of your data exposure. If it shows details you never consented to publishing, you'll be able to take action and get them removed. Get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web: CyberGuy.com.
What the numbers actually show

A data removal service research team analyzed FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center data and found that 72% of the crimes reported by Americans over 60 in 2024 were facilitated or made worse by victims' personal data being available online. That's roughly 82,000 complaints out of 113,906. Those data-facilitated crimes accounted for $4.2 billion of the $4.9 billion older Americans reported losing that year. The average victim lost about $33,200. And this problem is growing, not shrinking. Reported elder fraud victims rose 45% in a single year. What the fall adds isn't a new kind of crime. It's a schedule.

The Federal Trade Commission puts it plainly: "Every year, scammers get more active around Medicare Open Enrollment Period, trying to get your money, information or both." The agency warns that callers pose as Medicare representatives, pressure people about a "new" or "updated" Medicare card, and spoof caller ID so the call appears to come from an official number.

Meanwhile, the Social Security version writes itself. Every October, a wave of "Claim Your COLA" scams tells retirees they have to take action to receive their increase or they'll lose it. They don't. The adjustment is automatic. But by October, that call arrives sounding perfectly timed, because it is.
'I'll worry about this when the calls actually start'

That's the natural reaction. October feels like the real deadline. Why act now? Because the targeting gets locked in before the calls do. If your name, age, address, relatives and financial profile are sitting on broker sites this month, they're available to be compiled, sorted and resold well before anyone picks up a phone in October.

And removal isn't instant. Brokers have to process opt-out requests, and they re-list information on a rolling basis, which means the process works best when you start it early and let it run. Beginning in August means you're being scrubbed from the pipeline while it's still being assembled. Beginning in November means you're filing paperwork while the calls are already coming in. The point isn't to react faster. It's to be a worse target before anyone goes looking.
How to get ahead of the cycle now
These steps can help reduce the personal information scammers may use and prepare your family before fall fraud attempts begin.
Go to Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified or a similar site and look up your own name. See exactly what a caller would see this month, before they do.
If you have older relatives, their profiles are the ones worth the most to a scammer. An August check-in beats an October warning.
WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES
Personal details available through data brokers and people-search sites can help criminals tailor scams involving Medicare, Social Security and other benefits. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Every major broker is required to honor removal requests. The catch: there are hundreds of them, each with its own process, and they re-list your information regularly. Starting now gives the process time to work before the fall surge.

Removing your information from data brokers one site at a time can take hours. A reputable automated data removal service can submit opt-out requests on your behalf and continue checking participating sites in case your information reappears.

Some services also accept custom removal requests for people-search sites and other websites that publish personal details. Before signing up, compare the number of brokers covered, how often the service checks for new listings, whether it handles custom requests and whether independent experts have reviewed its privacy and security practices.

A family plan may offer better value when you want to protect parents, children or other members of your household. No service can remove every piece of information from the internet, but ongoing removals can reduce the personal details scammers may use to create convincing calls, messages or emails.
Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
Agree on a code word with elderly parents or relatives today, while there's no pressure. It's a much easier conversation in August than in the middle of a panicked phone call in November.

If your bank still verifies you with "mother's maiden name" or "city you were born in," that information is likely already on a broker profile. Switch to answers that aren't true and store them in a password manager.
Kurt's key takeaways

Medicare Open Enrollment runs from Oct. 15 through Dec. 7, while the 2027 Social Security COLA is expected to be announced on Oct. 14. Those public dates give scammers predictable events to reference in calls, texts and letters. Justice Department cases involving Epsilon, KBM Group and Macromark show that consumer information has been sold to fraud operations and used to identify older or vulnerable targets. The FBI received 201,266 complaints from people 60 and older in 2025, with reported losses reaching $7.748 billion. Incogni separately estimated that exposed personal information may have facilitated or worsened 72% of the 2024 crime categories it analyzed. Removing information from people-search sites cannot prevent every scam. However, reducing exposed details can make it harder for a criminal to create a convincing personal story. Social Security COLA increases are automatic. Medicare cards are mailed automatically and are free. Anyone demanding information or payment to activate either one should be treated as a potential scammer. You still have time before this year's open enrollment period begins. title: Survivor's Christian Hubicki marvels at China's robotics games records: 'Willing to break the robots to do it'
summary: The World Humanoid Robot Games' crashes show how far the technology still needs to go to be useful, "Survivor" reality TV star and robotics scientist Christian Hubicki says.
story: Florida State robotics professor Christian Hubicki, a star from reality TV's "Survivor," breaks down why humanoid robots can now outrun Usain Bolt — but still lack the intelligence to reliably think, react and stop.

The World Humanoid Robot Games made headlines this week, putting robotics experts in awe and leaving social media scrollers laughing at the robots’ histrionics, viral stumbles, and dramatic crashes and burns.

In its second year, it is making an annual event out of stress-testing the limits of technological advancement, while allaying fears to the public that SkyNet is not on the verge of taking over the world.

"The goal of this event really was to show how fast we can get robots to go," Christian Hubicki, Florida State University mechanical-engineering professor and robotics lab director, told Fox News Digital on the final day of the five-day event. "What happens to them afterwards? Well, as we can see, it's a bit dramatic.
"They didn't care so much how they stopped. In fact, they had this big wall that they just smashed into."
LET'S LOOK BACK ON THE BEST MOMENTS (READ: CRASHES) FROM THE WORLD HUMANOID ROBOT GAMES

The robots might be running faster than Usain Bolt before they know how to stop, but the tech is still at the stage of standing up from a crawl, according to Hubicki, who is also known for being a past contestant on the CBS reality TV show "Survivor."

"They wanted to break the record, and they're willing to break the robots to do it," Hubicki said. "You can see robots are sparking, limbs are flying off. It's incredibly kinetic. It's like these things are almost like missiles flying at this wall. All to break the record."
The record broken was Bolt's 9.58 seconds in the 100-meter dash, but in a show of just how fast the robots can go and technology can advance, Saturday's 9.39 mark only lasted a few days.

A Chinese humanoid robot – Tiangong Ultra, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Centre – on the event's final day won the large-size robot 100-meter final at 8.64 seconds, almost a second faster than Bolt's human world-record time.
CHINESE MARATHON ROBOT FALLS, BREAK DANCES ITSELF TO PIECES

"This is a major milestone that people who work in specifically legged robotics, like I do, have wanted to see for a long time – just to prove that we could do this," Hubicki said. "So this is big deal. I watched this. This is incredible, how fast they get these robots to go.

"At the same time, we're not terribly surprised. We've known for a while that motors and gears and joints of robots could outperform people. We've known this. There have been papers specifically published that are titled, 'Why Robots Don't Outrun People Yet.' And the answer was we've just got to make them just a little bit smarter."
Artificial intelligence is helping, but the games also show how far the technology remains from reliable, practical use.
CHINESE HUMANOID ROBOT BREAKS USAIN BOLT'S 100M DASH RECORD AT 9.39 SECONDS

"There's still a lot of human intelligence built into how these things are moving around," Hubicki said. "They're being told exactly what to do, go forward, rotate around the course, right? The higher level intelligence, we would say, is still very limited. And you can see this in the other events as well.

"You can see when they're playing robot tennis – and by the way, I'm very impressed with what they've been able to accomplish – they had to have these sort of external cameras pointing out exactly where the ball is so they know where to hit the ball. And that's OK, it's work in progress," he said.
"There's still a lot of limited intelligence on the robots, but of course they are getting better."
As in human athletics, the 100 meters was one of the highlights of the Beijing games, underscoring advances in robot mobility, balance and control systems.
NEW AI BRAIN LETS ROBOTS MOVE LIKE HUMANS
Christian Hubicki made his name on reality TV's "Survivor," but he makes his living running a robotics research lab at Florida State University. (Todd Owyoung/NBC)

"The organizers of this event did a great job of highlighting specifically the types of tasks that Chinese robotics companies are great at doing, which are the athletic events," Hubicki said. "They focus a lot on robots that do these fantastic athletic stunts."

"And you might be wondering, couldn't robots already go faster than people? Well, yes, wheeled robots absolutely could," he explained. "We have had RC cars that outpace people for a very long time. But the challenge with humanoids has been coordinating all the motors, all the joints.

"We are so good at this as people, but thanks to the AI boom of the last handful of years, we figured out smarter and smarter ways to make robots coordinate their motion so they don't fall down while moving faster and faster, and squeeze out every last bit of performance that you can out of the motors – and that's why we're starting to see faster and faster robots."

The event, dubbed the "Robot Olympics," brought together more than 2,000 robots from 666 teams, most of them Chinese. Its 51 disciplines included sports contests as well as task-based challenges in simulated factories, restaurants, offices and emergency settings.
ROBOT SOCCER PLAYER DENTS WALL WITH TERRIFYING KICKS

"They are getting smarter," he said. "The challenge is to get them smarter in a way that is really practical for us. I mean, it's fun for me to watch a robot going Usain Bolt speeds down a runway, but it doesn't really help us too much. The real challenge is how can we get them to be reliable and practical to help us."
Step one was to make them run as fast as they can – and look good doing it – before they knew how to stop.
"Last year's robots looked a little stiff and uncoordinated," Niu, 34, told Reuters. "This year, they are much better. They are like healthy newborn babies growing up."
UNITREE G1 HUMANOID ROBOT ICE SKATES AND ROLLERBLADES
Eventually, the tech will require getting them to think for themselves about how to stop.

"The thing that's important to say about the smarts is it's a very specific kind of smarts – they're only figuring out how to coordinate their motion to the point where these robots, when they're running around, they don't even remember what happened a second ago," Hubicki said. "All they're looking at is like, 'Right now, what do I need to do to keep moving forward?'"

"And so I think it's important for people to realize that when we see something that kind of moves like a duck, quacks like a duck, like a person here, it's not actually thinking like a duck in this particular case – it's very purpose-built, specific intelligence to keep this thing running and boy does it go fast. It's incredible."
The kinetic robots will eventually have AI processing added in.
AI BUILDS VIRTUAL HOMES WHERE ROBOTS LEARN FROM THEIR MISTAKES

"The AI of these robots is so much simpler than what you would experience interacting with like a chatbot or Chat GPT," according to Hubicki. "It frankly doesn't need to. It would take too long on the computer to think as hard as those things. They just have to go quick, quick, quick, quick. So it's very simple. It's just saying, 'Hey, what's my pose? How fast am I moving? Where do I put my leg?' That's it."
The intelligence tech still is artificial and just not "reliable" yet, Hubicki warned, as anyone who has seen the "nonsense" AI can sometimes produce.

"You'll use some of these tools and it'll come up with something like, 'Wow, that's actually pretty brilliant,' and sometimes you're like, ‘Wait a second, that is nonsense,’ and it's only as good as you can verify," he said.

"That's why it's not a particularly good fit right now to put on a robot – not because it's going to be coming up with some kind diabolical scheme but it just doesn't understand reality in the same way that we do."
HUMANOID ROBOT SKIN SENSES PEOPLE BEFORE CONTACT
Hubicki pointed to a viral social media video of a humanoid robot that looked like it went rogue.

"We do see what happens when you put these robots in the real world," he said. "There was one of these humanoids, it just went and just kicked a kid in the stomach, and it didn't know the kid was there.

"It wasn't even using the cameras. It's just interacting in a complicated world it doesn't even understand. So that's where a lot of the work has to go in order to actually have robots be able to interact with us in a way that is useful and helpful. Otherwise, you know, it's just a bull in a china shop."

Recently, there was a New York Times report of Russia using AI-guided drones that killed three civilians in Ukraine, leading a Ukrainian military leader to warn that "we will be living in a 'Terminator' movie" before long.
HUMANOID ROBOT VIDEOS SHOW MACHINES LASHING OUT

"Certainly there's a lot of people, certainly governments are looking for all kinds of applications of AI and robotics, and that includes the battlefield," Hubicki said. "The war in Ukraine right now, it's a drone war. And I mean people talk about humanoid robots right now on the battlefield, there are unmanned aerial vehicles, little quadcopter drones that are just everywhere. And it's a brave new world.

"As much as these humanoids get a lot of headlines because they kind of hit us in a part of our brain where like, wow, that's a thing we can do, the robots can do that, there's a lot more practical and scary ways that robots are being used right here and right now."

title: Humanoid robot outruns Usain Bolt record as China races ahead
summary: X-Humanoid's TianGong Ultra ran 100 meters in 9.32 seconds at Beijing's World Humanoid Robot Games, beating last year's winner by more than half.
story: Kurt Knutsson, 'The CyberGuy', joins 'Fox & Friends' to showcase the World Humanoid Games in Beijing, China. Over 2,000 robots and 600 teams from 16 countries compete in athletic competitions including sprinting, boxing, and soccer. Knutsson discusses how the U.S.-China tech race is expanding into humanoid robotics as developers push the boundaries of artificial intelligence.

If your mental image of a humanoid robot still involves stiff knees and awkward demos, you may want to update it. A Chinese humanoid robot has now covered 100 meters faster than Usain Bolt's 9.58-second human world record. At the opening of Beijing's World Humanoid Robot Games, an X-Humanoid robot completed the 100-meter sprint in 9.39 seconds. Then the number dropped again.

X-Humanoid announced on Aug. 25 that TianGong Ultra ultimately posted a 9.32-second time during the competition. The company says its robots reset the mark several times during roughly two hours of racing. Before anybody starts rewriting the Olympic record books, keep some perspective. Bolt still holds the official men's 100-meter world record recognized by World Athletics. These robots compete under their own rules in a separate event.
CHINESE ROBOT BREAKS HUMAN WORLD RECORD IN BEIJING HALF-MARATHON

Still, look at how quickly this technology is moving. For me, the bigger story goes far beyond a robot beating Bolt's time. We are watching humanoid machines go from clumsy demonstrations to increasingly capable physical systems at remarkable speed.

Robots from Team Tiangong Ultra compete in the 4x100-meter relay final on day 4 of the 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games at National Speed Skating Oval in Beijing, China, on Aug. 25, 2026. (VCG via Getty Images)
