title: Massive garbage heap collapses onto homes, killing at least 30 as rescuers search for survivors
summary: A mountain of garbage collapsed after heavy rain at a major landfill site in Conakry, Guinea, burying nearby homes and launching a search for survivors.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
At least 30 people were killed in a massive landslide in Guinea on Sunday when a mountainous open-air landfill collapsed and buried nearby shacks, trapping numerous victims beneath a mass of garbage.
The incident happened at Dar Es Salam, the largest waste dump in the West African country's capital, Conakry, according to a report from The Associated Press (AP).
Guinea News reported that the weight of the waste caused a three-story building beneath it to cave in.
Authorities said heavy rainfall also washed over the refuse overnight, creating hazardous conditions at the landfill, according to the AP.
EARTHQUAKE SHAKES PERU'S ANDES REGION, KILLING AT LEAST 5, DISPLACING HUNDREDS
Residents and rescuers use an excavator to search for victims after a landslide struck the Dar Es Salam dumpsite in Conakry, Guinea, on Aug. 23, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
Six people were seriously injured and several homes were destroyed in the incident, according to reports. Officials launched a search-and-rescue operation to find any survivors.

The AP reported that the landfill was originally scheduled to close Sunday after officials warned of hazardous conditions, citing Lt. Col. Baldé Mamadou Bailo, the sanitation officer for the military engineering battalion.
The decision followed reports of a similar incident at the landfill in recent years, raising concerns about its safety.
Thirty people were killed and six others seriously injured after a landslide struck the Dar Es Salam dumpsite in Conakry, Guinea, on Aug. 23, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
As a precautionary measure, residents who lived near the site had also been given eviction notices and were forced to vacate the area, the AP said.
However, many people remained nearby at the time of the disaster, according to reports.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Dar Es Salam landfill collapsed following heavy overnight rain in Conakry, Guinea, on Aug. 23, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
"We will ensure that the remaining families are relocated elsewhere," Dienabou Touré, the minister of territorial administration and decentralization, said at the scene, according to the AP.
Reuters reported that the landfill suffered a similar incident in 2017, when torrential rains caused a mudslide that killed at least eight people.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Mexican governor facing US drug charges seeks leave just one day after returning to office
summary: Embattled Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya's abrupt reversal follows pointed remarks from Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum about putting nation above personal interest.
story: Mexican Senator Lilly Tellez discusses the indictment of a Sinaloa governor and nine officials for alleged fentanyl trafficking. She blasts President Claudia Sheinbaum's refusal to extradite, asserting Mexico operates as a 'narco-state.' Tellez warns of deep corruption and the dire implications for bilateral relations and border security.

Embattled Sinaloa, Mexico, Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya abruptly requested an indefinite leave of absence Saturday, just one day after returning to office following a three-month absence triggered by U.S. drug trafficking charges against him.
Rocha, 77, shared a letter on social media asking for "temporary leave of an indefinite nature, for more than 30 days" from his position as governor.
The letter, dated Aug. 22 and stamped received by the Sinaloa State Congress that day, does not say when Rocha plans to return or why he is stepping away again.
MEXICAN SENATOR ACCUSES SHEINBAUM OF SHIELDING 'NARCO-POLITICIANS' AFTER US CARTEL INDICTMENT

Sinaloa Gov. Ruben Rocha Moya speaks as he leaves the inauguration ceremony of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum in Mexico City, Mexico, on Oct. 1, 2024. (Jose Luis Torales/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
The request came just a day after Rocha announced his return and said it was his "duty to fulfill the mandate" of voters who elected him to serve through Oct. 31, 2027.
"Today, I return to the exercise of my responsibility as Governor of Sinaloa with a clear conscience and head held high, with the strength of truth on our side," Rocha wrote Friday on X.
Rocha said he spent 112 days away from office while making himself available to Mexican authorities investigating what he called "false accusations" by the U.S. government.
He said he personally appeared before Mexico’s Attorney General’s Office and answered investigators’ questions.

Rocha insisted the investigation had produced no evidence that he committed a crime and accused political opponents in Mexico and abroad of trying to damage both the country’s sovereignty and the left-wing movement he represents.
MEXICAN PRESIDENT IN THE DARK ABOUT DRUG OPERATION AFTER WHICH US, MEXICAN OFFICIALS WERE KILLED
"I am unrelated to and innocent of the fabrications woven against me," Rocha wrote.
Rocha’s return Friday did not get a warm reception from Mexico’s ruling Morena party or the government of President Claudia Sheinbaum.

Morena said it had no advance knowledge of Rocha’s decision and distanced itself from the move, according to Reuters. Mexico’s Interior Ministry said returning to office was Rocha’s decision alone and noted that the attorney general’s investigation remained open.
5 MEXICAN CARTEL BOSSES CHARGED IN WEAPONS, DRUG TRAFFICKING, TIMESHARE FRAUD SCHEMES, DOJ SAYS
Sheinbaum also posted a pointed message on X.
"No personal interest can ever stand above the interests of the people and the Nation," she wrote.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum responded to Rocha's return to office on Saturday. (Daniel Cardenas/Getty Images)
"Mexico deserves public servants who understand that positions are temporary, but responsibility to the Nation is eternal," Sheinbaum added.

U.S. prosecutors charged Rocha and nine other current and former officials in April with drug trafficking and related weapons offenses. The current and former high-ranking government and law enforcement officials are alleged to have partnered with the Sinaloa cartel to distribute massive quantities of narcotics to the United States.
U.S. prosecutors charged Rocha and nine other current and former officials in April with drug trafficking and related weapons offenses linked to the Sinaloa cartel. (Solidago/Getty Images)
Rocha is the first sitting Mexican governor to face charges from the U.S., according to Reuters.

The case has strained relations between the U.S. and Mexico. Sheinbaum has called the charges foreign interference, while Mexico says Washington has not provided enough evidence to justify Rocha’s arrest or extradition.

title: Hormuz crisis hides a deeper oil threat that could outlast the war
summary: Art Berman warns that 8 million barrels shut in near the Strait of Hormuz may never fully recover, even after a ceasefire reopens the waterway.
story: Art Berman says millions of barrels of production remain shut in and warns some wells could take months to restart — while others may never fully recover.

As global attention remains fixed on tankers moving through the Strait of Hormuz, a petroleum geologist is warning that the more consequential energy story may be unfolding thousands of feet underground — and could continue long after any political agreement ends the fighting.

Art Berman, a petroleum geologist and energy consultant with more than four decades of industry experience, told Fox News Digital that millions of barrels of Persian Gulf oil production remain shut in and warned that restoring those wells is far more complicated than simply reopening the strategic waterway.
"This is potentially a kind of a world-changing event, even if we resolve the political issues," Berman said.

"The bigger story and the more important one long term is that 8 million barrels of Persian Gulf production is currently shut in and world production is down about 10 million barrels a day," Berman explained.

In an aerial view, Marathon Petroleum Corp's Los Angeles Refinery, one of the largest oil refineries in North America, operates as gas prices rocket upward due to worldwide oil supply disruptions caused by the U.S. and Israeli attack on Iran, on March 10, 2026 in Carson, California. (David McNew/Getty Images)

"We can move tankers around and we can obsess about, you know, are there 4 million barrels getting through or are there 6 million or 9 million or whatever the right number is," he added. "But eventually, those tankers have to be filled with oil."

A White House official, speaking on background, pointed to the sharp decline in oil prices following the signing of the MOU and said the Strait of Hormuz is open, with the U.S. naval blockade in full effect.

Berman's estimate of Gulf shut-ins is broadly consistent with the latest assessment from the International Energy Agency. The IEA said in its Aug. 12, 2026, Oil Market Report, "Gulf oil production rose by a further 2.5 mb/d in July to 23.9 mb/d, still 8.3 mb/d below pre-war levels."
Global oil supply remained 6.3 million bpd below year-earlier levels, according to the agency.
The U.S. Energy Information Administration offers a somewhat different estimate.

EIA assessed production shut-ins at an average 5.5 million bpd in July, while warning that continuing constraints on Hormuz transit had forced the agency to increase its forecast for shut-in production in August. EIA expects production and trade patterns to generally return to pre-conflict conditions in early 2027, but says some Gulf producers may not regain their previous output during its forecast period.
Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on Aug. 3, 2026. (Reuters)

The distinction is important because much of the public discussion has centered on what the industry calls the midstream problem — whether tankers can safely transport oil through Hormuz — while Berman argues that the upstream problem of producing the oil itself could prove more enduring.
"The very last thing in the world I ever want to do is to shut in a well," Berman told Fox News Digital.

Restarting a well requires restoring communication between equipment at the surface and reservoirs thousands of feet underground, he explained, and extended shutdowns can create complications inside the reservoir and well.
"This is not like turning on a switch for a light bulb," Berman said. "It's a complicated, high-risk, relatively long-term process, and we don't know the outcome."

Berman estimated that roughly 80% of affected wells could return close to their previous production levels, although he said that could take weeks or months. He said many of the remainder could require additional engineering work and some could ultimately produce at lower rates.
"Some of that production will never come back," he predicted.
Other energy analysts agree that restarting Gulf production presents substantial technical challenges. But Wood Mackenzie is more optimistic than Berman about the ultimate recovery.

Its analysis projects that fields affected by the Hormuz closure could return to approximately 70% of their previous production within three months and 90% within six months, assuming a controlled restart. The final roughly 1 million bpd could take considerably longer.
Oil tankers and cargo ships line up in the Strait of Hormuz as seen from Khor Fakkan, United Arab Emirates, Wednesday, March 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Altaf Qadri)
Berman also warned against assuming that a ceasefire or political agreement would immediately restore pre-war energy flows.

Shipowners, insurers and crews would first have to become confident that tankers could safely navigate the waterway, while other logistical and security issues could continue even after governments reached an agreement.
"A simple political agreement doesn't mean the problem's over," Berman said.
Berman's argument goes considerably further than predicting a slow oil-market recovery.
He contends that the Persian Gulf conflict represents a fundamental shock to the global energy and economic system — one whose consequences will persist even after the immediate crisis ends.

Asked about his comparison with the COVID-19 pandemic, Berman told Fox News Digital that the scale of oil production affected by the current crisis makes it comparable to the largest economic disruptions of recent years.
"This is not just a news cycle," Berman said. "This is potentially a kind of a world-changing event, even if we resolve the political issues."
IRAN DEAL CLOCK HITS ZERO AS TRUMP DEMANDS ‘WHITE FLAG’ WITH NEW PRESSURE CAMPAIGN LOOMING
The ConocoPhillips Oil Refinery is seen in Wilmington, California on April 11, 2026. (Etienne Laurent / AFP via Getty Images)
The United States is the world's largest oil producer, but Berman argues that does not isolate American consumers from the disruption.
"The oil market and the refined products market is global," he told Fox News Digital.

Berman noted that U.S. refineries require different grades of crude to produce the country's mix of gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other petroleum products, meaning domestic production alone cannot eliminate America's exposure to international markets.
"The problem for the U.S. isn't that we don't have enough oil, we almost do," Berman said. "It's that the oil we have isn't the right kind" for everything American refineries produce.

EIA reported July 15 that Hormuz disruptions had already pushed international buyers toward alternative sources of petroleum products, contributing to higher U.S. refinery margins, production and exports.

Whether that recovery proceeds as EIA expects or encounters the technical obstacles Berman warns about could determine how long the economic consequences of the conflict linger after the shooting stops.
For Berman, the question is no longer simply when tankers return to Hormuz. It is whether the global energy system that emerges afterward will ever operate quite the way it did before.

The White House pushed back on concerns that the disruption represents a lasting threat to U.S. energy security, pointing to record American production and blaming Iran for instability in the critical shipping corridor.

"Thanks to President Trump, the United States is now the world’s number-one producer and exporter of oil and gas. Record oil and gas production strengthens our energy independence and national security," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital.

"The Iranian regime’s terrorist actions in the Strait of Hormuz have proven that our allies need to invest in reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources and advance new partnerships with the United States that enhance the world’s energy security," Rogers added.
Children swim as ships are seen anchored in the Strait of Hormuz on August 10, 2026 off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. ( )
Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House, U.S. Energy Information Administration and Defense Intelligence Agency for comment.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Woman in her 30s who pretended to be a child and lived with family found guilty of fraud
summary: Amanda Maria Souza de Oliveira, 37, lived with a family as their daughter for 14 months before her elaborate child identity fraud was uncovered.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A woman in Brazil was found guilty this week of living with a foster family for more than a year while pretending to be a child, officials said.

Amanda Maria Souza de Oliveira, who is in reality 37 years old, was convicted of fraud and false identity on Thursday, according to a translated release from the Court of Justice of Santa Catarina in Brazil.
Oliveira, who the family took in as their daughter for 14 months until her scheme was uncovered, claimed she had fled abuse.

Amanda Maria Souza de Oliveira was convicted of fraud and false identity in Brazil. (Campo Grande Civil Police)
The woman later admitted to creating a false identity and age, the court said.

Oliveira had been living falsely as a child for 15 years in an "elaborate fraud," the Washington Post reported, using a high-pitched, childlike voice and even telling people she had been forced to get hormones to make her look older.
COLLEGE FOOTBALL NATIONAL CHAMPION WHO WORE WIGS IN FRAUD SCHEME PLEADS GUILTY TO CHARGES
She was sentenced to one year, six months and 10 days in prison, along with four months and 18 days of detention.
One of her lawyers, Lúcio Sousa, said that Oliveira’s scheme was how she "survived."
Amanda Maria Souza de Oliveira was sentenced by a court in Brazil to one year, six months and 10 days in prison, along with four months and 18 days of detention for fraud and false identity. (iStock)
"She admits that she invented an identity," Sousa said before the verdict, according to the Post. "It was the way she found to survive. But she has been a vulnerable person for more than 20 years.

"She has lived on the streets, and there has been no allegation that she obtained any financial advantage, or committed robbery or theft, which, in theory, means the elements of fraud have not been established."
Oliveira said she never meant to hurt anyone.
"Of course, I deceived people, I lied," she said, according to police, the Post reported. "But I didn’t intend to scam anyone."

Amanda Maria Souza de Oliveira is photographed in jail after she was convicted of fraud and false identity by pretending to be a child while living with a foster family in Brazil. (Campo Grande Civil Police)
She said she wanted to experience the love she never got as a child.
"There was a certain void in me, a need to have that kind of care, so I always sought it out," she said.

title: ICE arrests far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos
summary: The far-right commentator and self-described internet troll was arrested at the airport in New Orleans for staying in the country after his visa expired, according to DHS.
story: Milo Yiannopoulos, a self-described libertarian and professional internet troll who became known for his controversial right-wing political views, is in ICE custody.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News that ICE arrested Yiannopoulos, a United Kingdom national, on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport in Kenner, Louisiana.
The DHS spokesperson said Yiannopoulos legally entered the U.S. on May 14, 2019, through New York City, but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws.”

Yiannopoulos was taken into ICE custody Thursday after “failing to show up for his immigration hearing” on July 22, prompting an immigration judge to issue a final order of removal against him, according to the spokesperson. “He will remain in ICE custody pending removal,” the spokesperson added.
TMZ first reported Yiannopoulos’ ICE arrest.

Yiannopoulos has ties to Kanye West, known now as Ye, and  previously served as the rapper’s chief of staff when Ye tried to run for president in 2020 and 2024. He also worked at Ye’s clothing brand “Yeezy,” but resigned from that job two years ago after the singer announced he was launching an adult entertainment studio under his Yeezy brand, TMZ reported.
Ye is scheduled to perform in Louisiana Friday night at the New Orleans Caesars Superdome. It’s unclear if Yiannopoulos was in the state to attend the concert.

A former editor of Breitbart, the conservative internet publication President Donald Trump once considered as one of his favorite news sources, Yiannopoulos resigned from Breitbart in 2017 amid backlash to his reported comments about teens and sexual abuse.
The DHS spokesperson said that the Trump administration is “working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”

title: Kevin Warsh walks a fine line on inflation in key speech
summary: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said measures of inflation are still elevated, but it is not yet clear that the Fed must take action to address rising prices.
story: JACKSON HOLE, Wyo. — President Donald Trump’s new Federal Reserve chair said Friday that although measures of inflation are still elevated, it is not yet clear that the central bank must take urgent action to address rising prices.

The speech at the Fed’s yearly retreat at Jackson Hole had been eagerly anticipated after a rocky start to Kevin Warsh’s tenure. Market observers were concerned that he had downplayed the risk of rising prices.

There were also calls for an interest rate hike from economists, including some within the Fed. Trump has routinely called for lower rates that would spark the economy but risk even greater inflation.
Warsh noted that the labor market looks “stable” and said this was one reason that he saw prices as “more concerning.”
The Fed chairman noted that while readings of inflation this summer were “better than expected, they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.”
Warsh did not say how the Fed would react if prices keep rising at rates above the target of 2%. But he underscored that the chief tool for tackling inflation was rate hikes.
“We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do,” he said.
Following Warsh’s speech, the odds increased that the Fed would raise its benchmark interest rate next month in order to cool inflation.

Warsh reiterated his preference for a “quieter Fed,” doing away with his predecessor Jerome Powell’s use of “forward guidance” to let markets and the general public know what the central bank planned to do in the near future.

“If markets rely materially on the Fed’s guidance and the Fed relies on market prices, we are all more likely to be blinded to new developments, more likely to be caught unprepared for a turn of events, and more likely to commit errors in policymaking,” Warsh said.

title: Elon Musk enters the midterm chat: From the Politics Desk
summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
In today’s edition, we dive into Elon Musk’s first foray into this year’s midterms. Plus, Kristen Welker digs into how voters are feeling about the Iran war six months in.
Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.
Elon Musk enters the midterm chat
Elon Musk is back.
The tech billionaire’s super PAC launched digital ads this month in three states with key Senate races: Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire.
The effort from America PAC targets specific lists of people and urges viewers to register to vote, according to a review of Meta political ad data.

Some ads are generic, featuring reminders that the Senate races in their states could decide control of the chamber. Others go on the attack against socialism, including one ad that features an image of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, warning that “if you don’t vote in November, socialism could declare victory over America.”

The campaign marks America PAC’s first significant ad spending since the April 2025 Wisconsin Supreme Court election. Musk injected himself into the center of that race, spending millions of dollars and traveling to the state. But his endorsed candidate, conservative Brad Schimel, ultimately fell well short of Susan Crawford, allowing liberals to maintain their majority on the swing state court.

Musk spent a quarter-billion dollars to boost Trump and the GOP in the 2024 election. He then went on to serve as an adviser to Trump at the outset of his second term, before having an on-again, off-again relationship with the president after leaving the White House.

It remains to be seen exactly how much Musk will spend this time around. But as the Republicans prepare to face a daunting political environment this fall, any financial involvement from Musk in battleground contests will be a welcome development for the party.
Read more →
Voter frustrations with Trump and the GOP reshape the midterm map

As the war with Iran hits the six-month mark, Americans appear to have reached a consensus: They don’t support it. That was the case when the war started, and it remains so in recent polling over the last few weeks.

Poll after poll shows that President Donald Trump’s handling of the war is deeply underwater and that voters are skeptical it will come to an end any time soon. It’s a reminder of the political headwinds Trump and Republicans face across multiple fronts. In addition to this conflict, Trump continues to escalate trade wars with countries like Canada, while capturing headlines for trying to rename Lake Ontario or threatening to demolish the Kennedy Center.

We’ve spoken with voters across the country who keep making the same point — they’re laser-focused on the economy and frustrated about the war, with many worried the administration’s efforts aren’t hitting the mark.

Those frustrations are one reason why even traditionally red states like Texas — the home of one of my guests this Sunday, Republican Sen. Ted Cruz — appears to be in play this cycle. Democratic state Rep. James Talarico is waging a tough battle there against state Attorney General Ken Paxton in what’s become a major proving ground for so many of these issues.

Most recently, Talarico has blasted Trump’s effort to suspend tariffs on beef exports as part of a broader attempt to hit the GOP on the issue of rising costs. But that issue in particular has scrambled the usual party lines: A chorus of Republican lawmakers around the country has also warned the plan could hurt American farmers and ranchers.

Paxton, meanwhile, has countered with an affordability pitch of his own centered on lowering taxes, as he and Trump try to frame Talarico as too extreme on social issues. In a sign of how competitive the race has become, Trump also traveled to the state for a fundraiser yesterday.
Cruz and Rep. James Clyburn, D-S.C., will join me on “Meet the Press” this Sunday to discuss all of this and more.

title: Wisconsin dad cited after tripping 9-year-old during youth football game
summary: Poor parental behavior in youth sports reached a new low near Milwaukee when a father ran onto the field and tripped a 9-year-old football player racing for the end zone, police said.
story: Poor parental behavior in youth sports reached a new low near Milwaukee when a father ran onto the field and tripped a 9-year-old football player racing for the end zone, police said.
Video of the incident, which quickly went viral, captured the moment Saturday at Case High School in Racine, where the Racine Youth Eagles  hosted the Milwaukee Colts.
An Eagles ball carrier had turned the left edge and had a clear path to the pylon when, out of nowhere, a man wearing black shorts and a black T-shirt ran onto the field, video showed.
The man extended his left and swept the runner’s legs out from under him, causing the player to crash to the grass short of a touchdown.
“During the game, a parent from the visiting team became upset over a play, walked onto the field, and tripped a 9-year-old player,” according to a Mount Pleasant police statement.

​”A spectator captured the incident on video, while another parent followed the suspect’s vehicle as he left the grounds. Officers located the vehicle shortly after and conducted a traffic stop. The suspect, a 41-year-old Milwaukee man, admitted to the act and was issued a citation for disorderly conduct.”
The Colts were awarded a touchdown on that play, and referees called the game early in hopes of defusing tensions between the victorious hosts and the defeated visitors.
Terrence Ryan Bradshaw was pulled over at 11:07 a.m. Saturday on Highway 20 near Oakes Road, less than half a mile away from Case High School, Mount Pleasant police records show.

Bradshaw told officers he apologized to players and coaches for losing his cool because  “there was just some bigger kids (on the other team) than my kid,” according to police body camera footage of the stop.
Bradshaw said he was only trying to “stop the game,” though his actions stunned officers.
“I mean it’s kids, kids!” police officer Nicole Knierim told Bradshaw.
Bradshaw explained he was afraid his son might get hurt.
“I got scared, really,” he told police. “My son broke his arm twice already, so when I saw him flip like that it just — I was trying to stop the game, really.”
Knierim and her partner discussed the case and agreed Bradshaw deserved a disorderly conduct citation.
“So there were these kids playing a game. The kids on the other team are bigger than his kids, and it was he felt it was just like getting a little too much or whatever,” Knierim said to her partner.
“And he says ‘I got my feelings or whatever’ so he didn’t kick him. He says he went out there to stop the play, and they kind of slid together. He says ‘I apologize to everybody.’ “
Bradshaw does not have to appear in court if he pays the $313 fine, police said.
The 9-year-old player “was thankfully not injured,” police added.
Prosecutors reviewed the incident and determined it did not amount to  felony child abuse, letting the disorderly conduct citation stand, the Racine County District Attorney’s Office said.

title: Trump signs order to create space-focused military academy
summary: President Donald Trump on Friday announced that he would sign an executive order to create a new military academy, the U.S. Space Academy.
story: President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order to create a new military academy — the U.S. Space Academy — to train people for the U.S. Space Force, NASA and the civilian space industry.

Speaking at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, Trump said “the rapid growth of the Space Force and the commercial space industry and the expansion of our ambitions to the moon and far beyond the moon” inspired the new academy.
“It’s clear that we need to educate and train an entire generation of skilled service members, engineers, civil operators and everything else to do what we have to do,” he added.

Later in the day, Trump made history by becoming the first president to call U.S. astronauts on the International Space Station from the NASA facility’s Mission Control Center. He also awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the crewmembers of NASA’s Artemis II mission, who flew around the moon earlier this year.
“I just congratulate everybody. And be careful. Be safe. And we love you all,” the president told the astronauts aboard the space station, telling them about the new service academy.

Astronaut Jack Hathaway, who is also an officer in the U.S. Navy, celebrated the news, telling Trump, “I graduated from the Naval Academy. I’m sure they’re more than excited to support it and have it on board.”
Astronaut Jessica Meir, the current space station mission commander, said the crew “will continue doing our best to inspire all of the bright minds and the next generation as well.”
Trump offered few details about the future space academy, telling the audience in Houston that he would be choosing a location “very shortly.”
During his appearance at the space center, which saw the Artemis II crew present Trump with his own NASA flight jacket, the president expressed optimism about the future of U.S. space exploration.
“Far beyond the moon will someday be thought of a close location, like, like in the old days, the subway, the first stop, the moon will be a close location,” Trump said.

title: Lindsay Clancy’s jury ends the week without verdict, will return Monday
summary: PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy was “scared” as the jury deliberated for a second day to determine whether she is guilty of killing her three children in 2023, her defense lawyer said Friday.
story: PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy was “scared” as the jury deliberated for a second day to determine whether she is guilty of killing her three children in 2023, her defense lawyer said Friday.
“She’s nervous. Sad. Scared. Same as she has been,” Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington told reporters at the courthouse Friday, according to NBC Boston.

Before the jury went home without a decision Friday afternoon, there was an anxiousness in the air and reporters lining the hallways at Plymouth Superior Court. The murder trial is in its home stretch after five weeks of testimony from more than 80 witnesses.
Deliberations resumed Friday at 9:15 a.m., and the jury had its  first question around 10 a.m., about four hours into deliberations.

Judge William Sullivan called a recess after the question was brought to his attention, just after he sought the opposing attorneys for a sidebar. The question was not publicly disclosed, and the jury was never brought into the courtroom.
Clancy’s mother, father and sister sat in court Friday behind her.

Reddington, however, told reporters in Plymouth that the jury wanted to see the bag of pills he showed during closings, as well as some other pill bottles and a knife that were all entered as evidence in the case.

It’s typical for a jury to have questions as it deliberates, especially in such a winding case with competing storylines and troves of evidence. Juries are also known to ask questions about the instructions given by the judge, and the law and how to apply it.
Clancy, 36, is facing charges of fatally strangling her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — on Jan. 24, 2023.

The jury — comprised of nine women and three men — must decide if Clancy is guilty of first-degree murder in relation to the killings. If she is convicted of first-degree murder, she faces life in prison.

Throughout the trial, the defense has argued that she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis when she killed her children, before trying to kill herself by hurling herself out of her Duxbury, Massachusetts, home’s second-story window.
Reddington has said that Clancy was compelled to act on auditory hallucinations, a symptom of the postpartum psychosis, while her then-husband was out running errands that night.

The prosecution, though, argued that even though Clancy was clearly struggling with her mental health, she was not actually in psychosis and therefore had control over her actions. Prosecutors have said that Clancy deliberately chose to kill her kids before trying to kill herself and that she planned their murders earlier that evening.

The jury also has the option to convict her of lesser charges, including second-degree murder and manslaughter, or to deem her not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility — meaning that they believe she did kill the children, but couldn’t control her actions due to being in psychosis.
Both the prosecution and the defense offered their closing arguments Thursday morning, and the jury began deliberating that afternoon.

Sullivan has said that if Clancy is found not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, the district attorney or another authority will likely petition the court to commit her to a mental health facility. It is unclear what her sentencing will look like if she is convicted of a lesser charge.

Frequently asked questions
The best Labor Day sales to shop this year are:

Summer-related products: Summer is officially coming to an end, and retailers are desperate to get rid of related products to make room for fall inventory, says Porwal. Because of this, you’ll see huge clearance sales on grills, patio furniture, pool and beach accessories and outdoor sports equipment.   Warm-weather clothing, footwear and accessories: Summer fashion usually makes up the biggest portion of retailers’ summer clearance sections, says Porwal. Use it as your chance to stock up on basics and buy discounted pieces you’ve had your eye on to save for next year. If you see something you’re interested in, be sure to jump on it — the most popular brands, styles, colors and sizes sell out very quickly.Mattresses, furniture and major appliances: Deals on these categories are the bread and butter of all three-day holiday weekend sales. Shoppers tend to wait on purchasing mattresses, furniture and major appliances because they’re pricey, says Stephanie Carls, a retail insights expert at RetailMeNot. By offering deep discounts across a few days, retailers give customers time to compare prices and weigh options, plus, on top of deals, they offer add-ons like free delivery and installation, which could be the thing that finally makes someone take the leap. Porwal says using Labor Day to buy mattresses, furniture and major appliances is especially important this year — he expects prices to increase by the end of 2026 due to ongoing economic issues, so this may be the last time you see deals this low.

The Labor Day sales you should skip this year are:

Tech: Retailers offer the lowest prices of the year on items like TVs, gaming consoles, smart home devices, earbuds and Bluetooth speakers during Black Friday and Cyber Monday, says Carls. Unless you need something immediately, don’t add tech to your cart just yet. The only exception is laptops. “Higher memory costs are putting pressure on notebook pricing, so if you find a strong Labor Day deal on the exact laptop you want, I’d take it seriously,” says Carls. “I wouldn’t assume November automatically gets you a lower final price.”Toys: Toy deals are the most competitive leading up to the holidays, especially during Black Friday and Cyber Monday, says Carls. There are comparable Labor Day sales online and in stores, especially at big box retailers, so you’re guaranteed to find strong deals wherever you shop. A few things to keep in mind while deciding whether to leave your couch:

Shopping online makes comparing prices and stacking savings easier, letting you consider the total value of a deal, not just the sale price, says Ashley Feinstein Gerstley, a shopping and savings expert at Rakuten. Open a few tabs and search for the exact same product at a handful of retailers to weigh which one offers the lowest price and lowest shipping fee. You can also shop through cash back apps and browser extensions online, which help you find additional promo codes and rewards, she says.Shopping in stores lets you try out big ticket items like furniture, mattresses and major appliances, giving you more confidence in pricey purchases. You can also ask a store associate about lower-priced floor models and open-box inventory, which you may never see advertised online, says Carls.Shipping fees add up, especially if you’re placing online orders at numerous retailers or buying big-ticket products that require installation. Shipping fees add up, especially if you’re placing online orders at numerous retailers or buying big-ticket products that require installation. If your total goes up drastically once you consider shipping fees, see if you can buy online and pick up in store instead.

Some early Labor Day sales have already started, but the majority of them begin between Tuesday, Sept. 1 and Friday, Sept. 4. Retailers typically consider the Friday before the official holiday, which lands on Monday, Sept. 7 this year, the start of the long weekend, so all sales will be live by Sept. 4.

Plan for most Labor Day sales to end on the holiday, Monday, Sept. 7. Some may extend longer into the week, but don’t plan on it — aim to get all your shopping done by Labor Day, but shop sooner if you can, says Carls. “Summer clearance is already working with fewer sizes, colors and models, so the thing you actually want can disappear before the promotion does,” she says. “The discount may hang around, but your exact patio set, for example, may not.”

All the experts I talked to agree that the best way to save the most money during Labor Day sales is to stack your savings. That means looking at the deal price as the starting point and combining it with additional offers to save even more, says Gerstley. For example, search for promo codes to lower prices further, shop through cash back apps and browsers to put money back in your pocket, and pay with credit cards that let you earn rewards as you spend.

Additionally, make sure you’re comparing prices across retailers before buying anything, says Porwal. Since so many retailers are hosting sales right now, they’re all competing for your attention, and you never know when one might lower prices just a little bit more to give themselves an edge, or throw in extras that make a purchase more worthwhile, like free shipping, delivery, install or haul-away. Don’t be afraid to ask about price matching, too, says Carls. If a retailer really wants your business, they’ll be open to negotiating with you.

Last but not least, don’t feel like you absolutely have to buy something if deals aren’t compelling, says Gerstley. As we enter the final quarter of the year, sales are plentiful with early Black Friday and Cyber Monday offers starting in October, and Amazon Prime Big Deal Days might be around the corner (it hasn’t been confirmed yet, however). There will be more promotional moments in the near future, and waiting might be key to maximizing your savings.

title: Lindsay Clancy’s jury ends the week without verdict, will return Monday
summary: PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy was “scared” as the jury deliberated for a second day to determine whether she is guilty of killing her three children in 2023, her defense lawyer said Friday.
story: PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy was “scared” as the jury deliberated for a second day to determine whether she is guilty of killing her three children in 2023, her defense lawyer said Friday.
“She’s nervous. Sad. Scared. Same as she has been,” Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington told reporters at the courthouse Friday, according to NBC Boston.

Before the jury went home without a decision Friday afternoon, there was an anxiousness in the air and reporters lining the hallways at Plymouth Superior Court. The murder trial is in its home stretch after five weeks of testimony from more than 80 witnesses.
Deliberations resumed Friday at 9:15 a.m., and the jury had its  first question around 10 a.m., about four hours into deliberations.

Judge William Sullivan called a recess after the question was brought to his attention, just after he sought the opposing attorneys for a sidebar. The question was not publicly disclosed, and the jury was never brought into the courtroom.
Clancy’s mother, father and sister sat in court Friday behind her.

Reddington, however, told reporters in Plymouth that the jury wanted to see the bag of pills he showed during closings, as well as some other pill bottles and a knife that were all entered as evidence in the case.

It’s typical for a jury to have questions as it deliberates, especially in such a winding case with competing storylines and troves of evidence. Juries are also known to ask questions about the instructions given by the judge, and the law and how to apply it.
Clancy, 36, is facing charges of fatally strangling her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — on Jan. 24, 2023.

The jury — comprised of nine women and three men — must decide if Clancy is guilty of first-degree murder in relation to the killings. If she is convicted of first-degree murder, she faces life in prison.

Throughout the trial, the defense has argued that she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis when she killed her children, before trying to kill herself by hurling herself out of her Duxbury, Massachusetts, home’s second-story window.
Reddington has said that Clancy was compelled to act on auditory hallucinations, a symptom of the postpartum psychosis, while her then-husband was out running errands that night.

The prosecution, though, argued that even though Clancy was clearly struggling with her mental health, she was not actually in psychosis and therefore had control over her actions. Prosecutors have said that Clancy deliberately chose to kill her kids before trying to kill herself and that she planned their murders earlier that evening.

The jury also has the option to convict her of lesser charges, including second-degree murder and manslaughter, or to deem her not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility — meaning that they believe she did kill the children, but couldn’t control her actions due to being in psychosis.
Both the prosecution and the defense offered their closing arguments Thursday morning, and the jury began deliberating that afternoon.

Sullivan has said that if Clancy is found not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, the district attorney or another authority will likely petition the court to commit her to a mental health facility. It is unclear what her sentencing will look like if she is convicted of a lesser charge.

title: Wisconsin dad cited after tripping 9-year-old during youth football game
summary: Poor parental behavior in youth sports reached a new low near Milwaukee when a father ran onto the field and tripped a 9-year-old football player racing for the end zone, police said.
story: Poor parental behavior in youth sports reached a new low near Milwaukee when a father ran onto the field and tripped a 9-year-old football player racing for the end zone, police said.
Video of the incident, which quickly went viral, captured the moment Saturday at Case High School in Racine, where the Racine Youth Eagles  hosted the Milwaukee Colts.
An Eagles ball carrier had turned the left edge and had a clear path to the pylon when, out of nowhere, a man wearing black shorts and a black T-shirt ran onto the field, video showed.
The man extended his left and swept the runner’s legs out from under him, causing the player to crash to the grass short of a touchdown.
“During the game, a parent from the visiting team became upset over a play, walked onto the field, and tripped a 9-year-old player,” according to a Mount Pleasant police statement.

​”A spectator captured the incident on video, while another parent followed the suspect’s vehicle as he left the grounds. Officers located the vehicle shortly after and conducted a traffic stop. The suspect, a 41-year-old Milwaukee man, admitted to the act and was issued a citation for disorderly conduct.”
The Colts were awarded a touchdown on that play, and referees called the game early in hopes of defusing tensions between the victorious hosts and the defeated visitors.
Terrence Ryan Bradshaw was pulled over at 11:07 a.m. Saturday on Highway 20 near Oakes Road, less than half a mile away from Case High School, Mount Pleasant police records show.

Bradshaw told officers he apologized to players and coaches for losing his cool because  “there was just some bigger kids (on the other team) than my kid,” according to police body camera footage of the stop.
Bradshaw said he was only trying to “stop the game,” though his actions stunned officers.
“I mean it’s kids, kids!” police officer Nicole Knierim told Bradshaw.
Bradshaw explained he was afraid his son might get hurt.
“I got scared, really,” he told police. “My son broke his arm twice already, so when I saw him flip like that it just — I was trying to stop the game, really.”
Knierim and her partner discussed the case and agreed Bradshaw deserved a disorderly conduct citation.
“So there were these kids playing a game. The kids on the other team are bigger than his kids, and it was he felt it was just like getting a little too much or whatever,” Knierim said to her partner.
“And he says ‘I got my feelings or whatever’ so he didn’t kick him. He says he went out there to stop the play, and they kind of slid together. He says ‘I apologize to everybody.’ “
Bradshaw does not have to appear in court if he pays the $313 fine, police said.
The 9-year-old player “was thankfully not injured,” police added.
Prosecutors reviewed the incident and determined it did not amount to  felony child abuse, letting the disorderly conduct citation stand, the Racine County District Attorney’s Office said.

title: Jake Reiner says he hasn’t spoken to his brother as he opens up about grief
summary: “I will never understand why this happened,” Jake Reiner told KABC-TV of Los Angeles about the murders of Rob Reiner and Michelle Singer Reiner. His brother has been charged in their deaths.
story: It has been eight months since beloved Hollywood director Rob Reiner and his wife, Michele Singer Reiner, were killed and their son Nick Reiner was arrested in their deaths.

But for Jake Reiner, the couple’s 35-year-old son, the nightmare feels like “eight years at the same time, and it also feels like eight minutes,” he told KABC-TV of Los Angeles in his first sit-down interview since the family tragedy.
“Every moment that I wake up, I’m reminded of my reality, and you’re living through that every single day,” he said.
Jake said he hasn’t spoken to his brother. Nor has he attended any of his brother’s court hearings, the station reported.
“He’s in jail, so, you know, it’s like I physically lost my parents and then Nick was arrested. And it’s like now, it’s just me and Romy,” he said, referring to his 28-year-old sister.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Jake opened up to KABC in the interview, which aired Thursday, about navigating grief and how it can manifest into anger.
“I’ll never understand. I don’t care how it’s explained to me. I don’t care what facts come out. I will never understand why this happened,” he told the station.

“It manifests into rage, into how unfair this was. How I didn’t get a say in what happened. I didn’t get to stop it from happening. I had no choice in the matter, and I just have to accept the reality of it. And to me that is just one of the most infuriating parts of all this,” he said.
Rob Reiner, 78, and Michele Singer Reiner, 70, were found brutally stabbed in their home in the Brentwood neighborhood of Los Angeles on Dec. 14. Nick was arrested hours later.
Jake was at Los Angeles’ Union Station for a celebration of life event for a friend when his sister called. He didn’t pick up.

“She called immediately again, and I knew at that point something immediately was wrong. Romy told me our dad was dead, and then she said, ‘I can’t find Mom.’ And I immediately went into shock. I need to get out of this train station, and I need to get to my parents’ house,” he recalled.
Asked whether he was surprised to learn that his brother was the main suspect, Jake took a deep breath and said, “I feel like that’s something I don’t really want to answer right now.”
In April, Jake wrote about his heartbreak on Substack, saying, “We lost more than half of our family that night in the most violent way imaginable.” He affirmed that that included Nick.

Nick Reiner, 32, has a long history of drug addiction and has struggled with his mental health. He co-wrote the 2016 movie “Being Charlie” with his father, who directed it, about the experiences of a young man who struggles with recovery.

“I can tell you, they never stopped wanting to help him. They never stopped helping him,” Jake said of his parents’ supporting Nick. “And I think that project was a way for my dad to try and connect with him.”
Asked whether it was ever a fear that something like the murders could ever happen, Jake declined to answer.
Now his focus is on following in his parents’ footsteps working with the Children’s Institute, an organization that supports children and families. He’ll be at its gala in November.
“It’s going to be hard. I think everything that we’ve done so far without them has been hard and weird. But I do feel responsible for making sure people know them and they remember them,” he said.

Nick Reiner has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder in connection with special circumstance allegations of multiple murders and lying in wait. His case continues in court. Earlier this summer, he filed a petition seeking access to his more than $1.5 million trust fund to help pay for his defense.
KABC reported that Jake Reiner isn’t commenting about his brother’s attempts to access money from the trust.

title: Judge hits DOJ lawyers with barrage of questions on Kennedy Center changes
summary: Justice Department lawyers said in a court filing this week that keeping Trump’s name off the performance center could lead to its being demolished.
story: The judge in a court battle over efforts to add Donald Trump’s name to the front of the Kennedy Center peppered the administration’s lawyers with questions Thursday on their rush to put his name back on it.

The Trump-appointed board at the performance venue voted this month to add the words “renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump” to the building and to rename the property “President Donald J. Trump Plaza” by Sept. 8.
“What’s magic about that date?” U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper asked Justice Department attorney Brantley Mayers, noting that it seems “expedited.”
Mayers said that was the date the board had voted on and a timetable it plans to stick to.

Cooper then asked why adding Trump’s name to the building — the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts — would not violate federal appropriations rules that prevent aggrandizement, promoting a specific individual within a federal agency.
Mayers said it would not be in violation because it would be honoring Trump in his role as president, not as chairman of the board of the Kennedy Center.
“That’s cutting it a little fine, isn’t it?” Cooper asked.
Mayers said he was being true to the statute.
Cooper did not rule on any of the issues at the hearing but said he was considering a temporary pause on the Sept. 8 date so he can fully weigh the legal issues.
“There may be a temporary holding pattern while we can give the issues the attention they deserve,” he said.
A Justice Department lawyer suggested in a court filing this week that the center may have to be demolished if Trump’s name isn’t allowed to be added to the site.

“The Board also underscores, and the undisputed evidence demonstrates, that without the prominent recognition of The Trump Administration, and President Trump’s efforts, the donors will not contribute, and the Center will continue to be in a financial and structural death spiral,” the filing said.

“Without those efforts, the Center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years,” Mayers wrote in the filing.

Attorneys for ex officio board member Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, argued in court filings that the financial problems were the result of Trump’s name’s being added to the building in the first place. Now, they said, the defendants “openly threaten to do further damage to this sacred memorial if they do not get their way in emblazoning that historic marble with Trump’s name once again and renaming the grounds for him.”

“In plain English, Defendants have not-so-subtly said: ‘What a nice Kennedy Center you have here. What a shame should something happen to it.’ This is a breathtaking assault on the rule of law. It is delusional. And it must stop,” the filing said.

Mayers said Thursday that the new addition isn’t a renaming — it’s just a recognition. Beatty attorney Nathaniel Zelinsky said additional names are banned from being displayed on the outside of the building and can be displayed only in certain areas inside the facility.
He said the board’s move shows “outright defiance” of Cooper’s earlier order to remove Trump’s name from the front portico. The center is appealing that ruling.

Meeting minutes the Kennedy Center submitted to the court showed that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told board members that Trump — who threatened to walk away from the center after his name was removed from the facade — wanted the recognition.

“Secretary Lutnick introduced a discussion regarding recognition of the Chairman, stating that if the Chairman is to complete the renovation in two years for $257 million, and has further committed to help raise money to endow the institution, it is appropriate that he be recognized. It is important to President Trump that if he’s going to put his time and effort into the building and fundraising, that he be recognized,” the minutes said.

Trump then addressed the meeting virtually, and after “commenting on prior management and spending at the Center, the condition of the building including the parking structure, and the White House ballroom project,” he “stated his commitment to complete the renovation within two years with the building closed, and to reopen it in a substantially improved condition,” the minutes said.

The board, including Trump, then voted to pass a resolution honoring his “current and future existential and unprecedented contributions to the survival of the Center” by adding his name to the front of the building — twice.
Beatty said in a court filing that Trump was putting the cart before the horse.

“I find it particularly galling that President Trump is seeking to be recognized in this manner when the funds were appropriated by Congress and paid for by the American people, and when President Trump has not successfully renovated the Kennedy Center,” she wrote.
Lutnick told reporters before the hearing that the message is designed to “induce” and “entice” Trump.

“The idea, when you have the greatest philanthropist, the guy who’s going to raise you $500 million, you just need him to agree. And whatever the terms are, since you know he is the most credible person in the world, when he says, ‘I’m going to raise the money,’ you know he’s going to raise the money,” he said.

Lutnick, who said he’d gotten involved with the center at Trump’s request, told reporters: “There are two things that he does for enjoyment: He plays golf on the weekend, and he builds. He loves to build. So why are we talking about this? This is what he enjoys.”
“It’s fun for him,” Lutnick said. “I’m helping so he can enjoy constructing the Kennedy Center.”

title: Judge blocks Trump’s Postal Service regulation on mail-in ballots
summary: The judge said the regulation is most likely unlawful because the president can’t insert the federal government into elections without Congress’ approval.
story: A federal judge Thursday blocked a Postal Service regulation that would exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections in the latest setback on the issue for President Donald Trump.

The recently finalized measure would implement a key provision of Trump’s executive order on mail-in ballots that would add a new level of bureaucracy to the elections process, which is typically administered by states.
The executive order directed the U.S. Postal Service to, among other things, track mail-in ballots and potentially reject those submitted by people not on a federal list of eligible voters.

The decision by Boston-based U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in one case brought by the League of Women Voters and other groups and another brought by a coalition of states means part of the executive order remains blocked for at least 14 days, with time running out to implement it ahead of the November election.

“This rule is a clear attempt by the federal government to interfere in elections it has no power to control,” New York Attorney General Letitia James said in a statement. “Today, a federal court halted it before this administration could wreak havoc on our elections.”
Talwani wrote that the regulation is most likely unlawful because the president cannot insert the federal government into elections without the express authorization of Congress.
“The court finds plaintiffs likely to succeed on the merits of their claims,” she said.
The Trump administration could seek to quickly overturn her decision by rushing to the Supreme Court.
Trump often criticizes mail-in ballots, claiming without evidence that there is rampant fraud even though they are widely used by Republicans and Democrats all across the country.
Talwani noted in her ruling that the administration had not offered “any evidence regarding fraudulent absentee or mail-in voting.”
The government’s interest in “correcting an unsubstantiated problem through likely unconstitutional means is dwarfed by the overwhelming risk of pervasive disenfranchisement,” she added.

Directly addressing the short time frame ahead of the election, Talwani said states “have neither time nor funds” to meet the necessary requirements, including updating election management systems and training staff members.
Based on the evidence before her, states’ compliance with what the Trump administration is asking of them before the 2026 midterms would be “practically impossible,” Talwani wrote.
In a separate decision Wednesday, Talwani lifted an earlier injunction she had imposed that blocked vital elements of Trump’s executive order in the case.
It is a different injunction from the one the Supreme Court lifted Monday in a similar case brought by California and 22 other states. Talwani is overseeing both cases.
The Supreme Court found that Talwani had acted too hastily in ruling on the executive order but did not weigh in on whether the underlying proposal or the Postal Service regulation is lawful.

While the Postal Service regulation is now blocked, a provision of the executive order requiring the Department of Homeland Security to compile lists of eligible voters and send them to states remains in effect.

title: Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’
summary: The move comes as Trump and Canada have become embroiled in a trade war.
story: President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America.”
The move comes amid the president’s repeated threats and taunts that he would do so amid his escalating trade war with Canada.
“This is official, effective immediately,” Trump said after signing the order in the Oval Office.
The president said he’d “filed all the necessary papers, documents, everything else” for the name change.
“We notified all of the various people that we have to notify. So we’ve done everything that you have to do, and this is official, effective immediately,” he said.

The order says that with “the deepest parts of the Lake’s waters lying within United States territory, the United States claims most of the Lake’s volume,” and that the “Lake has long been an integral asset to American exploration, settlement, commerce, and defense.”
Asked what message he was trying to send Canada by renaming the Great Lake, Trump said, “No message. As you know, Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade.”
“They don’t pay for anything, and they want to be treated like a state, but they’re not a state,” Trump said.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted on X a short time after Trump’s action that the name predates Canada — and the U.S.

“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big’. The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” he wrote.

“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always,” he wrote.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Lake Ontario has been called Lake Ontario since at least the 1600s, and it is the inspiration of the name for Canada’s most populous province, Ontario, which is home to Ottawa and Toronto.

Trump made a similar move last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America.” The Interior Department, Google and Apple complied with that directive, while the rest of the world largely has not.
Trump suggested Thursday other larger renamings could follow.

“So, the lake change, Lake of America, was something I’ve been thinking about for a long time. Actually, as you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico. We changed it, and now it’s very routinely the Gulf of America. So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake,” he said. “Now, all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.”

Canadian maritime attorney Marc Isaacs told NBC News this week that a U.S. move on a name change of Lake Ontario wouldn’t affect other countries, including Canada, saying that no officials in either country own the naming rights to the lake.
“The Americans can call it whatever they want to call it,” Isaacs said. “It is Lake Ontario.”
Canadian Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly shrugged off Trump’s initial threats to change the name earlier this week.
“We’ll always call it Lake Ontario. Period,” she said. “We’re proud of our Great Lakes.”

title: When Is the ‘Love Island USA’ Season 8 Reunion?
