title: Dolly Parton Had a Well-Documented Love Affair With Food. These Were Her Favorites
summary: Dolly Parton loved to cook and eat foods like chicken and dumplings, funnel cake, fried chicken, potatoes (in any form), milk gravy and more Southern staples.
story: Dolly Parton was a meat-and-potatoes kind of woman.
The iconic singer, songwriter, actor and philanthropist died at the age of 80 on Aug. 25 following a “brief battle with cancer,” her estate announced.
Over her spectacularly rhinestone-speckled life, she appeared on TODAY over 50 times, sometimes with a plate full of muffins or a cake in tow.
After Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver shared the news of her death in an Instagram video, fans shared their condolences — and many of them made food that reminded them of her.

Parton and the Southern food she grew up on were intrinsically linked, leading to several food partnerships, a line of Lodge cooking pans, and two cookbooks from the “9 to 5” singer, including one with her sister, Rachel Parton George.
In those books and in interviews over the years, the “Jolene” singer shared some of her favorite dishes. Here is a selection of them from over the years — a “Coat of Many Colors,” if you will.
Fried Chicken
Parton told TODAY.com more than once that fried chicken was at the top of her family’s favorite foods list.

“Growing up in the South with my mom being the greatest cook in the world — and my aunts and my grandmas — I just remember things like fried chicken on Sunday was one of the greatest things ever,” she told TODAY.com in January 2022.

Later, in September 2024, she said, “I think there’s something about Sundays and fried chicken — even in the country — that was just a special treat … The preacher in our family happened to be our grandpa, and grandpa loved fried chicken.”
Funnel Cake

Dollywood, Parton’s theme park, offers some irresistible foods. From cinnamon bread at The Grist Mill or pot roast at Aunt Granny’s Restaurant, guests could snack on any of a number of Dolly’s delicacies. In January 2025, Parton revealed which food she always has to have when she sets foot in her eponymous park.

“The funnel cakes we’re famous for, so I never go there … even if I’m in my bus or if I’m in my suite, The Dolly Suite, I say, ‘Run and get me some funnel cakes. I can’t leave here without funnel cakes,’” she said.
Banana Pudding, Coconut Cake and Chocolate Cake
Parton stopped by TODAY in 2022 to chat about her line of cake mixes and frostings with Duncan Hines, and shared her love for another dessert.
“Everybody in the South — but everywhere, really — we love bananas, and we love banana pudding,” she said. “When you have a good banana pudding, it’s great.”
She also expressed her adoration for cake during the segment.

“I always think of Sundays when I think of coconut cake,” she said. “My mom always made either chocolate cake or coconut cake on Sundays, but on Easter, we always had a coconut cake. So we just felt that it was really a nice start for me to do something more Southern, and they’re beautiful.”
Milk Gravy
“Every now and then I’ll make my husband, Carl, an extra special breakfast,” she said on TODAY.com in 2020 while sharing her own recipe.
She added that, when she made Southern staples like sausage patties or flaky biscuits for her husband Carl Dean, who died in 2025, she would make an easy, creamy milk gravy as the “perfect” topping.
Get The Recipe
Taco Bell
Parton told Insider in January and April 2022 that when she wasn’t cooking, she and her husband would sometimes hit up Taco Bell.

“I like soft-shell tacos,” Parton said. “I like the others, but they fall apart so bad, especially if you’re riding around. So I always get a Taco Supreme, with the sour cream and all that, in the soft shell. I love that.”
She also revealed she loved the then-discontinued Mexican Pizza, which may have convinced the chain to resurrect the dish in May 2022.
Potatoes, in Any Form
In 2025, she told TODAY.com that every day, she had “to have something with potatoes.”
“I mean, I’m just one of those people that I have to either have a baked potato, some mashed potatoes, or some french fries, or something to do with potatoes,” Parton told TODAY.com.
Earlier, in 2022, she also said she enjoys the tuberous starch at barbecues, in the form of a mayo-based potato salad, along with a vinegar-based coleslaw.

“When that happened at our church, and that big bowl of potato salad got there, you didn’t have to worry,” she said. “Even it was sunny, it wasn’t gonna last that long! It wasn’t gonna go bad … not if I was around!”
Chicken and Dumplings and Peanut Butter Fudge

Chicken and Dumplings, which appears in her recipe book, “Good Lookin’ Cookin,’” was also a favorite on the movie sets she graced. She would also whip up a sweet treat that co-stars like Lily Tomlin or Jane Fonda may have snacked on while filming “9 to 5”: peanut butter fudge.

“I cook a lot when I’m on my movie sets,” she said in 2022. “So I guess it would be a long list of famous people, because whoever the stars and co-stars are. I have this huge big pot, and I make chicken and dumplings. I’m famous for it, so everybody wants me to make that or a peanut butter fudge that I love and take on set with me. Everybody asks, ‘When are you going to do the dumplings?’ I always announce it a couple of days before so they all look forward to it. So, I’ve had my dumplings eaten by a lot of famous people.”

title: Tim Curry Was the World’s Scariest Clown. It Surprised Him Until the Very End
summary: Tim Curry was terrifying playing the clown Pennywise in “IT,” the 1990 TV-movie adaptation of Stephen King’s book.
story: Coulrophobia is the fear of clowns. There is, however, no known name for the specific condition of coulrophobia, as brought on by Tim Curry.
Curry, of course, may have generated more than a few cases of coulrophobia all by himself, thanks to one of his most memorable parts.
The actor’s manager shared on Aug. 26 that he had died at the age of 80.
In 1990, Curry took on a role that was as frightening as something you would read in a Stephen King book, which is not a coincidence because it came from a Stephen King book.

In “IT,” based on King’s 1986 book of the same name, Curry portrayed Pennywise, the demonic clown terrorizing a group of child outcasts in 1960s Maine, and resurfaces decades later to wreak more havoc.

“IT” was a four-hour movie that aired over two nights. Curry was the linchpin of the film, which also starred John Ritter, Tim Reid, Richard Thomas, Harry Anderson, Annette O’Toole, as well as child stars Jonathan Brandis and Seth Green.
Pennywise is as scary as scary can be, and Curry was often taken aback at the effect the character had long after the movie aired.

“The majority of people who want to talk to me about being Pennywise are either notably odd people, who sort of revel in his evilness, or else they want me to know that I’ve really traumatized them, or made it impossible to sleep, or something of that variety,” he wrote in his 2025 memoir, “Vagabond.”
“I don’t blame them — one of my lines is literally ‘I’m your worst dream come true.’ But I’ve never really known how to respond to that.”
Curry, who already had a following for his work in “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” and “Clue,” seemed to have mixed feelings about “IT,” which was remade for the big screen in 2017.

“I haven’t had much to say about it publicly for many years, which many people misread as my carrying some sort of deep conflict about the role,” he wrote in “Vagabond.” “That’s really not the case, but I didn’t revel in the role, either.”
Imagine, though, if Curry did revel in it. He was mesmerizing in his portrayal of the clown who lured in children with his menacing smile and balloons.

“My job was to give Tim the stage and not get in his way too much,” “IT” director Tommy Lee Wallace told The Hollywood Reporter in 2017. “He was like Robin Williams in the way he brought a spontaneous improvisation to the part.”

This was transcendental stuff. Curry reached a level of terror that the slasher films of the ‘80s aspired to — and he did it in a TV movie that preyed on the visceral over the physical. It would’ve been right at home had people coughed up a few bucks to see it on the big screen.
“Beep beep, Richie.”
“They all float down here.”
“I’m every nightmare you’ve ever had. I’m your worst dream come true. I’m everything you ever were afraid of.”
If you’ve seen the movie, you can see and hear Curry delivering those lines. They still echo more than three decades later.
The Hollywood Reporter applauded the film, calling it “one big kicky ride thanks to the charismatic acting of Curry as savage, sneering malevolence.”

“I don’t like clowns. I never did,” he told The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences earlier this year. “But I liked doing that show a lot because you have immense freedom, really, as a clown.”

Curry was so on point that he recalled scaring Tony Dakota, one of his co-stars, in a scene that takes place early in the movie when Georgie (played by Dakota) chases his toy boat after it goes into the sewer, where Pennywise is holed up.

“He stopped in the middle of the scene and said, ‘Mr. Curry, you’re scaring me.’ I said, ‘Well, ‘I’m supposed to scare you, but I don’t mean to harm you in any way,” he told The Academy, echoing a story he also shared in “Vagabond.”

“IT” earned two Emmy nominations, winning one for outstanding achievement in music composition for a miniseries or a special. It was also nominated for best editing. It’s amazing to think that Curry did not earn a nomination, given the enduring nature of the part.

Interestingly, Curry would earn one Emmy in his career — and it was connected to horror. He garnered a nod in 1994 for outstanding guest actor in a drama series for appearing on the HBO anthology series “Tales from the Crypt.”

Curry called “IT” “very original, very audacious, and yes, legitimately frightening” in “Vagabond.” He would go on to write that fans often ask him to do Pennywise’s voice when he goes to conventions, which he called “a weird phenomenon.” It shows the power of the part and the connection fans still feel to this very day.
“I never would have imagined that out of my whole body of work, that clown would end up being so memorable to audiences,” he wrote.

title: Bob Barker Reflects on 3 Decades of Hosting ‘The Price Is Right’ in 2002 TODAY Interview
summary: On April 1, 2002, Bob Barker stopped by TODAY to look back at his experiences, a mere 30 years into his tenure.
story: Welcome inside the TODAY Vault, where we revisit memories from our show when celebrities and newsmakers started discourse, made us laugh or shaped our culture. This latest installment aired April 1, 2002 and features Bob Barker talking to Al Roker about “The Price is Right” 30 years into his run as host of the beloved game show.
The history of game shows can’t be told without Bob Barker.
Barker, who helped make “The Price is Right” a staple of daytime television during his 35-year run as host, died Aug. 26, 2023, at the age of 99.
He began his stint on the show in 1972 and remained on the job until 2007, a vital part in turning the show into the smash hit it remains to this day with current host Drew Carey.
On April 1, 2002, Barker stopped by TODAY to look back at his experiences, a mere 30 years into his tenure.
“Sometimes it seems much longer,” he said while laughing. “And sometimes it seems like only yesterday that we started.”
Barker also spoke about what had changed over the years, why young people loved the show and how he broke into the business.
How Had ‘The Price is Right’ Changed Since He Began Hosting?
Barker noted that the set remained the same, but the cost of the items on the show had evolved.

“The prices, that’s what has really changed,” he said. “The first car I gave away was $2,465. We had car after car, four digits. Two was the first number. Then 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Now we’ve had to change our props to accommodate five digits.”
‘The Price is Right’ Appealed to Young People

It’s lore that kids watched the show when they stayed home sick from school. That love didn’t dissipate over time, either, as evidenced by the young people and college students who appear on the show. Barker couldn’t explain why a younger demographic was so drawn to the series, but he was glad it was.
“We’re blessed. It happened. We don’t know how it happened. If we did, we could bottle it and sell it. But it became a cult thing with the college youngsters,” he said.
“And now they come from all over the country — East Coast, Midwest, and, of course, the West Coast — and they give our show great energy. It’s just wonderful,” he added.
How Did Bob Barker Wind Up Hosting Game Shows?

Prior to “The Price is Right,” Barker hosted “Truth or Consequences” for 18 years. He began his career in radio and ultimately made the move to the small screen with encouragement from his wife, Dorothy Jo Gideon.
“I started working at a radio station when I was in college. They didn’t call them game shows. They were audience participation shows,” he said.

“The first audience participation show I did, my wife heard and she said, ‘That’s what you should do.’ She said, ‘You do that better than you’ve ever done anything else.’ Now she didn’t say I was good,” he joked. “She just said I did it better than I’ve ever done anything else. And I set out to do precisely what I’m doing.”

title: Young Dolly Parton Photos: See the ‘Queen of Country’ Through the Years
summary: See pictures of Dolly Parton from the earlier part of her life as a child into adulthood when she posed with some huge stars.
story: The world continues to mourn Dolly Parton’s death of cancer at the age of 80.

Tributes for the icon — who was a TODAY staple and sage speaker — have poured in from across all corners, as the global superstar leaves behind a legacy in which she was known not just for her music and acting, but for her humility and generosity.

Parton was married to Carl Dean for 60 years before his death in 2025. There was another Dolly Parton, though, long before they tied the knot and long before she became a worldwide superstar who wrote over 3,000 songs.

Parton was Dolly Rebecca Parton on Jan. 19, 1946, the fourth of 12 children. She grew up in rural Sevierville, Tennessee and sang on local television and radio while still a child. At 13, Johnny Cash introduced her for her 1959 debut at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville.

Stardom awaited her. Parton moved to Nashville to pursue a music career after graduating high school in 1964. In 1967, country star and TV personality Porter Wagoner handpicked her to be his new duet partner on “The Porter Wagoner Show.”

That same year, she released her debut solo album, “Hello, I’m Dolly,” which rose to the number 11 spot on the Billboard Top Country Albums chart and announced her arrival as a star for years to come.
Take a look at Parton throughout her younger years below.
Dolly Parton From Her 1st Recording to Co-Starring with Porter Wagoner
Parton’s first single, “Puppy Love,” came out in 1955, when Parton was about 9 years old. When she was 21, Wagoner offered her a life-changing spot on his syndicated show.
Dolly Parton Went Solo in 1974 and Became a Star

Parton became a solo act and rocketed to stardom in the 1970s, propelled, in part, by the success of her songs “Joshua,” “Coat of Many Colors,” “Jolene” and “I Will Always Love You.” Those tracks would remain some of her signature songs throughout her career.
Dolly Parton Hobnobbed With Celebrities for Years

As her star rose, so did her profile. Parton was not known for appearing in the tabloids, but she did cross paths with several stars over the years as she crossed into the mainstream by making the jump into film with ‘9 to 5” in 1980. Even before that, she had emerged as a superstar.

title: Miley Cyrus Honors Late Godmother Dolly Parton After Her Death: ‘I Have an Angel By My Side’
summary: Singer Miley Cyrus shared a heartfelt tribute after the passing of her “fairy godmother,” Dolly Parton.
story: To the world, Dolly Parton was a country music legend. To Miley Cyrus, she was her “fairy godmother.”
Parton’s nephew shared that she died “peacefully” on Aug. 25 at the age of 80. And today on Instagram, Cyrus gave Parton her “flowers.”

“The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share. Our most sacred moments were private and they’ll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour & between our hearts,” she began.

“What I KNOW is Dolly would want me to feel it, write a song about it, and then continue on and be strong. I have an angel by my side. I always have. One of our last conversations was about music and metamorphosis. 🦋

“I will always love her and want to make her proud. My heart breaks for the world, her family and friends who will miss her deeply. We’re in this loss together and we will see her in all of the most beautiful things. 💖”

Parton had a long-standing friendship with the singer’s parents, Billy Ray Cyrus and Tish Cyrus-Purcell, and she shared the story of becoming a godmother during an interview in 2023 on SiriusXM’s “The Howard Stern Show.”

“We just got to be good friends because he’s a Kentucky boy, I’m from Tennessee,” Parton said at the time. “And he said … ‘We’re having a girl, and you’ve got to be her godmother!’ And I said, ‘Well, I’d be honored.’ So actually, Miley and I took over from there.”
Miley Cyrus and Dolly Parton have a long history of gushing over one another, both personally and professionally.

They collaborated in front of the cameras when Parton guest starred on three episodes of “Hannah Montana” as her character’s fictional on-screen godmother. And together they sang Parton’s 1973 hit “Jolene” with Pentatonix on “The Voice” in 2016.
When Parton was honored by as one of Time’s Most Influential People of 2021, Cyrus wrote a tribute to her.

“There’s a theory that you shouldn’t meet your heroes, but I wish everyone had the chance to meet Dolly Parton, because she’s even better than your sparkliest dreams,” Cyrus wrote. “She may be my fairy godmother, but I think she’s that to everyone else too. I am happy to share her with the world.”
Cyrus shared a message that her godmother sent her a few years later.
“Dolly’s been like a mother to me. Actually, I was just reading this fax that she sent me two Mother’s Days ago,” Cyrus told W Magazine in 2024.
“Dolly wrote to me to say: ‘How much do I love you? As much as my heart can hold and as far as my arms can reach,’” Cyrus recalled. “It gets me choked up. I just love her so much.”
In a Facebook tribute, Billy Ray Cyrus said that he grew up watching Parton on his living room TV, and shared a memory from a meeting with her in 1992.

“I’ll never forget walking into her dressing room to apologize for all the tabloid stories which claimed I was having an affair with her. In true Dolly fashion, she just looked at me, winked and said, ‘Honey, this trash sells records!’” Billy Ray Cyrus wrote.
The singer added that Parton recently sent him a message telling him that she “loved me with her whole heart.”
“I will always love her in the same way ….. with my whole heart … and I always will,” he said.

title: TODAY Anchors Honor Dolly Parton and Her Life Spent Spreading Joy: ‘She Was an Original’
summary: Following the death of beloved country music icon Dolly Parton, the TODAY family took a trip down memory lane to reflect on the many ways she had touched their lives.
story: Following the death of beloved country music icon Dolly Parton, the TODAY family took a trip down memory lane to reflect on the many ways she had touched their lives.
“It goes without saying how much we love Dolly Parton,” Hoda Kotb said on TODAY Aug. 26. “Her music was the soundtrack of so many lives, and that’s just one small part of her incredible legacy.”
Carson Daly highlighted the “rhinestone-studded trail” Parton had blazed for countless entertainers who had followed her, many of whom had shared their personal tributes to Parton.

“It’s crazy, from all walks of life ... all genres of music,” Carson said of the music industry’s admiration for Parton. He recalled how she initially turned down her nomination for the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame because she didn’t feel her music was worthy. Parton later accepted the nomination — and then she proceeded to put out a rock album in 2023.

“I don’t think she cared about any accolades,” Hoda said. “It was as if the accolades didn’t mean much to her because she often said, ‘If I didn’t get paid or if I wasn’t that good, I would still be singing.’”
Kristen Welker also shared about Parton’s legacy, including what her fans meant to her.

“She was just so humble,” Kristen said, reflecting on Parton’s response when asked if she felt bothered when people recognized her. “She said, ‘Are you kidding? That’s why I’m here.’ She loved just being with the people and spreading that love.”
Craig Melvin highlighted Parton’s family background, being one of 12 children, as a possible source of her humility.
Carson then chimed in, further commemorating Parton’s reach.

“Country music was regional, it was walled off of mainstream,” he said. “She comes in and owns her masters, she owns her likeness, she owns her rights. She’s a business savant. ... And by the way, her greatest legacy might be what she’s done for literacy.”

Parton founded the Imagination Library, a book gifting program that grants young children around the country access to free books. Carson continued to list Parton’s contributions to society beyond entertaining, including her donations to fund a COVID vaccine and helping those impacted by natural disasters.
“She didn’t want the accolades,” Carson said. “She wanted to help.”
Later on TODAY, “9 to 5” played on the Plaza, with Craig shouting out Parton as a “national treasure.”
Hoda, who has interviewed Parton many times, reflected on a moment when Parton made an impact on another member of the TODAY family, Megan Stackhouse, who is head of public relations.

“She walked up to Dolly and said, ‘You raised me.’” Hoda remembered. “And Dolly enveloped her, hugged her, and I remember Megan crying. We all got to sit and chat with her, but those are the moments I think stick out the most for me.”

title: Oil prices dip as cautious optimism over Iran trumps new fears of Russian escalation in Ukraine
summary: Oil prices tumbled as headlines from the Middle East renewed optimism in global energy markets, and muted fears of a Russian escalation in Ukraine.
story: Crude oil prices dropped for a third day Wednesday as markets weighed a series of potentially positive developments in the Middle East against new fears of Russian escalation in Ukraine and dwindling U.S. reserves.
U.S. crude oil fell as low as $79 per barrel early Wednesday for the first time since Aug. 13. The international oil benchmark Brent dropped to around $85 a barrel.

But around midday Wednesday, oil prices made an unexpected U-turn and moved slightly higher on reports of a plan by Russian President Vladimir Putin to escalate his war with Ukraine, 4½ years after the Kremlin invaded its former Soviet satellite.
Prices ended the day slightly lower. U.S. crude oil fell to $82.23 per barrel, while Brent fell to $87.84.

NBC News has not independently verified Bloomberg News’ reporting, which was a timely reminder of the pressure global energy markets face from conflicts and supply disruptions far outside the Middle East.

Also driving oil prices was the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s announcement that oil stockpiles had risen by fewer barrels than analysts were expecting. The report also caused prices to briefly move higher, as it underscored the mammoth task ahead to replenish U.S. reserves that have been drained in recent months.

Prices were notably lower early in the day after reports from several outlets that, taken together, signaled a potential shift in how both Tehran and Washington are approaching the war after six months.
The first of those developments was a reported renewal of talks between Iran and Oman about reopening the critical Strait of Hormuz in recent days.
The State Department is also preparing to return American diplomats to their posts at embassies across the Middle East, The New York Times reported Tuesday.
And Secretary of State Marco Rubio told U.S. allies that the Trump administration does not expect to resume military strikes on Iran, according to comments reported by Axios.
Before the latest developments in Eastern Europe buffeted oil prices, President Donald Trump’s comments on social media had helped boost Iran sentiment.
“I have just been informed by the United States Navy that all mines have been removed and/or detonated from within the International Waters of the Strait of Hormuz,” Trump posted Tuesday.
The timing of the post raised eyebrows, however, because the text mirrors a Trump post on Aug. 18, when he wrote that “all water mines have been removed or detonated.”

The shipping analytics firm Kpler reported Wednesday that “Strait crossings remain subdued.” The firm assessed that just five vessels had transited the strait Tuesday, down from seven on Monday and nine on Sunday.
Those figures are just a tiny fraction of the pre-war daily average of 130 vessels.

Wednesday’s oil price action mirrored what has been a roller-coaster ride of a year for energy markets. Crude oil futures are down more than 5% since Sunday. Still, since the start of the year, oil prices overall have risen more than 40%.
After having soared to more than $110 per barrel in early April, U.S. crude oil dropped to the low $80s by the middle of that month before it rebounded again to more than $100.

By the end of May, crude oil prices had come down into the $80s. But it was the ceasefire announcement in mid-June that pushed oil prices down further, to near pre-war levels of around $70 a barrel for WTI crude.

But the low prices did not last long. Throughout July, the lack of progress in U.S.-Iran negotiations and renewed U.S. strikes on Iran pushed prices back up. By the end of the month, a barrel of U.S. crude was trading up into the low $90s.
The whipsawing energy prices helped keep inflation high in July, the Bureau of Economic Analysis reported Wednesday.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures index was unchanged from June, stuck at 3.7%. The lack of movement even extended to core PCE, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, which excludes the more volatile categories of food and energy and came in at 3.3%.

“The United States still has an inflation problem. PCE inflation came in hotter than expected,” said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. “The impacts of the war in Iran are still apparent.”

The multiday move lower in oil prices has also dragged bond yields lower. After having traded at decades-high levels for days, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was trading around 4.6%, down from nearly 4.75%. The 30-year yield had fallen to around 5.18%, down from its recent high of more than 5.3%.
Mortgage rates also trended lower for a second straight day. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.74% early Wednesday.

“When yields are falling, mortgage lenders are generally able to offer lower rates than they otherwise would have, depending on the timing and size of the move,” Matthew Graham of data provider Mortgage News Daily wrote Tuesday.
Yet even as oil prices, bond yields and mortgage rates are falling, gas prices remain high for consumers.
Since Sunday, prices have largely remained flat, and on Wednesday, the national average price per gallon ticked up to $4.10, AAA data shows.

title: Families wait in agony as Nepal floods leave hundreds missing
summary: A New York couple traveling to Mount Kailash is among 65 Americans missing after a catastrophic flood along the Nepal-Tibet border.
story: The last time Radhika Sharma heard from her parents, they had just crossed from Nepal into Tibet.

Ramesh Sharma, 65, and Neelam Sharma, 64, who live in New York and are U.S. citizens, were making a religious pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a peak in Tibet considered sacred by Hindus, Buddhists and other faiths. Shortly after their border crossing Wednesday, a towering torrent of water, rock and mud tore through the same Himalayan corridor.

Videos from the hardest-hit border regions showed people running as the debris flow swallowed buildings and vehicles, devastated towns and settlements, and severed roads, power and communications. The suspected collapse of a melting glacier shook the ground so violently that seismic monitors initially registered it as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake.

In one video from Mailung, in Nepal’s Rasuwa region, a group of construction workers was seen walking down a mountain path before noticing giant plumes of brown debris in the distance, rapidly cascading toward them. The men reversed course to flee uphill, one briefly stopping to film before realizing the scale of the danger.
He shouts in Nepali: “Oh, my God, the flood is getting so big! Let’s run — run fast, guys! Oh, my God, get back quickly!”

As of Friday morning local time, authorities had recovered 469 bodies in Nepal and confirmed three deaths in Tibet. Hundreds more remained unaccounted for. Nepal’s Tourism Board said 644 travelers, including 65 Americans, were missing.
Sharma’s parents were among a group of seven people making the journey to Mount Kailash, visited by tens of thousands of pilgrims each year.
“It has probably been the worst 24 hours of my life,” Sharma, 32, a doctor based in North Carolina, said in an interview as she continued an anxious wait for news.

The hardest part, she said, was the not knowing. She has contacted the U.S. embassies in Nepal and China, as well as American officials domestically. “I haven’t heard anything back,” Sharma said initially, although later added that embassy officials in Beijing had been in regular touch with her.

After posting pleas on social media, Sharma has been put in contact with people in Nepal “who are trying to help track down my parents,” she said. “I’ve given them my parents’ information, their photos. I’m on the phone now, just waiting to hear someone say that they’ve even seen them.”
Sharma is far from alone in desperately seeking information about loved ones.

The State Department has urged U.S. citizens “currently in, or recently traveling through Rasuwa or another affected area” to get in touch, and encouraged loved ones of those missing to contact U.S. officials via various means.
It was “working closely with local tour agencies and local authorities to assist Americans in the affected areas. Nepali-led search and rescue operations continue,” a State Department spokesman said.

As of 2 p.m. ET Thursday, it was aware of 90 Americans who may have been “impacted” by the floods on the Nepal-China border. Three American citizens had been safely rescued by that time, the spokesperson added.
Add to Google
Add to Google
In Baidur, Nepal, Shova Shrestha, 33, has spent more than a day waiting for news of her missing husband, Rajan Shrestha, as rescue efforts continue.
“I keep looking at each helicopter, hoping he will step out of it,” she told The Associated Press.
Sagar Pandey, chief executive of the tour company escorting travelers from Australia, India, the U.S., Canada and Singapore, could only assess the devastation where they had been from a helicopter.
“There are no human-made things, no human settlement left. Everything is just flat,” he told Reuters. “So anyone in the hotel, the restaurant or the car, I believe that everybody is gone.”
Syed Sadique, who runs a tour agency based in southern India, was waiting anxiously for news on the fate of 57 people traveling with his company, including his tour guide son, Sayed Umar Farook.

“The group ⁠was traveling on three buses in Nepal,” he told Reuters. “A member of the group told us that one vehicle carrying about 20 people managed to get through safely, while passengers saw another bus plunge ​into a gorge.”
Amid the carnage and chaos, and her desperate outreach to authorities and locals, Sharma sent a message to her missing parents themselves.
She said she told them: “I love you. I am looking for you. I will keep looking for you. I  just hope you’re OK.”
Sharma added: “I know that wherever they are, they’re probably a lot more worried about my brother and I, because that’s just the type of people they are.”

title: Harry and Meghan arrive for ‘extended’ stay in the U.K. six years after royal exit
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan arrived back in the U.K.  after six years in California, a source close to the family confirmed to NBC News.
story: LONDON — Prince Harry and his family sought to begin a new life for a second time as they arrived back in the United Kingdom on Wednesday after six years in California, a source close to them confirmed to NBC News.
The Duke of Sussex, 41, and his wife, Meghan, 45, flew in on a private plane with their two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, according to several media reports.

A spokesperson for the Sussexes declined to comment on where the family would be living, citing privacy and security concerns. However, the spokesperson did confirm that they brought their dogs with them, although their chickens would remain in Montecito, California, where the family had been living since 2020.
A source close to the couple told NBC News last week that they were moving back for an “extended period” of time.
Harry and Meghan rattled the British royal family six years ago when they opted to step down as working royals, eventually choosing a quieter life in the affluent coastal enclave in Santa Barbara.

Relations have been strained in the years since, worsened in part by explosive allegations of racism and bullying made by the couple in their Netflix documentary “Harry & Meghan” and in Harry’s memoir, “Spare.”
After years with few signs of a royal rapprochement, Britain was shocked last week when it emerged they were planning a return.

Harry and Meghan will remain private individuals and nonworking members of the royal family, a source familiar with the couple’s plans told NBC News last week, while reports in British media indicated that Archie and Lilibet have been enrolled in schools in the country.

Questions remain over what security arrangements will be in place for the couple, after a protracted legal battle between Harry and the British government over the removal of their security protection.
Asked about their security last week, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: “This is a private matter, it’s a matter for Harry and Meghan, and we wish them well in the moves that they’re making.”

The couple’s planned return had sparked a slew of media coverage, with front pages dominated by unconfirmed reports that Meghan could return to acting for the first time since she departed the television show “Suits” ahead of her 2018 wedding to Harry.

Harry’s return to Britain also comes after he and several other claimants were ordered to pay a combined £34.5 million ($46 million) to a major newspaper publisher after losing a High Court battle over alleged breaches of privacy. That battle was one of several salvos between Harry and the British press.

title: Iran vows retaliation after U.S. widens sanctions, fueling fears of escalated war
summary: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran has vowed to retaliate against widened U.S. sanctions, saying Washington should “expect an attack” in response.
story: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran has vowed to retaliate against widened U.S. sanctions, saying Washington should “expect an attack” in response.

“We know how to play the game, too,” Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said in an interview televised by state media late Monday as he condemned the U.S. measures as an “economic terrorist attack.”
The U.S. has imposed sanctions on Iran since 1979, after Iranian students stormed the American Embassy in Tehran, taking U.S. diplomats hostage.

Madanizadeh said at least two countries — China and Russia — have so far given no indication that they plan to fall into line. At a news conference Tuesday, Chinese Foreign Affairs Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said Beijing was firmly opposed to “illegal unilateral sanctions,” according to Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency.
Madanizadeh warned that “they should not think that our response will be defensive and that we will only defend ourselves.” He added, “They should expect an attack from our side, as well.”
Madanizadeh did not specify what sort of attack.
He added that Tehran had been preparing for such an economic assault and that it had a two-year plan in the works to deal with the impact, which he did not expand on.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the fresh battery of measures against Iran on Monday, calling it an “economic D-Day” and warning that any country financially partnering with Tehran would be isolated. The U.S. stopped short of imposing actual penalties.

Bessent provided limited details about the measures and did not identify countries that could be targeted with secondary sanctions. He said President Donald Trump was “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime.”

The Treasury Department confirmed Monday that it had launched Operation Economic Outcast. It said in a news release that it was expanding the categories of Iran-related conduct that could be subject to secondary sanctions, with determinations issued against “five critical sectors — digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping.”

It added that the Office of Foreign Assets Control had also sanctioned nearly 60 entities, people and vessels in multiple jurisdictions that it said “enable the Iranian regime’s recklessness,” in addition to other measures.
The United Arab Emirates, which has long maintained close economic ties with Iran, announced last week that it would be halting all financial transactions with Tehran.
On the ground in Tehran, some Iranians expressed resignation at the U.S. announcement, which Bessent described as “the single greatest financial offensive ever” against Iran.
“It’s nothing new,” Farzin, 27, a mechanic, told NBC News on Tuesday. “The country is already locked, and the psychological effect is worse than the actual outcome.”
Farzin said U.S. sanctions had yet to yield any significant impact on his business, with car parts still making their way into the country.
“You find a route and you find a market inside the country,” he said, adding that many parts were being imported through land borders, whether legally or illegally.
Farzin declined to give his last name. Many Iranians are wary of speaking with and identifying themselves to U.S. media.
Hamid Ebrahimi, a retired lawyer and university professor, said many Iranians felt there was little they could do to make their lives any better.

“We are just getting by day to day and can’t keep up with inflation,” said Ebrahimi, 63. “Sanctions have had an effect, and the government says it can manage them, but they have always hurt the people, and they will continue to do so.”
Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at King’s College London’s School of Security Studies, said Washington’s latest moves were unlikely to achieve the desired results.
“Iran’s response so far suggests Washington’s ‘Economic D-Day’ is producing pain, but not the behavioral effect the administration is looking for,” he said.
Tehran appeared to be interpreting the measures as “economic warfare” aimed at its “regime survival rather than as bargaining pressure designed to produce a compromise,” Krieg added.
As a result, its response “has consequently been defiance rather than accommodation.”

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in comments the semiofficial Tasnim news agency published Monday that the U.S. “must correct its tone and approach in dealing with Iran, because relying on force and bullying will only complicate the process.”

Krieg said the global community could expect Tehran to increase pressure on the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial trade route through which 20% of the world’s oil ran before the war, which began in late February after the U.S. and Israel launched punishing strikes on Iran.
The stated reason for waging war was to prevent Iran from building a nuclear weapon. Tehran has long denied it is seeking to build a nuclear arsenal.

Since then, the key waterway has largely been strangled by a blockade imposed by Iran, sending energy prices soaring, with the U.S. also launching its own blockade in Iranian ports in response to Iranian attacks along the strait. Hormuz was open and without tolls when the U.S. and Israel triggered the war.
“Tehran cannot prevent Washington from imposing sanctions, but it can make those sanctions expensive for everybody else,” Krieg said.
Meanwhile, Iranian media have repeatedly aired content threatening the life of Trump’s son Barron Trump, fueling fears over the escalating rhetoric surrounding the conflict.
U.S. Secret Service spokesperson Nate Herring said Monday that the agency was “aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees.”
“Out of concern for operational security, we do not discuss matters of protective intelligence,” Herring added.

title: CIA director flies unannounced to Moscow to hold talks, source says
summary: CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Russia to holds talks in Moscow, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.
story: WASHINGTON — CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Russia to hold unspecified talks in Moscow, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.
The person declined to say whom Ratcliffe was meeting with or what the focus of the talks was. The CIA declined to comment.

It’s Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Moscow as CIA director. He made headlines with a visit to Venezuela in January to meet with interim President Delcy Rodríguez about two weeks after the U.S. military seized President Nicolás Maduro in a raid in Caracas.

He also traveled to Cuba in May to meet with government leaders. He was the highest-ranking Trump administration official to visit the island, which is under severe economic pressure after the U.S. tightened sanctions.
News of Ratcliffe’s travel came as mystery swirled around a U.S. military transport aircraft that landed in Moscow, according to tracking data.
It was not known who was on board the plane and why it was in Moscow. When asked, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he did not have information about the aircraft.
Neither U.S. military officials, the White House, the U.S. Embassy in Moscow nor the Russian Embassy in Washington immediately responded to questions about the flight’s mission.
Two planes, a C-130 cargo plane and a C-40, landed in Riga, the capital of Latvia, as part of the same mission, according to a U.S. official. The C-130 then went on to Russia, the official said.
Data from FlightRadar24 tracking site showed a plane approached Vnukovo International Airport in Moscow just after 10 a.m. local time (3 a.m. ET) after taking off from Riga two hours earlier.

It had departed from the U.S. Air Force’s Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Sunday just before 5 p.m. ET, the data showed. That plane had apparently left Moscow on Tuesday afternoon, according to flight radar data.
CBS News and Axios first reported on the CIA chief’s unannounced visit.

CIA directors sometimes act as envoys for presidents in high-stakes talks with adversaries. Former President Joe Biden turned to then-CIA Director William Burns to relay stern warnings to Russia before and after President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

title: As Ukraine’s allies gather for big anniversary, one key backer is absent
summary: The lack of visible senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine.
story: Leaders of Ukraine’s international allies on Monday marked 35 years since the country broke away from the Soviet Union to become an independent nation.
The U.K.’s Andy Burnham flew in, while France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz joined a call to reaffirm commitments to Kyiv.
But senior officials from one longtime backer were notably absent from the public show of support: the United States.
Add to Google
Add to Google

While U.S. senators and former officials visited Ukraine ahead of the commemorations, the apparent lack of senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine.
The message sent was especially pointed as Monday also marks 4 1/2 years since President Vladimir Putin launched his large-scale invasion of Russia’s much smaller neighbor.

Negotiations to reach a peace deal, which President Donald Trump once promised to achieve within 24 hours, have stalled as supplies of U.S. air defense missiles dwindle and the Russian leader ramps up threats to Ukraine’s allies.
Britain’s Burnham was the highest-profile Western leader to fly in and co-chair a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing,” a group of countries backing Ukraine.

European Council President António Costa, as well as the heads of nearly a dozen European nations, was also in Kyiv, despite the country’s air force reporting Russian rocket and drone strikes overnight.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated Ukraine in a statement.
“The United States is committed to Ukraine’s sovereignty and continues to work to support a negotiated settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war that establishes a lasting and durable peace,” it said.
